To date, several antiviral engineering strategies have been developed, including dominant resistance (R) genes, pathogen-derived resistance (PDR), RNA interference (RNAi), CRISPR-Cas–based genome editing, host susceptibility factor engineering, and immune signaling enhancement. Among these approaches, NLR-mediated resistance can provide strong protection against viral infection (9); however, resistance-breaking viral variants frequently emerge and compromise its durability (27, 43, 46, 47). Classical PDR and cross-protection approaches exhibit favorable biosafety and practical applicability but suffer from narrow antiviral spectra and potential risks of viral recombination and virulence reversion under field conditions (48, 49). RNAi-based strategies enable flexible and sequence-specific viral suppression; however, their efficacy can be compromised by viral sequence variation and diverse viral suppressors of RNA silencing that antagonize host silencing pathways (50, 51). CRISPR-Cas systems provide high-precision and multiplex editing for viral and host target modification, yet mutations within gRNA target sites frequently generate viral escape variants, and constitutive Cas expression may raise biosafety and regulatory concerns (52–54). Engineering host susceptibility factors, such as eIF4E family proteins, can confer durable resistance against specific groups of viruses, but their effectiveness is often limited to particular virus taxa (55–58). Likewise, manipulation of host proteins involved in virus infection through overexpression or knockout can enhance antiviral resistance, although such modifications rarely provide complete immunity (59). In addition, constitutive activation of immune pathways can confer broad-spectrum disease resistance but often results in notable growth penalties because of the well-known growth-defense trade-off (60, 61). To address these limitations, pathogen-responsive resistance systems that activate defense responses only upon pathogen infection have attracted increasing attention. Recent studies have demonstrated that translational regulation mediated by uORFs can effectively control the expression of immune-related genes and enhance resistance against fungal, bacterial, and DNA viral pathogens without obvious fitness costs (34, 35). Likewise, engineered NLRs and inducible elicitor peptide systems can provide strong resistance to potyviruses while minimizing growth penalties by activating defense responses only after infection (29, 36). These findings collectively highlight the potential of pathogen-responsive defense systems to overcome the limitations associated with constitutive resistance. Nevertheless, virus-responsive antiviral systems specifically designed for +ssRNA viruses that produce sgRNAs remain limited.Compared with existing approaches, the virus-responsive RIP system developed in this study has several notable advantages (Fig. 6). First, antiviral activity is activated only after viral infection, thereby minimizing developmental abnormalities under normal growth conditions. Second, unlike RNAi and CRISPR-based technologies that directly target viral nucleotide sequences, our strategy exploits the conserved process of viral sgRNA synthesis to activate defense responses, potentially reducing the likelihood of resistance breakdown caused by single mutational events. Third, because sgRNA production is a common feature among many +ssRNA viruses, this platform may have broader applicability than virus-specific resistance mechanisms. Additional specificity assays demonstrated that the TI-TA system was not activated by unrelated viruses, bacterial or fungal pathogens, or abiotic stresses including heat and drought (figs. S8 and S9), indicating that viral mini-replicon recognition is highly specific and that the TI-TA system is unlikely to be ectopically activated by nontarget biotic or abiotic stimuli. Such stringent specificity minimizes the risk of unintended HR activation and enhances the biosafety and practical potential of this strategy for agricultural applications. However, several limitations should also be acknowledged. Differences in the abundance, timing, and regulatory mechanisms of sgRNA accumulation among viruses may substantially influence the activation efficiency of the TI-TA system. In addition, plant species may differ in their sensitivity to RIP-induced immune responses, which could further affect system performance. Moreover, all experiments in the present study were conducted under controlled greenhouse conditions using laboratory-maintained viral isolates. Therefore, the stability, durability, and practical performance of the TI-TA system under field conditions remain to be evaluated. In agricultural environments, fluctuating temperatures, mixed infections involving multiple pathogens, and genetically diverse viral populations may influence viral replication dynamics, sgRNA production, and consequently the activation efficiency of the TI-TA circuit. Field trials using diverse viral isolates and representative environmental conditions will therefore be essential to assess the robustness and long-term effectiveness of this strategy. Another limitation is that the current study used constitutive transgenic expression of TI-TA components, which facilitated proof-of-concept validation but may not fully satisfy future regulatory requirements for commercial crop deployment. Future optimization could explore tissue-specific or infection-responsive promoters to restrict transgene expression to relevant tissues or infection sites, as well as minimized expression cassettes to simplify genetic constructs and improve biosafety and regulatory compatibility. The current TI-TA system is designed to target a specific virus or closely related viruses within the same genus. Therefore, achieving resistance against multiple unrelated viruses will likely require stacking several TI-TA modules using strategies such as tRNA- or ribozyme-mediated polycistronic expression. Although the system conferred effective immunity resistance against CMV, it did not provide complete protection against PepMV or TMV. Accordingly, further efforts are required to improve the virus-responsive activation efficiency of TI-TA upon viral challenge. Artificial intelligence–assisted screening can be adopted to identify more efficient RIPs that can potently trigger immune responses across diverse plant species. Furthermore, combining the TI-TA platform with complementary antiviral strategies, including host susceptibility factor engineering, RNAi, and CRISPR-Cas–based technologies, may provide broader-spectrum and more durable resistance against emerging plant viruses.Fig. 6.Schematic working model of the TI-TA synthetic immune module conferring plant resistance to viral infection.Our innovative system integrates three key components that combine uAUG-ds as TI, Virusmini as virus-activated transcription (TA), and RIPs to create a targeted defense that only activates upon infection. NMD is known to target viral RNAs containing premature termination codons (PTCs), including those of PVX, TCV, and CGMMV (68–71). For example, PVX RNAs carrying extended 3′ UTRs are degraded through NMD (72), whereas the PEMV2 P26 protein counteracts NMD to protect viral RNAs (73). Moreover, m6A modification promotes NMD-mediated degradation of PepMV RNA (74). Because Virusmini constructs contain PTCs, it is plausible that they are recognized by the NMD machinery, thereby contributing to the reduced accumulation of GFP mRNA. Insertion of GFP between INF1 and the 3′ UTR may disrupt this putative structure and restore repression. Although this hypothesis requires further experimental validation, it highlights the importance of local RNA structural context in determining TI-TA performance. In addition, our results indicate that the optimal positioning of dsBC may vary among different viral mini-replicons. Unlike PepMVmini and TMVmini, in which placement of dsBC at the 5′ terminus enabled efficient virus-responsive activation, CMVminiRNA3 required internal insertion of dsBC to achieve functionality (figs. S12, B to D, and S4, B to D). Therefore, the current design principles should be considered empirical guidelines rather than fully predictive rules, as they were derived from a limited number of viral mini-replicon configurations tested in this study. The requirement for internal dsBC placement in CMVminiRNA3 highlights the current limitation that the optimal architecture for a different virus cannot yet be reliably predicted solely from viral sequence information or known regulatory elements. Specifically, 5′-terminal dsBC insertion represents a useful initial design strategy because of its successful performance in two independent viral backbones, whereas internal dsBC insertion provides an alternative configuration when 5′-terminal placement compromises mini-replicon activity or virus-responsive expression. Establishing more generalizable and predictive design principles will require systematic evaluation of diverse viral mini-replicons combined with computational analyses of RNA sequence features, secondary structures, and potential interactions between dsBC elements and viral regulatory regions. This work innovatively fuses the dsBC translational repression module with viral mini-replicons to assemble the TI-TA synthetic immune circuit, which drives strict virus-specific activation of RIP effector expression exclusively during viral infection (Fig. 6). The dsBC-PepMVmini-BAX construct confers robust PepMV resistance in transgenic N. benthamiana and tomato lines. Separately, dsBC-TMVmini-INF1-2A-GFP and dsBC-TMVmini-NLPPya grant TMV resistance in stably transformed N. benthamiana. CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-NLPPya delivers near-complete immunity against systemic CMV infection. Furthermore, the TI-TA architecture mediates partial cross-resistance against phylogenetically related viruses within the same genus. Collectively, this programmable synthetic immune strategy provides a conceptual framework for engineering resistance against sgRNA-producing +ssRNA viruses and establishes a foundation for future optimization toward agricultural applications. Beyond agricultural deployment, this experimental framework also provides a tractable system to dissect how growth-regulatory cytotoxic proteins modulate +ssRNA virus infection dynamics in plant hosts. Last, the core TI-TA design logic offers conceptual reference and design inspiration for developing RNA-targeted synthetic immunotherapies against animal RNA viral pathogens.MATERIALS AND METHODSPlant growth conditions and plant materialsThe WT and transgenic N. benthamiana plants were grown in a climate chamber with a 15-hour daylight and 9-hour dark photoperiod at 23° to 25°C as described previously (75). Solanum lycopersicum (microTom) was grown under the same conditions as N. benthamiana. Generation of transgenic N. benthamiana plants and S. lycopersicum was completed by BioRuan (Wuhan, China). T2 transgenic N. benthamiana and S. lycopersicum plants were inoculated with PepMV or TMV by rubbing plant leaves with virus-infected N. benthamiana crude sap (76). A. thaliana seedlings were vernalized in the darkness at 4°C for 2 to 3 days and then grown in soil at 22° to 23°C with a 10/14-hour light/dark cycle (76). All A. thaliana WT and transgenic plants are in the Col-0 background. To generate CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-RIPs overexpression lines, CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-RIPs were inserted into pCAMBIA1300 vector and then transformed into Col-0 plants using the flower dip method (77). Progeny seeds were screened on 1/2 Murashige and Skoog medium plates supplemented with hygromycin B (50 ng/ml), 3% sucrose, and 1.2% agar with pH 5.8 to 6.0 (78). T3 transgenic A. thaliana plants were inoculated with CMV by rubbing plant leaves with virus-infected N. benthamiana crude sap. qRT-PCR was conducted to detect these transgenic plants using the corresponding primers listed in table S1.Plasmid constructionTo systematically validate the TI-TA concept and identify optimal regulatory components, we constructed a series of vectors following a stepwise design logic: starting with core TI elements (uAUG-ds), then integrating viral TA elements, and last, assembling full Virusmini backbones for functional verification. Construction of core TI element vectors (screening potent uAUG-ds) We first generated basic vectors to evaluate the inhibitory efficacy of different uAUG-ds elements. The GFP coding sequence was amplified from TMV-GFP and inserted into pCAMBIA1300 at the Sac I and Bam HI sites using Vazyme’s DNA seamless cloning kit (catalog no. C117) to serve as a control (79). The 5′ UTRs of TUB7 and TBF1 contain uAUG-ds elements (designated dsA, 144 nt; dsB, 105 nt), and a synthetic class I uAUG-ds (dsC, 54 nt) was also used (33). To enhance translational repression, we tandemly fused dsC to dsA, dsB, and dsC, generating dsAC, dsBC, and ds2C, respectively. All single/dual uAUG-ds elements were synthesized and cloned into pCAMBIA1300 at Sac I/Bam HI sites, with a Kpn I site inserted between the uAUG-ds and PepMV 3′ UTR. The resulting vectors were named pCAMBIA1300-Sac I-dsA/B/C/AC/BC/2C-Kpn I-3′ UTR-Bam HI. Subsequently, the GFP fragment was inserted into the Kpn I and Bam HI sites of these vectors, yielding dsA/B/C/AC/BC/2C-GFP, which were used to screen for the most potent TI elements (fig. S1A). Integration of viral TA element (PepMVSP1) and initial functional test To examine whether viral subgenomic promoters (TA elements) can drive gene expression under TI control, the PepMV CP subgenomic promoter (PepMVSP1) was fused with GFP by overlap PCR, and the resulting cassette was inserted into the Kpn I site of the pCAMBIA1300-Sac I-dsA/B/C/AC/BC/2C-Kpn I-3′ UTR-Bam HI vectors, generating dsA/B/C/AC/BC/2C-PepMVSP1 (Fig. 1B). A control vector containing only PepMVSP1-GFP without TI elements was also constructed. Compared with dsB, dsBC further reduced GFP protein accumulation and exhibited the strongest inhibitory effect among all tested uAUG-ds elements. Therefore, pCAMBIA1300-Sac I-dsBC-Kpn I-3′ UTR-Bam HI was selected for subsequent experiments. To determine whether the 36-nt sequence at the C terminus of the CP protein enhances viral activation, the PepMVSP1-GFP fragment was fused with 3′ UTR-B (the 3′ UTR with the CP C-terminal 36 nt appended to its 5′ end) via overlap PCR. The fused product was then seamlessly cloned into pCAMBIA1300-Sac I-dsBC-Kpn I-3′ UTR-Bam HI linearized with Kpn I/Bam HI or Sac I/Bam HI, yielding dsBC-PepMVSP1-GFP-B and the corresponding control PepMVSP1-GFP-B, respectively (fig. S2D). Assembly of PepMVmini backbone and dual-site GFP insertion To further enhance the efficiency of virus-activated target protein expression and recapitulate authentic viral transcriptional regulation, we synthesized PepMVmini, which comprises the PepMV 5′ UTR, the 45-nt sequence from the N terminus of RdRP, the TGB1 subgenomic promoter (PepMVSGP192), the CP subgenomic promoter (PepMVSP1), the 36-nt sequence from the C terminus of CP, and the 3′ UTR-B. PepMVmini was then cloned into pCAMBIA1300-Sac I-dsBC-Kpn I-3′ UTR-Bam HI linearized with Kpn I/Bam HI or Sac I/Bam HI, generating dsBC-PepMVmini and PepMVmini, respectively (Fig. 1F). Two unique restriction sites were engineered in PepMV: Kpn I (downstream of PepMVSGP192) and Pst I (downstream of PepMVSP1). GFP was inserted at the Kpn I site to generate PepMVmini-192-GFP, which tests TGB1 promoter-driven expression (Fig. 1F). GFP was inserted at the Pst I site to generate PepMVmini-GFP, which tests CP promoter-driven expression and serves as the core TA reporter. GFP was further inserted into Kpn I– or Pst I–linearized dsBC-PepMVmini vectors, yielding dsBC-PepMVmini-192-GFP and dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP, respectively, to validate TI-TA synergy (Fig. 1F). RIP expression vectors for PepMV resistance To test antiviral function, we replaced GFP in dsBC-PepMVmini with RIPs (BAX, INF1, and NLPPya), generating dsBC-PepMVmini-RIPs. For transient cell death assays, RIPs with N/C-terminal 3×HA tags were constructed into pCAMBIA1300 (fig. S4). Universal TI-TA vectors for TMV and CMV To establish a TI-TA system for TMV-activated expression, we synthesized TMVmini, a mini-replicon containing the TMV 5′ UTR, the N-terminal 60 nt of ORF1, the subgenomic promoters of MP and CP, the CP C-terminal 36 nt, and the TMV 3′ UTR. A unique Pst I site was engineered immediately downstream of the CP subgenomic promoter to allow reporter/effector insertion. The TMVmini fragment was cloned into the pCAMBIA1300-Sac I-dsBC-Kpn I-3′ UTR-Bam HI backbone at two different positions: at Sac I/Bam HI sites to generate the control vector pCAMBIA1300-TMVmini (without the TI module) and at Kpn I/Bam HI sites to generate the TI-containing vector pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-TMVmini (Fig. 3A). GFP was inserted into the Pst I site of both vectors to yield pCAMBIA1300-TMVmini-GFP and pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-TMVmini-GFP, respectively. For antiviral assays, RIPs (including BAX, INF1, and NLPPya) were cloned into the Pst I site of pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-TMVmini to produce pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-TMVmini-RIPs. To monitor INF1 expression and leakage, we also constructed pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-TMVmini-GFP-2A-INF1 and pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-TMVmini-INF1-2A-GFP using an overlapping PCR strategy with the 2A self-cleaving peptide (Fig. 3H).To develop a TI-TA system responsive to CMV, we constructed CMVminiRNA3-RZ, a mini-replicon derived from CMV RNA3 (1 to 221 nt, 639 to 1256 nt, and 1914 to 2216 nt) with a ribozyme (RZ) at the 3′ end, containing Spe I, Mlu I, and Xba I restriction sites (Fig. 4A). First, GFP was inserted into the Mlu I/Xba I sites to generate pCAMBIA1300-CMVminiRNA3-GFP-RZ (Fig. 4A). To test different TI modules, the full CMVminiRNA3-GFP-RZ cassette was cloned into the Kpn I/Bam HI sites of pCAMBIA1300-dsBC/A/B/C-Kpn I-3′ UTR-Bam HI, yielding a series of TI-containing reporter vectors (fig. S12A). To position dsBC upstream of the viral regulatory elements without disrupting promoter activity, we inserted dsBC into the Spe I site of pCAMBIA1300-CMVminiRNA3-GFP-RZ, generating pCAMBIA1300-CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-GFP-RZ (Fig. 4A). Last, RIPs were cloned into the Mlu I/Xba I sites to produce the effector vectors pCAMBIA1300-CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-RIP-RZ.All constructs were verified by DNA sequencing. Primers and sequences are listed in tables S1 and S2.Agrobacterium infiltration and GFP imagingAgrobacterium tumefaciens cultures [optical density at 600 nm (OD600) = 0.5] containing pCAMBIA1300-GFP, pCAMBIA1300-uAUG-ds-GFP, and pCAMBIA1300-uAUG-ds-PepMVSP1-GFP plasmids were infiltrated into 5- to 6-week-old N. benthamiana leaves. A. tumefaciens (OD600 = 0.5) harboring pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-PepMVSP1-GFP, pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP, and pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-PepMVmini-192-GFP plasmids were separately co-infiltrated with A. tumefaciens containing EV or PepMV plasmids (OD600 = 0.5) into N. benthamiana leaves. A. tumefaciens (OD600 = 0.5) containing the pCAMBIA1300-dsBC-TMVmini-GFP plasmid was separately co-infiltrated with A. tumefaciens (OD600 = 0.5) harboring EV or TMV into N. benthamiana leaves. Similarly, Agrobacterium strains containing GFP controlled by uAUG-ds and CMVminiRNA3 were separately co-infiltrated with A. tumefaciens containing EV or CMV (pCB301-CMV RNA1, pCB301-CMV RNA2, and pCB301-CMV RNA3 plasmids, with a final OD600 of 0.2 for each plasmid) and co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves. At 2 dpi, the agroinfiltrated leaves were illuminated under a long-wavelength ultraviolet lamp (UVP) and photographed under a yellow filter.Western blot analysisTotal protein was extracted from infiltrated N. benthamiana leaves as described previously (76). Immunoblotting was performed with the primary mouse polyclonal antibodies: anti-GFP polyclonal antibodies from ROCHE (1:5000, catalog no. 11814460001), anti-actin polyclonal antibodies from Abclonal (1:5000, catalog no. AC009), anti-PepMV CP polyclonal antibodies (1:5000, custom-made antibodies) (74), and anti-TMV CP and anti-CMV CP polyclonal antibodies (1:5000, custom-made antibodies). The membranes were then incubated with anti-mouse immunoglobulin G horseradish peroxidase–linked antibodies obtained from Easybio (1:5000, catalog no. BE0102).RNA extraction and qRT-PCRRNA extraction was performed as described previously (76), and qRT-PCR was conducted according to previously described methods (80). Total RNA was extracted from the collected leaf samples, and qRT-PCR was performed using gene-specific primers listed in table S1. The NbActin2, AtActin2, and SlActin genes served as endogenous controls (74). For PR1 expression analysis in N. benthamiana, two experimental setups were used. In transient expression assays, A. tumefaciens cultures (OD600 = 0.5) carrying the indicated constructs (EV, dsBC-Virusmini-GFP, or dsBC-Virusmini-RIPs) were co-infiltrated with Agrobacterium carrying the corresponding virus (PepMV, TMV, or CMV) at OD600 = 0.5 (for PepMV and TMV) or final OD600 = 0.2 per CMV component (total OD600 = 0.6). Inoculated leaves were collected at 2 dpi for qRT-PCR analysis. In transgenic plant assays, Agrobacterium suspensions harboring the corresponding virus (OD600 = 0.1) were infiltrated into leaves of WT, dsBC-Virusmini-GFP, and dsBC-Virusmini-RIP transgenic N. benthamiana plants. For CMV, virus sap was rub-inoculated onto transgenic A. thaliana lines and Col-0 WT plants. Inoculated leaves were collected at 3 dpi for qRT-PCR analysis. Gene-specific primers for NbPR1 (in N. benthamiana) or AtPR1 (in A. thaliana) were used, with the corresponding Actin genes as endogenous controls. In all qRT-PCR graphs, error bars represent means ± SD, and detailed information on biological replicates is specified in the corresponding figure legends. Statistical analyses were performed according to the experimental design. For comparisons among multiple groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) test was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 27 (P < 0.05). For selected pairwise comparisons between two groups, Student’s t test was performed using GraphPad Prism 8 when appropriate. One gram of infected systemic leaves was homogenized in 100 ml of 10 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.2) and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 5 min at 4°C. A total of 10 μl of the virus-containing supernatant was mechanically inoculated onto the leaves of 4- to 5-week-old N. benthamiana seedlings. Subsequently, 1 g of CMV-infected systemic leaves was ground in 100 ml of 10 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.2) supplemented with 2% PVP-40. The supernatant-containing CMV obtained from the same process was mechanically inoculated into two expanded leaves of 4-week-old A. thaliana seedlings (78).

source_paper.title: Specific and efficient translation inhibition–transcription activation resistance module against viruses in plants
source_paper.abstract: Positive-sense RNA viruses using subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs) cause severe crop losses, yet this conserved feature has rarely been exploited for antiviral engineering. Here, we constructed a virus-activated synthetic immune circuit, wherein viral sgRNA production drives host defense responses via a translation inhibition–transcription activation (TI-TA) module. An optimized translational repression element (dsBC) minimized basal expression while enabling virus-specific activation of resistance-inducing proteins (RIPs) by cognate viral sgRNA promoters. This circuit functioned against three major sgRNA-producing viruses—pepino mosaic virus (PepMV), tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), and cucumber mosaic virus (CMV)—in Nicotiana benthamiana, tomato, and Arabidopsis thaliana, with cross-resistance to related viruses. RIP expression was strictly triggered by viral infection, conferring robust resistance without detectable growth penalties. This programmable strategy provides a versatile platform for engineering resistance against diverse sgRNA-producing RNA viruses and offers a conceptual framework for developing synthetic antiviral immunity in plants.
source_paper.full_text: INTRODUCTIONDuring the long-term coevolution of plants and pathogens, plants have developed two major layers of innate immunity: pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) and effector-triggered immunity (ETI) (1, 2). PTI is triggered by plasma membrane–localized pattern recognition receptors, which perceive conserved microbial patterns, including flagellin, elongation factor Tu, peptidoglycan, chitin, and lipopolysaccharides, thereby conferring basal immunity against a broad spectrum of nonadapted pathogens (3, 4). In contrast, ETI represents a more robust and specific immune response mediated by resistance (R) proteins. Most proteins belong to the family of nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors (NLRs), which recognize pathogen effectors and initiate potent defense responses, typically accompanied by a hypersensitive response (HR) to restrict pathogen proliferation (5, 6). Recent studies have revealed that PTI and ETI function interdependently rather than independently, resulting in largely overlapping and integrated immune responses (7, 8). NLR-mediated plant immunity induces HR, which serves as an effective defense against viral infections. However, only a small number of viral proteins can be recognized by limited NLRs to initiate ETI signaling (9). Several exogenous proteins, including BAX, INF1, and NLPPya are capable of rapidly inducing plant HR through PTI/ETI-dependent or independent pathways. As a mammalian Bcl-2 family protein, BAX localizes to mitochondria and triggers cell death upon heterologous expression in plants, followed by the up-regulation of defense-related genes and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation (10, 11). INF1, a 10-kDa extracellular elicitor widely distributed across Phytophthora species, induces HR in a restricted number of plants, particularly in the genus Nicotiana. INF1-triggered immune responses include PTI activation, ROS burst, and elevated expression of ethylene (ET)– and jasmonic acid (JA)–responsive genes (12–16). NLPPya derived from the phytopathogenic oomycete Pythium aphanidermatum, triggers leaf necrosis in diverse plant species. It functions by forming transient small pores on lipid membranes, leading to plasma membrane destruction, cytolysis, and the activation of plant defense–related genes. This cellular damage–triggered immune activation is analogous to inflammasome activation in vertebrates (17, 18). Whether resistance-inducing proteins (RIPs) from different biological sources, such as INF1, BAX, and NLPPya can be harnessed to combat viral infections remains an intriguing scientific question.Positive-sense single-stranded RNA (+ssRNA) viruses constitute the vast majority of plant viruses and impose severe threats to global crop production. A large proportion of these viruses, encompassing over 1000 characterized plant +ssRNA viral species, use subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs) promoters to generate sgRNAs for the expression of internal and 3′-proximal open reading frames (ORFs) (19, 20). The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) of +ssRNA viruses recognizes the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the viral genome and synthesizes a complementary negative-strand viral RNA genome. Subsequently, RdRP recognizes specific internal subgenomic promoters (SPs) on the negative-strand RNA template to initiate the synthesis of truncated positive-strand RNA transcripts, termed sgRNAs. Through sgRNA biogenesis, viruses efficiently orchestrate viral gene expression and ensure the timely synthesis of structural and nonstructural proteins during infection, thereby expanding their genomic coding capacity (21). Most economically destructive plant viruses fall into this category, including tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), cucumber mosaic virus (CMV), brome mosaic virus (BMV), and potato virus X (PVX) (22). Additionally, multiple emerging crop-damaging viruses, such as pepino mosaic virus (PepMV), tomato brown rugose fruit virus (ToBRFV), cucumber green mottle mosaic virus (CGMMV), and maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV), also use the sgRNA-dependent gene expression strategy (20, 23). Due to the intrinsically high mutation rates of +ssRNA viruses, which primarily result from the lack of proofreading activity in viral RdRP (24, 25), viral populations exist as dynamic quasispecies capable of rapid adaptation to diverse selective pressures. This potent evolutionary plasticity allows viruses to evade NLR-mediated host resistance. For example, resistance-breaking strains have been documented to overcome host resistance conferred by tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) and ToBRFV resistance genes (26, 27). Recent advances in plant immune engineering have facilitated the optimization of NLR-mediated resistance through multiple strategies, including random mutagenesis, structure-guided receptor engineering, integrated decoy engineering, and effector-mediated derepression of autoactive NLRs (28, 29). Despite these advances, durable and broadly applicable resistance approaches specifically targeting sgRNA-producing RNA viruses remain largely undeveloped.Plants maintain a dynamic balance between growth and immunity to optimize environmental adaptation. Robust immune responses strengthen disease resistance but frequently penalize plant growth and yield, a trade-off universally recognized as the “growth-defense trade-off” (30). Fortunately, multiple strategies have been developed to boost plant immunity without incurring substantial fitness costs (31). A typical paradigm is the “TBF1-cassette,” which exploits pathogen-responsive translational regulation mediated by upstream open reading frames (uORFs) within the 5′ leader sequence of the TBF1 (TL1-binding transcription factor 1). TBF1 acts as a core transcription factor that regulates the transition from growth to defense upon immune activation. Although its translation is constitutively repressed by two conserved uORFs under normal conditions, it is rapidly activated in response to pathogen challenge, ensuring the timely accumulation of defense regulators. Engineering this regulatory module to control the expression of immune genes, such as NPR1, confers broad-spectrum disease resistance without compromising plant growth (32). Further studies have revealed that uORF-dependent translational regulation is tightly associated with RNA secondary structures. Specifically, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) hairpin structures immediately downstream of the upstream AUG codons (uAUGs) of uORF, termed uAUG-ds, are critical for selective translation initiation. These structural motifs facilitate ribosome recognition of uAUGs, thereby promoting uORFs translation and repressing the translation of downstream main ORF under normal growth conditions. Upon immune activation, RNA helicases unwind these dsRNA structures, enabling ribosomes to bypass uAUGs and initiate translation of defense-related proteins. Notably, uAUG-ds serves as a functional structural partner of uORFs rather than being functionally equivalent to uORFs. While uAUGs define the start codon of uORFs, the downstream dsRNA structures modulate translational efficiency, and, together, they constitute a dynamic regulatory module that fine-tunes protein abundance (33). Previous studies have reported advanced pathogen-responsive resistance strategies. Mei et al. exploited uAUG-mediated translational regulation to modulate the expression of plant immune genes, successfully enhancing resistance against fungal, bacterial, and DNA viral pathogens with negligible fitness penalties (34). Liu’s group used the pathogen-responsive TBF1 promoter coupled with its endogenous uORFs to drive MCD1 expression in Nicotiana benthamiana, achieving broad-spectrum resistance against cross-kingdom pathogens without affecting normal plant growth (35). Engineered NLRs or elicitor peptides also confer potent resistance to potyviruses without growth penalties by activating postinfection defense responses (29, 36). Nevertheless, efficient virus-responsive resistance systems specifically tailored for sgRNA-producing RNA viruses remain largely underexplored to date.In this study, we developed a dual-layer translation inhibition–transcription activation (TI-TA) strategy for engineering resistance against sgRNA-producing +ssRNA viruses. This design is built upon two core biological principles. First, uAUG-ds elements robustly repress downstream protein translation under normal growth conditions, thereby minimizing constitutive expression-driven growth penalties typically induced by RIPs. Second, sgRNA-producing viruses specifically activate viral subgenomic promoters during infection, providing a virus-dependent transcriptional activation (TA) signal. Based on these two principles, we used uAUG-ds elements as translational inhibition (TI) modules to repress RIP expression in the absence of viral infection, while viral subgenomic promoters were used as TA modules to drive RIP expression specifically upon viral infection. For systematic evaluation, uAUG-ds motifs derived from the 5′ UTRs of TUB7 and TBF1 were designated as dsA and dsB, respectively, and a synthetic 54–nucleotide (nt) class I uAUG-ds element was named dsC and generated the enhanced translational repression module dsBC. Using this TI-TA framework, we demonstrated that the combination of dsBC with viral subgenomic promoter modules confers potent basal repression and robust virus-responsive expression. Substituting green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporters with RIP effectors (e.g., BAX) conferred effective resistance against PepMV in N. benthamiana and tomato. Furthermore, the strategy exhibits partial broad applicability toward diverse sgRNA-producing viruses, including TMV and CMV, with protective efficacy extending to other closely related viruses within the corresponding genera. Collectively, this synthetic system integrates three advantageous features: (i) potent basal translational repression, (ii) strict virus-specific activation, and (iii) partial broad-spectrum antiviral activity without detectable growth penalty. Our work therefore establishes a programmable framework for engineering durable resistance against sgRNA-producing plant RNA viruses.RESULTSStepwise optimization of TI and TA modules yields a PepMV-responsive expression systemGiven the persistent and severe threat to crop production posed by +ssRNA viruses that produce sgRNAs, we sought to develop a virus-responsive system capable of specifically activating the expression of RIPs upon viral infection. To achieve this goal, two requirements needed to be fulfilled: (i) RIP expression should remain strongly suppressed in the absence of viral infection through TI; and (ii) RIP expression should be specifically activated upon viral infection through TA. To establish an efficient TI module, we evaluated several uAUG-ds elements. The 5′ UTRs of TUB7 and TBF1 contain naturally occurring uAUG-ds elements, designated dsA (144 nt) and dsB (105 nt), respectively, whereas a 54-nt class I uAUG-ds element was designated dsC (33). The PepMV coat protein (CP) subgenomic promoter (PepMVSP1) was selected as the initial TA module (Fig. 1A). To assess the translational inhibitory activities of these elements, GFP was inserted between PepMVSP1 and the 3′ UTR to generate PepMVSP1-GFP (Fig. 1B). Individual or tandem uAUG-ds elements were subsequently fused to the 5′ end of PepMVSP1-GFP, generating dsA-, dsB-, dsC-, dsAC-, dsBC-, and ds2C-PepMVSP1-GFP constructs (Fig. 1B). Transient expression assays in N. benthamiana revealed that tandem uAUG-ds elements (dsAC, dsBC, and ds2C) conferred substantially stronger translational repression than individual elements, as evidenced by reduced GFP fluorescence and protein accumulation (Fig. 1, C and D). Among them, dsBC exhibited the strongest inhibitory effect on GFP protein accumulation (Fig. 1, C and D). Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis showed that dsBC did not substantially affect GFP transcript abundance (Fig. 1E), indicating that its inhibitory effect primarily occurred at the translational level. In addition, independent verification assays confirmed that uAUG-ds elements, in the absence of PepMVSP1, could significantly reduce GFP protein accumulation without altering mRNA levels, solidifying the translational inhibitory function of uAUG-ds modules (fig. S1). Collectively, dsBC was selected as the optimal TI element for subsequent system construction due to its strong and specific translational repression activity.Fig. 1.PepMV strongly restores GFP expression in the dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP system.(A) Schematic of the PepMV genome. TGB1–3, triple gene block proteins; CP, coat protein. (B) Schematic of uAUG-ds, PepMVSP1, and GFP constructs. The uAUG-ds elements include 144-nt dsA from the TUB7 5′ UTR, 105-nt dsB from the TBF1 5′ UTR, and a 54-nt class I element dsC (33). Tandem fusion of these elements with dsC produced dsAC, dsBC, and ds2C. Blue line indicates PepMVSP1 and 3′ UTR; pink box indicates the first 36 nt of the CP N terminus. (C to E) GFP fluorescence, protein accumulation, and mRNA levels in N. benthamiana leaves infiltrated with Agrobacterium (OD600 = 0.5) carrying GFP, PepMVSP1-GFP, or uAUG-ds-PepMVSP1-GFP constructs. EV served as the negative control. Fluorescence was observed at 2 dpi under UV light, GFP accumulation was detected by Western blot using anti-GFP and anti-actin antibodies, and GFP mRNA levels were analyzed by qRT-PCR. (F) Schematic of PepMVmini and derivatives. PepMVmini contains the 5′ UTR, 45 nt of the RdRP N terminus, PepMVSGP192, PepMVSP1, the 36-nt CP C-terminal sequence, and the 3′ UTR (648 nt total). Kpn I and Pst I sites are located downstream of PepMVSGP192 and PepMVSP1, respectively. (G to I) PepMV infection restores GFP expression from dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP. Agrobacterium carrying dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP (OD600 = 0.5) was co-infiltrated with EV or PepMV (OD600 = 0.5). GFP fluorescence (G), protein accumulation (H), and mRNA levels (I) were analyzed at 2 dpi. GFP and PepMVmini-GFP served as controls. Data are presented as means ± SD (n = 3). Statistical significance was determined by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD test (P < 0.05) using IBM SPSS Statistics 27; different letters indicate significant differences among treatments. Selected pairwise comparisons were performed using Student’s t test in GraphPad Prism 8 when appropriate.Having identified dsBC as the most effective TI module, we next evaluated whether PepMVSP1 could function as a virus-responsive TA module. To this end, dsBC-PepMVSP1-GFP was co-infiltrated with either an empty vector (EV) or PepMV into N. benthamiana leaves. Unexpectedly, PepMV infection failed to restore GFP fluorescence, protein accumulation, or transcript levels relative to the EV control (fig. S2, A to C). These results indicated that PepMVSP1 and 3′ UTR were insufficient to support efficient virus-dependent activation, revealing a critical limitation of the initial system design. To identify additional cis-regulatory elements required for PepMV-dependent activation, we considered previous reports showing that efficient transcription from the PepMV CP subgenomic promoter requires the N-terminal 36-nt sequence of the CP coding region (37). This observation suggested that sequences adjacent to the CP transcription unit may contain additional cis-elements involved in promoter recognition or activity. Therefore, we tested whether incorporation of the 36-nt sequence immediately upstream of the 3′ UTR could improve PepMV-dependent activation of the dsBC-PepMVSP1-GFP construct. However, this modification resulted in only weak GFP activation following PepMV infection (fig. S2, D to G), suggesting that partial sequence optimization was insufficient to restore effective virus-responsive expression activation. These results suggested that additional viral cis-elements were required. We therefore reconstructed a larger PepMV-derived mini-replicon, designated PepMVmini, consisting of the 5′ UTR, the first 45 nt of the RdRP coding sequence, the TGB1 subgenomic promoter (SGP192), the CP subgenomic promoter (SP1), the 36-nt CP-terminal sequence, and the 3′ UTR (Fig. 1F). GFP was fused downstream of PepMVmini to generate PepMVmini-GFP, and dsBC was subsequently introduced to generate dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP (Fig. 1F). To date, several antiviral engineering strategies have been developed, including dominant resistance (R) genes, pathogen-derived resistance (PDR), RNA interference (RNAi), CRISPR-Cas–based genome editing, host susceptibility factor engineering, and immune signaling enhancement. Among these approaches, NLR-mediated resistance can provide strong protection against viral infection (9); however, resistance-breaking viral variants frequently emerge and compromise its durability (27, 43, 46, 47). Classical PDR and cross-protection approaches exhibit favorable biosafety and practical applicability but suffer from narrow antiviral spectra and potential risks of viral recombination and virulence reversion under field conditions (48, 49). RNAi-based strategies enable flexible and sequence-specific viral suppression; however, their efficacy can be compromised by viral sequence variation and diverse viral suppressors of RNA silencing that antagonize host silencing pathways (50, 51). CRISPR-Cas systems provide high-precision and multiplex editing for viral and host target modification, yet mutations within gRNA target sites frequently generate viral escape variants, and constitutive Cas expression may raise biosafety and regulatory concerns (52–54). Engineering host susceptibility factors, such as eIF4E family proteins, can confer durable resistance against specific groups of viruses, but their effectiveness is often limited to particular virus taxa (55–58). Likewise, manipulation of host proteins involved in virus infection through overexpression or knockout can enhance antiviral resistance, although such modifications rarely provide complete immunity (59). In addition, constitutive activation of immune pathways can confer broad-spectrum disease resistance but often results in notable growth penalties because of the well-known growth-defense trade-off (60, 61). To address these limitations, pathogen-responsive resistance systems that activate defense responses only upon pathogen infection have attracted increasing attention. Recent studies have demonstrated that translational regulation mediated by uORFs can effectively control the expression of immune-related genes and enhance resistance against fungal, bacterial, and DNA viral pathogens without obvious fitness costs (34, 35). Likewise, engineered NLRs and inducible elicitor peptide systems can provide strong resistance to potyviruses while minimizing growth penalties by activating defense responses only after infection (29, 36). These findings collectively highlight the potential of pathogen-responsive defense systems to overcome the limitations associated with constitutive resistance. Nevertheless, virus-responsive antiviral systems specifically designed for +ssRNA viruses that produce sgRNAs remain limited.Compared with existing approaches, the virus-responsive RIP system developed in this study has several notable advantages (Fig. 6). First, antiviral activity is activated only after viral infection, thereby minimizing developmental abnormalities under normal growth conditions. Second, unlike RNAi and CRISPR-based technologies that directly target viral nucleotide sequences, our strategy exploits the conserved process of viral sgRNA synthesis to activate defense responses, potentially reducing the likelihood of resistance breakdown caused by single mutational events. Third, because sgRNA production is a common feature among many +ssRNA viruses, this platform may have broader applicability than virus-specific resistance mechanisms. Additional specificity assays demonstrated that the TI-TA system was not activated by unrelated viruses, bacterial or fungal pathogens, or abiotic stresses including heat and drought (figs. S8 and S9), indicating that viral mini-replicon recognition is highly specific and that the TI-TA system is unlikely to be ectopically activated by nontarget biotic or abiotic stimuli. Such stringent specificity minimizes the risk of unintended HR activation and enhances the biosafety and practical potential of this strategy for agricultural applications. However, several limitations should also be acknowledged. Differences in the abundance, timing, and regulatory mechanisms of sgRNA accumulation among viruses may substantially influence the activation efficiency of the TI-TA system. In addition, plant species may differ in their sensitivity to RIP-induced immune responses, which could further affect system performance. Moreover, all experiments in the present study were conducted under controlled greenhouse conditions using laboratory-maintained viral isolates. Therefore, the stability, durability, and practical performance of the TI-TA system under field conditions remain to be evaluated. In agricultural environments, fluctuating temperatures, mixed infections involving multiple pathogens, and genetically diverse viral populations may influence viral replication dynamics, sgRNA production, and consequently the activation efficiency of the TI-TA circuit. Field trials using diverse viral isolates and representative environmental conditions will therefore be essential to assess the robustness and long-term effectiveness of this strategy. Another limitation is that the current study used constitutive transgenic expression of TI-TA components, which facilitated proof-of-concept validation but may not fully satisfy future regulatory requirements for commercial crop deployment. Future optimization could explore tissue-specific or infection-responsive promoters to restrict transgene expression to relevant tissues or infection sites, as well as minimized expression cassettes to simplify genetic constructs and improve biosafety and regulatory compatibility. The current TI-TA system is designed to target a specific virus or closely related viruses within the same genus. Therefore, achieving resistance against multiple unrelated viruses will likely require stacking several TI-TA modules using strategies such as tRNA- or ribozyme-mediated polycistronic expression. Although the system conferred effective immunity resistance against CMV, it did not provide complete protection against PepMV or TMV. Accordingly, further efforts are required to improve the virus-responsive activation efficiency of TI-TA upon viral challenge. Artificial intelligence–assisted screening can be adopted to identify more efficient RIPs that can potently trigger immune responses across diverse plant species. Furthermore, combining the TI-TA platform with complementary antiviral strategies, including host susceptibility factor engineering, RNAi, and CRISPR-Cas–based technologies, may provide broader-spectrum and more durable resistance against emerging plant viruses.Fig. 6.Schematic working model of the TI-TA synthetic immune module conferring plant resistance to viral infection.Our innovative system integrates three key components that combine uAUG-ds as TI, Virusmini as virus-activated transcription (TA), and RIPs to create a targeted defense that only activates upon infection. The virus-responsive resistance system conferred robust resistance in N. benthamiana, tomato, and A. thaliana plants against three economically important viruses—PepMV, TMV, and CMV—with effectiveness extending to other viruses within the respective genera. This adaptable strategy enables rapid development of virus-resistant crops and may inform new approaches against animal RNA viruses, advancing plant and animal disease control. Created in BioRender. Yang, X (2026) https://BioRender.com/7z4l4rd.In this study, we found distinct BAX-mediated responses in different plant hosts, with A. thaliana exhibiting markedly stronger responses than N. benthamiana (Figs. 2D and 4H and fig. S14). This interspecific difference might be attributed to a combination of intrinsic host-specific biological characteristics and virus-dependent variations in the activation efficiency of the TI-TA system. On one hand, interspecific variations in cell death signaling pathways, translational regulatory mechanisms, and immune response networks lead to divergent host sensitivity to BAX-induced cytotoxicity. On the other hand, the accumulation level of BAX effector protein is governed by the activation efficiency of the TA module triggered by different viral infections. Transient expression assays verified that CMV infection increased GFP transcript accumulation by ∼336%, while PepMV and TMV resulted in only 13 and 47% increases in transcript accumulation, respectively, demonstrating that CMV activates the TI-TA system far more efficiently than PepMV and TMV under the tested conditions (Figs. 4D, 1I, and 3D). Accordingly, CMV-infected A. thaliana accumulates higher levels of BAX than PepMV-infected N. benthamiana, which might be a key factor contributing to the more intense phenotypic responses in A. thaliana. The differential activation efficiency among the three viral systems may result from multiple virus-specific factors. One possibility is that differences in mini-replicon architecture, including viral UTRs, sgRNA promoter sequences, and regulatory elements required for replication complex assembly, affect the efficiency of viral activation. In addition, the ability of viral RdRps to recognize and use heterologous mini-replicons may vary among viruses, leading to differences in sgRNA production and subsequent TI-TA activation. Furthermore, virus-host compatibility and replication dynamics in different plant species may influence the abundance and timing of viral signals available for system activation. Therefore, the stronger resistance observed in the CMV system likely reflects more efficient activation of the corresponding mini-replicon rather than an inherent superiority of the TI-TA framework. Future optimization of viral regulatory elements and host-virus combinations may further enhance the performance of PepMV- and TMV-based TI-TA systems.Beyond interspecific response differences, the cross-species transferability of this TI-TA experimental platform is another critical issue worthy of discussion. Mechanistically, the platform consists of three core components: the TI module, the TA module, and the RIPs, which differ greatly in their cross-species adaptability. The TI module is based on uAUG-ds element, a mechanism that is expected to function broadly across plant species because it relies on conserved translational machinery (33). The TA module depends on viral RdRP activity and therefore should be functional in any compatible host-virus interaction (21). In contrast, the RIPs are the primary limiting factor for cross-species application. All RIPs tested in this study were only validated in dicot plants, and their functional activity in monocot crops remains uncharacterized. Meanwhile, our INF1-related experiments further confirmed the host specificity of effector proteins. In transient expression assays, CMV infection efficiently activated CMVminiRNA3-INF1 and triggered a typical HR in N. benthamiana (Fig. 4F); however, transgenic A. thaliana stably expressing CMVminiRNA3-INF1 showed no enhanced CMV resistance compared with the WT Col-0 (Fig. 4H), indicating that the ability of effectors to activate plant defense responses is highly host-dependent. Therefore, the cross-species deployment of this platform requires targeted screening and optimization of effector proteins to ensure stable biological activity in target host species. Notably, different RIPs also exhibit inconsistent antiviral efficacy even within dicot hosts. For instance, transgenic lines expressing INF1 displayed relatively weak resistance to PepMV, which was consistent with the finding that PepMV infection failed to significantly increase PR1 expression in INF1 transgenic plants (Fig. 2, D and G). An important limitation of the current study is that RIP protein accumulation could not be directly quantified after viral infection. Because specific antibodies or epitope-tagged versions of RIP proteins were unavailable in the current experimental system, we cannot exclude the possibility that the observed differences among RIPs result from variation in protein abundance, intrinsic effector activity, or downstream immune activation efficiency. Therefore, the relative contribution of these factors to RIP-mediated antiviral resistance remains unresolved. Future studies incorporating fluorescent protein fusions, optimized epitope-tagging strategies, or RIP-specific antibodies will enable direct monitoring of RIP accumulation and provide mechanistic insights into the differential performance of RIP effectors.The cross-protection spectrum of the TI-TA system is influenced by the evolutionary relatedness between the target virus and the virus-derived mini-replicon. Although TI-TA transgenic plants exhibited cross-resistance against related viruses, the extent of protection varied among virus pairs (Fig. 5). To explore the potential determinants of this variation, we compared the sequence homology of subgenomic promoters from three virus pairs: TMV/ToBRFV (69.08%), CMV-Fny/CMV-Q (65.3%), and PepMV/PVX (32.99%) (fig. S15, A to C). The relatively high promoter similarity between TMV and ToBRFV, as well as between CMV-Fny and CMV-Q, may increase the likelihood that viral replicases recognize heterologous mini-replicons. Although PepMV and PVX share relatively low promoter homology, conserved sequence elements required for potexvirus replication and sgRNA synthesis may still enable PVX RdRp to recognize the PepMV-derived mini-replicon (fig. S15D) (62, 63). Consistent with the activation efficiencies observed in Figs. 1I, 3D, and 4D, we speculate that related viruses differ in their ability to activate heterologous mini-replicons. CMV-Q most efficiently activated CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-RIPs, whereas PVX showed the weakest activation of dsBC-PepMVmini-RIPs, which may explain why CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-RIPs conferred nearly complete immunity against CMV-Q, while dsBC-TMVmini-RIPs and dsBC-PepMVmini-RIPs provided only partial resistance to ToBRFV and PVX, respectively (Fig. 5). Although the binding affinity of viral RdRps to noncognate mini-replicons was not examined in this study, it may contribute to differences in mini-replicon activation. Furthermore, variation in RIP expression levels following heterologous mini-replicon activation may further influence the final cross-resistance outcome.In addition to demonstrating the antiviral efficacy of the TI-TA system, our results also uncovered several unexpected RNA-level phenomena related to transcript stability, translational regulation, and construct architecture, which warrant further investigation. We found that PepMVmini (Fig. 1I), TMVmini (Fig. 3D), and CMVminiRNA3 (Fig. 4D) all markedly reduced GFP mRNA accumulation. In plants, RNA quality control is mediated by nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), no-stop decay (NSD), and no-go decay (NGD), with XRN4 serving as a key component of the 5′ → 3′ RNA decay pathway (64, 65). Using TRV-VIGS (66, 67), we showed that silencing NbXRN4 increased GFP mRNA levels in dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP, dsBC-TMVmini-GFP, and CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-GFP (fig. S16), indicating that XRN4-dependent RNA degradation contributes to the reduced transcript abundance of Virusmini-based constructs. NMD is known to target viral RNAs containing premature termination codons (PTCs), including those of PVX, TCV, and CGMMV (68–71). For example, PVX RNAs carrying extended 3′ UTRs are degraded through NMD (72), whereas the PEMV2 P26 protein counteracts NMD to protect viral RNAs (73). Moreover, m6A modification promotes NMD-mediated degradation of PepMV RNA (74). Because Virusmini constructs contain PTCs, it is plausible that they are recognized by the NMD machinery, thereby contributing to the reduced accumulation of GFP mRNA. Here, we also found that dsA, dsB, and dsC effectively suppressed GFP protein accumulation without reducing GFP transcript levels, suggesting that these elements primarily act through translational repression. However, tandem fusion of dsA/B/C with dsC did not further enhance TI (fig. S1). In the presence of the PepMV subgenomic promoter PepMVSP1, fusion of dsA/B/C with dsC resulted in an additional reduction in GFP protein accumulation, possibly due to the presence of a termination codon or specific RNA structural features associated with PepMVSP1. These observations suggest that combining uAUG-ds elements with viral regulatory sequences may provide a practical strategy for fine-tuning the expression of highly toxic proteins to biologically tolerable levels. In addition, unlike dsB and dsC, dsA not only inhibited GFP translation but also significantly increased GFP mRNA accumulation (Fig. 1E and fig. S1D), implying the existence of an as-yet-unknown mechanism linking dsA to transcript regulation. Another unexpected observation was that dsBC-TMVmini-INF1 lost its ability to suppress INF1 expression and triggered HR in the absence of viral infection (Fig. 3G). This leakage phenotype was eliminated in dsBC-TMVmini-INF1-2A-GFP but not in dsBC-TMVmini-GFP-2A-INF1 (Fig. 3H), suggesting that the INF1 coding sequence together with the TMVmini 3′ UTR may form a specific RNA structure that interferes with dsBC-mediated translational repression. Insertion of GFP between INF1 and the 3′ UTR may disrupt this putative structure and restore repression. Although this hypothesis requires further experimental validation, it highlights the importance of local RNA structural context in determining TI-TA performance. In addition, our results indicate that the optimal positioning of dsBC may vary among different viral mini-replicons. Unlike PepMVmini and TMVmini, in which placement of dsBC at the 5′ terminus enabled efficient virus-responsive activation, CMVminiRNA3 required internal insertion of dsBC to achieve functionality (figs. S12, B to D, and S4, B to D). Therefore, the current design principles should be considered empirical guidelines rather than fully predictive rules, as they were derived from a limited number of viral mini-replicon configurations tested in this study. The requirement for internal dsBC placement in CMVminiRNA3 highlights the current limitation that the optimal architecture for a different virus cannot yet be reliably predicted solely from viral sequence information or known regulatory elements. Specifically, 5′-terminal dsBC insertion represents a useful initial design strategy because of its successful performance in two independent viral backbones, whereas internal dsBC insertion provides an alternative configuration when 5′-terminal placement compromises mini-replicon activity or virus-responsive expression. Establishing more generalizable and predictive design principles will require systematic evaluation of diverse viral mini-replicons combined with computational analyses of RNA sequence features, secondary structures, and potential interactions between dsBC elements and viral regulatory regions. Such integrative approaches may ultimately enable rational optimization of TI-TA architectures for newly emerging viral pathogens without extensive empirical screening.In this study, we combined distinct uAUG-ds repressor elements with the viral PepMVSP1 promoter to achieve tunable, gradient attenuation of target protein expression, a tool that facilitates functional characterization of cytotoxic or growth-suppressive proteins in planta. This work innovatively fuses the dsBC translational repression module with viral mini-replicons to assemble the TI-TA synthetic immune circuit, which drives strict virus-specific activation of RIP effector expression exclusively during viral infection (Fig. 6). The dsBC-PepMVmini-BAX construct confers robust PepMV resistance in transgenic N. benthamiana and tomato lines. Separately, dsBC-TMVmini-INF1-2A-GFP and dsBC-TMVmini-NLPPya grant TMV resistance in stably transformed N. benthamiana. CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-NLPPya delivers near-complete immunity against systemic CMV infection. Furthermore, the TI-TA architecture mediates partial cross-resistance against phylogenetically related viruses within the same genus. Collectively, this programmable synthetic immune strategy provides a conceptual framework for engineering resistance against sgRNA-producing +ssRNA viruses and establishes a foundation for future optimization toward agricultural applications. Beyond agricultural deployment, this experimental framework also provides a tractable system to dissect how growth-regulatory cytotoxic proteins modulate +ssRNA virus infection dynamics in plant hosts. Last, the core TI-TA design logic offers conceptual reference and design inspiration for developing RNA-targeted synthetic immunotherapies against animal RNA viral pathogens.MATERIALS AND METHODSPlant growth conditions and plant materialsThe WT and transgenic N. benthamiana plants were grown in a climate chamber with a 15-hour daylight and 9-hour dark photoperiod at 23° to 25°C as described previously (75). TITLE:
Specific and efficient translation inhibition–transcription activation resistance module against viruses in plants

ABSTRACT:
Positive-sense RNA viruses using subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs) cause severe crop losses, yet this conserved feature has rarely been exploited for antiviral engineering. Here, we constructed a virus-activated synthetic immune circuit, wherein viral sgRNA production drives host defense responses via a translation inhibition–transcription activation (TI-TA) module. An optimized translational repression element (dsBC) minimized basal expression while enabling virus-specific activation of resistance-inducing proteins (RIPs) by cognate viral sgRNA promoters. This circuit functioned against three major sgRNA-producing viruses—pepino mosaic virus (PepMV), tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), and cucumber mosaic virus (CMV)—in Nicotiana benthamiana, tomato, and Arabidopsis thaliana, with cross-resistance to related viruses. RIP expression was strictly triggered by viral infection, conferring robust resistance without detectable growth penalties. This programmable strategy provides a versatile platform for engineering resistance against diverse sgRNA-producing RNA viruses and offers a conceptual framework for developing synthetic antiviral immunity in plants.

TITLE:
Dominant resistance against plant viruses

ABSTRACT:
To establish a successful infection plant viruses have to overcome a defense system composed of several layers. This review will overview the various strategies plants employ to combat viral infections with main emphasis on the current status of single dominant resistance (R) genes identified against plant viruses and the corresponding avirulence (Avr) genes identified so far. The most common models to explain the mode of action of dominant R genes will be presented. Finally, in brief the hypersensitive response (HR) and extreme resistance (ER), and the functional and structural similarity of R genes to sensors of innate immunity in mammalian cell systems will be described.

evidence_results.verification_source: IntroductionDuring the past decades it has become clear that plants have a unique and complex defense system that consists of several layers, which enables them to avoid, suppress, or actively defend against pathogens from all kingdoms like fungi, bacteria, nematodes, and viruses. Of all plant viruses known, only a few cause serious diseases and, if so, mostly limited to a very small number of crops. In general, most viruses have a limited (natural) host range and the number of so-called non-hosts exceeds those of hosts. In those plants that are hosts, viruses encounter different mechanisms of defense. Some act general against all viruses and this response is part of the innate immune system, while others are virus-specific and involve resistance genes. Triggering of the latter simultaneously mediates a rapid necrosis at the site of virus entry and prevents further spread of the virus throughout the host. In several cases resistance genes do not confer absolute resistance and low levels of virus replication can still be observed. In those cases the genes are referred to as partial resistance genes or tolerance genes.While throughout the years reviews on resistance genes have appeared with regular intervals, these mostly had their main focus on fungal and bacterial resistance genes, primarily due to the large amount of data available. This review aims to present an overview on the current status of resistance genes against plant viruses, with emphasis on single dominant resistance genes. The very basis of plant pathogens (among others plant viruses) not being able to infect all plants is due to a mechanism called non-host resistance (NHR) (For an extensive review on this, see Uma et al., 2011). NHR holds for all plant pathogens and is a generic, nonspecific resistance that can be divided into two main types, distinguished by the mechanism and mode of recognition (Mysore and Ryu, 2004). Type 1 is the most pre-dominant type of NHR and presents a basic defense mechanism that prevents pathogen invasion, e.g., thickening of the cell-wall, secondary metabolite production, etc. This type of resistance usually is symptomless. In contrast, type 2 NHR is associated with induction of necrosis at the site of infection, and is induced when pathogens overcome type 1 resistance. Here, the pathogen is recognized through specific structures or proteins that are associated with the pathogen. The recognition of these structures/proteins, so called microbe associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) or PAMPS (Pathogen), takes place by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) on plant plasma membranes. These PRRs recognize conserved structures of pathogens, like flaggelin from the flagella of bacteria or chitin from the cell wall of fungi, and induce a so called PAMP triggered immunity (PTI) response (Jones and Dangl, 2006). Since plant viruses need to overcome the physical barrier of a cell wall, they enter their host cells either via mechanical inoculation or the infection is mediated by vectors like insects, nematodes, or even fungi. Direct recognition of viruses probably does not occur in the apoplast. However, a study recently reported on the possible involvement of (intracellular) receptor-like kinases (RLKs), of the like that are involved in PAMP recognition by PRRs, in plant-virus interactions (Kørner et al., 2013).One of the first innate immune responses all plant viruses encounter when invading a host consists of antiviral RNA silencing [also called RNA interference (RNAi) and in the very early days post-transcriptional gene silencing (PTSG)]. RNA silencing is a host response triggered by double stranded (ds)RNA. These molecules thus act as a MAMP/PAMP and in which RNAi can be regarded as PTI. The main difference with pathogens such as fungi and bacteria is that recognition of viral MAMPs/PAMPs occurs intracellularly (Ding and Voinnet, 2007).RNA silencing consists of two major “branches”; the first one is that of small-interfering (si)RNAs, and one of the hallmarks for antiviral RNAi, and the second one is that of (host-gene encoded) micro (mi)RNAs involved in gene regulation. The antiviral RNAi response is induced by viral double stranded (ds)RNA molecules that arise from replicative intermediates or secondary RNA folding structures. These structures are sensed by a host RNase type III-like enzyme called Dicer-like (DCL) protein and cleaved into short interfering (si)RNA of 21–24 nucleotides (nt) in size (Sharma et al., 2013). The siRNAs generated are unwound and only one strand, the so-called guide-strand, is uploaded into a functional protein complex termed RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC). This activated complex next surveils and subsequently degrades (viral) RNA target molecules with sequence complementarity to the guide-strand. Degradation of the target RNA is mediated by slicer, the core component of RISC, which is represented by a member of the Argonaut (AGO) family of proteins (Vaucheret, 2008; Sharma et al., 2013). After primary siRNAs have been generated, in plants an amplification of siRNAs follows, which is required to mount an RNAi response to effectively combat virus infections locally and systemically. This amplification involves host RNA dependent RNA polymerases (RDRs) that are able to convert (aberrant) viral (m)RNAs into dsRNA in a siRNA-dependent and -independent manner (Csorba et al., 2009). Their subsequent processing by DCL leads to the generation of secondary siRNAs that correspond to sequences outside the primary target sequence, a process also called transitive silencing (Sijen et al., 2001). The antiviral RNAi response acts against all RNA and DNA viruses (Incarbone and Dunoyer, 2013), but in general is a relatively slow process that does not lead to complete clearance of viral infections. For an extensive description of RNAi readers are referred to nice reviews from e.g., Ding (2010) and Sharma et al. (2013).Besides RNAi, viruses may also run into another, second layer of defense that involves resistance genes. While most of these are triggered by and confer resistance to a specific virus only, some act against several (related) viruses. The major class of these genes represent single dominant resistance genes (and of which the biggest group consists of the NB-LRR type), while others are recessive, tolerance, or partial resistance genes. A very nice example of a dominant resistance gene of the latter case has recently been described with the cloning and characterization of the Ty-1 resistance gene from tomato against Tomato yellow leaf curl geminivirus (TYLCV) This gene encodes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) and is proposed to confer resistance to TYLCV by amplifying the RNAi signal (Verlaan et al., 2013). Tomato plants containing Ty-1 do not show symptoms upon a challenge with TYLCV, but low levels of virus can still be detected.Recessive resistance (Truniger and Aranda, 2009) acting against viruses, relies on the observation that viruses require host factors (also called susceptibility factors) to enable an infection. The inability of interaction between such host factor and the virus leads to resistance. Since susceptibility factors are dominant, a resistance based on these requires all gene copies to be in the (resistant) recessive state. This explains why such resistance is generally termed recessive resistance. The majority of the recessive resistance genes known against plant viruses have been reported for potyviruses (Kang et al., 2005) and encode translation initiation factors of the 4E or 4G family (eIF4E/eIF4G) (Truniger and Aranda, 2009). The latter proteins need to interact with the cap-structure on (viral) transcripts, to allow for translation. Potyviral transcripts do not contain a cap structure, but provide a VPg (Virus-protein genome linked) to render their transcripts translatable in a cap-independent manner. Potyvirus infection leads to host shut off of cap-dependent transcripts, but only allow the cap-independent transcripts to be translated mediated by a subgroup of translation initiation factors; eIF(iso)4E/G. Viruses that encode their own cap-like structure (like potyviruses: VPg) require interaction with the translation initiation factors eIF4E/eIF4G for translation, this in turn induces a selection pressure on the host to escape the interaction between VPg and eIF4e, leading to recessive resistance. Recessive resistance genes toward other pathogens, such as fungi and bacteria have only been described to a limited extent and their encoded susceptibility factors (S genes) are proposed to provide a more durable resistance than dominant R genes. However due to their functions they may cause pleiotropic effects when knocked out from the host genome (Gawehns et al., 2013).Dominant resistanceEffector-mediated triggering of single dominant resistance genesPlant pathogens need to evade or suppress the PTI response in plants and achieve the latter by encoding effector proteins that can interfere with the recognition by PRRs, usually by binding to the substrate that PRRs would otherwise recognize. This process allows the pathogen to establish a successful infection, and is referred to as Effector Triggered Susceptibility (ETS) (Figure 1): a strategy that also applies to antiviral RNAi. One of the most common strategies plant viruses use to counteract RNAi is to encode RNA silencing suppressors (RSS), viral proteins that interfere with a specific part of the RNAi pathway and thereby reduce its effectiveness against plant viruses (Burgyan and Havelda, 2011). The majority of plant virus RSS proteins exert this activity through binding of small interfering (si)RNAs, or sometimes (also) long dsRNA, and thereby prevent their uploading into RISC and Dicer-cleavage, respectively (Lakatos et al., 2006). In recent years some RSS have also been discovered to inhibit the RNAi pathway in other ways, e.g., by binding directly to key-enzyme proteins like AGO1, the core component of RISC during the antiviral RNAi response (Zhang et al., 2006; Giner et al., 2010). Viral suppression of RNAi leads to a stage of ETS during which viruses are able to establish a successful infection.Figure 1Zig-zag-model. A visual presentation of the arms race between pathogen and host according to Jones and Dangl (2006). Here, a slightly modified version of that model is presented and as described in this review. MAMPs/PAMPs, Microbe/Pathogen associated molecular patterns; PTI, PAMP triggered immunity; ETS, Effector triggered susceptibility; ETI, Effector-triggered immunity; RB, resistance breaker.Single dominant resistance (R) gene products (in)directly sense the presence of a specific pathogen by their effector, termed avirulence factors (Avr), as a counter defense against ETS, leading to a stage called Effector-Triggered Immunity (ETI) (Figure 1). Triggering of R genes is generally associated with a (concomitant) induction of a programmed cell death response, as visualized by the rapid appearance of necrotic lesions (a hypersensitive response, HR) or in rare occasions extreme resistance (ER) during which no necrosis is observed at all. However, more and more evidence is presented, that there is an uncoupling of the resistance response from the programmed cell death response, although both can work in concert. Due to these responses, viruses (and other pathogens) are confined to the site of entry/invasion where infections are prevented. In contrast to the slower onset of antiviral RNAi, the R gene response generally is rapid and within ~3/4 days lead to containment of the virus.Dominant R genes basically can be grouped into two classes, namely those that encode NB-LRRs and all others. The major class of R genes consists of the NB-LRR type and encode proteins that, irrespective of the pathogen they recognize, consist of three domains; (1) the Nucleotide Binding Site (NBS) in the center of the protein, (2) a Leucine Rich Repeat (LRR) at the C-terminal end, and (3) a Coiled-coil (CC) or Toll and Interleukin-1 Receptor (TIR) domain at the N-terminal end of the resistance gene product (Moffett, 2009). The LRR determines the specificity of the target protein and is the most variable part of the protein, therefore considered to be under selection pressure to evolve for recognition of (new) target proteins. The NBS is composed of a conserved part that contains the Nucleotide Binding site (NB) and an ARC-domain, both required to bind and hydrolyze ATP. R genes that contain an N-terminal TIR domain are only found in dicots from the angiosperms (Collier et al., 2011), and through this domain share homology to Toll-like receptor (TLR) proteins, that act as PRRs in the innate immunity response in animal systems. Those with no predicted structure at its N-terminus, are grouped with the CC-domain (Maekawa et al., 2011a; Hao et al., 2013) in the non-TIR group. All three domains are involved in an interaction with each other and change conformationally upon activation to subsequently induce the resistance response (Lukasik and Takken, 2009; Slootweg et al., 2010).Only a few cases have been described in which the dominant R gene product recognizes an Avr protein through direct interaction (Jia et al., 2000; Deslandes et al., 2003; Dodds et al., 2006; Krasileva et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012; Cesari et al., 2013), of which one is the TMV-p50 helicase domain (Ueda et al., 2006). In the majority of known R genes recognition of the pathogen occurs indirectly and involves host proteins, which are considered guardees, decoys, or baits, depending on the model, as further discussed below (Model of R Gene Recognition) (Van Der Biezen and Jones, 1998; Jones and Dangl, 2006; Van Der Hoorn and Kamoun, 2008; Collier and Moffett, 2009).Cloned R genes and their known Avr determinantsWhile for fungi and bacteria many resistance genes have been cloned and characterized, resistance genes against plant viruses have received growing interest during the last two decades, still only few of the latter have been cloned so far. Table S1.1 gives an up-to-date summary of all R genes against plant viruses, known or currently under investigation. For some of these genes the viral Avr determinant has been identified. From this large, extensive list of R genes (>200), only 22 have been cloned and characterized. Some R genes have functional alleles in other plant species, often showing a similar Avr recognition. The majority of the known R gene products are of the CC-NB-LRR type, whereas only a small group belongs to the TIR-NB-LRR group (Table 1).Table 1Cloned dominant resistance genes against plant viruses,
