retrieved_papers.title: Turnip mosaic virus alters phosphorus metabolism and shoot-root allocation without resource competition.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Plant viruses affect production through symptom induction in host plants. These symptoms could partially arise from nutrient deprivation: The resource competition hypothesis posits that massive viral replication deprives hosts of essential nutrients, yet direct evidence for phosphorus (P) competition is lacking. Moreover, it is reported that biotic stresses can lead to alterations on P metabolism. Using a hydroponic system enabling separate analysis of shoots and roots in adult Arabidopsis thaliana plants, we investigated whether Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) drawed significant P internal pools leading to P competition or altered P metabolism. TuMV genomic RNA represented < 0.3% of the P pool allocated to 18S rRNA, refuting the resource competition hypothesis. Instead, TuMV induced a marked shoot-to-root P redistribution: Shoot/Root Pi and Porg changed from 1.7 to 1.04 to 0.71 and 0.68, respectively. This altered partitioning correlated with organ-specific gene expression changes: high-affinity transporters PHT1; 4 and PHT1; 5 were co-induced in shoots, whereas immunity-related PHT1; 4 was uniquely repressed in roots. The senescence-associated gene SEN1 showed opposite regulation between organs (repressed in shoots, induced in roots), distinguishing virus-induced responses from canonical senescence. Multivariate analysis revealed that shoots and roots only partially share physiological and molecular responses to TuMV. The virus reprograms phosphorus metabolism through organ-specific changes, not through resource depletion, and roots act as a distinct hub integrating infection response, senescence, and nutrient dynamics. This study advances the understanding of growth-defense trade-offs in plant mineral nutrition and identifies new targets for maintaining crop productivity under biotic stress.

retrieved_papers.title: Evolution of virulence of a plant RNA virus in developmental stage-structured host populations.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Natural host populations are age-structured, and developmental stages differ in susceptibility and within-host pathogen dynamics, potentially imposing distinct selective pressures on viruses. However, the evolutionary consequences of host age structure remain poorly understood. We experimentally evolved turnip mosaic potyvirus for 5 passages in Arabidopsis thaliana populations spanning 7 demographic regimes, from juvenile- to mature-dominated cohorts. We quantified disease progression, symptom severity, and viral load, cross-inoculated evolved lineages across host stages to construct infection matrices, and performed whole-population sequencing at passages 1 and 5. Disease traits changed markedly with passage, demography, and their interaction. Disease progression evolved faster in older populations, whereas symptom severity was independent of median age, indicating demographic reweighting of virulence components. Viral load increased across passages and positively correlated with severity, linking within-host fitness to symptoms. Cross-inoculation assays revealed a modular infection network: juvenile-evolved lineages specialized on juvenile hosts, whereas lineages from intermediate and older populations were more generalist. Genomically, we detected both parallel and demography-specific adaptations, including recurrent changes in the viral protein VPg (involved in translation, replication, and host interactions) as well as synonymous variants showing consistent or opposing selection across host population stage structures. Overall, host age structure emerges as a major ecological driver of virulence evolution, shaping tradeoffs between disease progression and severity and determining specialization versus generalism. These results integrate phenotypic and genomic responses and suggest that manipulating crop age structure could steer virus evolution toward less damaging outcomes.

retrieved_papers.title: A viral infection reshapes Arabidopsis water management via root hydraulics, aquaporin downregulation and osmotic adjustment.
retrieved_papers.abstract: The effect of plant viruses on root water relations and root-shoot coordination remains insufficiently characterized. Using a hydroponic Arabidopsis thaliana-Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) pathosystem, we integrated biometric, anatomical, hydraulic, and gas-exchange measurements to dissect how viral infection reshapes root-shoot water relations. TuMV infection did not merely impose a generalized shutdown of plant growth but triggered a complex physiological reprogramming of water relations. The infection impaired root development, evidenced by an early plateau in primary root elongation. Functionally, infected plants exhibited a decrease in root hydraulic conductance per unit root mass, accompanied by transcriptional downregulation of root aquaporin genes. However, the relative contribution of aquaporin-mediated water transport, assessed via sodium azide inhibition, remained unchanged, indicating that the virus downregulates total hydraulic capacity without altering the apoplastic-symplastic partitioning of water flow. Gas-exchange analysis revealed a virus-induced decoupling between stomatal conductance and net CO2 assimilation, resulting in a non-adaptive increase in intrinsic water-use efficiency. This loss of photosynthetic plasticity, combined with shoot-localized osmotic adjustment (more negative leaf osmotic potential and higher relative water content), points to a constrained, suboptimal physiological state. Multivariate analysis confirmed that variation in physiological traits largely drives phenotypic divergence between treatments. Together, these coordinated alterations-reduced root hydraulics to match a stunted shoot and rigid gas-exchange relationships-are consistent with plants locked into a low-performance equilibrium, poorly equipped to compete for water and carbon. This work reveals a systemic hydraulic-photosynthetic reconfiguration that may account for compromises in plant resilience and resource competitiveness.

retrieved_papers.title: Contrasting Effects of Tagging Turnip Mosaic Virus Proteins.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Potyvirus rapae (turnip mosaic virus, TuMV) is widely used as a model system in plant-virus interaction studies. The TuMV RNA genome encodes 11 proteins, some of which remain poorly characterized, while the functions of others are well defined. Studying individual proteins in isolation may not recapitulate native expression levels, subcellular localization, and interaction with host factors during virus replication and movement. An alternative approach is to tag individual viral proteins in the context of an infectious clone. Epitope tags may alter protein functions and affect viral replication, movement, or a combination of essential steps, thus leading to changes in pathogenicity. Because they have central roles in viral infection, here we measured the effect of individually tagging the helper component proteinase (HC-Pro) and nuclear inclusion protein b (NIb) with a 6His-3xFLAG tag. Epitope tags were placed at the N-terminus of HC-Pro and the N- and C-termini of NIb within a TuMV infectious clone carrying coding sequences for the green fluorescent protein (TuMV-GFP). Constructs carrying a tagged HC-Pro displayed pathogenicity similar to that observed for TuMV-GFP in Nicotiana benthamiana and Arabidopsis thaliana plants. In contrast, infectivity of NIb-tagged clones became temperature sensitive and, even at the permissive temperature, showed reduced pathogenicity compared to TuMV-GFP. Providing a silencing suppressor in trans did not restore infection efficiency, suggesting reduced viral fitness due to structural or functional disruption caused by the epitope tags. Structural models generated using AlphaFold2 showed no effect of the tag on HC-Pro. In contrast, structural models illustrated tag interference with the NIb catalytic site. AlphaFold2 was further used to predict the structural impact of several tags on NIb and to predict the effect of a 6HIS-3xFlag tag on all other TuMV proteins. This study provides a broadly applicable framework for selecting suitable epitope tags to mark viral proteins and maintain function in the context of virus infection.

retrieved_papers.title: Turnip mosaic virus utilizes the lipid droplet biogenesis machinery to facilitate its propagation in plants.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Lipid droplets (LDs), which are dedicated to storing neutral lipids (NLs), are dynamic organelles involved in numerous other functions, including membrane remodeling during abiotic stress. While the hijacking of LDs by animal viruses is well documented, their role(s) in plant virus infection remains largely unexplored. Similar to animal viruses, plant potyviruses reroute host proteins, intracellular membranes, and lipids to create an optimized microenvironment for their efficient viral replication compartment (VRC) assembly and movement. We therefore investigated whether potyviruses can also exploit the LD biogenesis machinery for their own benefit, akin to some animal viruses. Utilizing lipid analyses, confocal and transmission electron microscopy, and viral propagation surveys in plants impaired in LD biogenesis, we show that potyvirus turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) infection induces a significant accumulation of NLs and a proliferation of LDs in Nicotiana benthamiana or Arabidopsis thaliana-infected leaves, which are often located in close proximity to VRCs. This suggests that there is a spatial and functional relationship between LDs and TuMV. We demonstrate also that two protein families crucial for LD biogenesis, namely the lipid droplet-associated proteins and SEIPINs, facilitate TuMV propagation in Arabidopsis thaliana. Taken together, our results indicate a pro-viral function for LDs in potyvirus-infected plants.

retrieved_papers.title: Specific and efficient translation inhibition–transcription activation resistance module against viruses in plants
retrieved_papers.abstract: Positive-sense RNA viruses using subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs) cause severe crop losses, yet this conserved feature has rarely been exploited for antiviral engineering. Here, we constructed a virus-activated synthetic immune circuit, wherein viral sgRNA production drives host defense responses via a translation inhibition–transcription activation (TI-TA) module. An optimized translational repression element (dsBC) minimized basal expression while enabling virus-specific activation of resistance-inducing proteins (RIPs) by cognate viral sgRNA promoters. This circuit functioned against three major sgRNA-producing viruses—pepino mosaic virus (PepMV), tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), and cucumber mosaic virus (CMV)—in Nicotiana benthamiana, tomato, and Arabidopsis thaliana, with cross-resistance to related viruses. RIP expression was strictly triggered by viral infection, conferring robust resistance without detectable growth penalties. This programmable strategy provides a versatile platform for engineering resistance against diverse sgRNA-producing RNA viruses and offers a conceptual framework for developing synthetic antiviral immunity in plants.
retrieved_papers.full_text: INTRODUCTIONDuring the long-term coevolution of plants and pathogens, plants have developed two major layers of innate immunity: pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) and effector-triggered immunity (ETI) (1, 2). PTI is triggered by plasma membrane–localized pattern recognition receptors, which perceive conserved microbial patterns, including flagellin, elongation factor Tu, peptidoglycan, chitin, and lipopolysaccharides, thereby conferring basal immunity against a broad spectrum of nonadapted pathogens (3, 4). In contrast, ETI represents a more robust and specific immune response mediated by resistance (R) proteins. Most proteins belong to the family of nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors (NLRs), which recognize pathogen effectors and initiate potent defense responses, typically accompanied by a hypersensitive response (HR) to restrict pathogen proliferation (5, 6). Recent studies have revealed that PTI and ETI function interdependently rather than independently, resulting in largely overlapping and integrated immune responses (7, 8). NLR-mediated plant immunity induces HR, which serves as an effective defense against viral infections. However, only a small number of viral proteins can be recognized by limited NLRs to initiate ETI signaling (9). Several exogenous proteins, including BAX, INF1, and NLPPya are capable of rapidly inducing plant HR through PTI/ETI-dependent or independent pathways. As a mammalian Bcl-2 family protein, BAX localizes to mitochondria and triggers cell death upon heterologous expression in plants, followed by the up-regulation of defense-related genes and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation (10, 11). INF1, a 10-kDa extracellular elicitor widely distributed across Phytophthora species, induces HR in a restricted number of plants, particularly in the genus Nicotiana. INF1-triggered immune responses include PTI activation, ROS burst, and elevated expression of ethylene (ET)– and jasmonic acid (JA)–responsive genes (12–16). NLPPya derived from the phytopathogenic oomycete Pythium aphanidermatum, triggers leaf necrosis in diverse plant species. It functions by forming transient small pores on lipid membranes, leading to plasma membrane destruction, cytolysis, and the activation of plant defense–related genes. This cellular damage–triggered immune activation is analogous to inflammasome activation in vertebrates (17, 18). Whether resistance-inducing proteins (RIPs) from different biological sources, such as INF1, BAX, and NLPPya can be harnessed to combat viral infections remains an intriguing scientific question.Positive-sense single-stranded RNA (+ssRNA) viruses constitute the vast majority of plant viruses and impose severe threats to global crop production. A large proportion of these viruses, encompassing over 1000 characterized plant +ssRNA viral species, use subgenomic RNAs (sgRNAs) promoters to generate sgRNAs for the expression of internal and 3′-proximal open reading frames (ORFs) (19, 20). The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) of +ssRNA viruses recognizes the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) of the viral genome and synthesizes a complementary negative-strand viral RNA genome. Subsequently, RdRP recognizes specific internal subgenomic promoters (SPs) on the negative-strand RNA template to initiate the synthesis of truncated positive-strand RNA transcripts, termed sgRNAs. Through sgRNA biogenesis, viruses efficiently orchestrate viral gene expression and ensure the timely synthesis of structural and nonstructural proteins during infection, thereby expanding their genomic coding capacity (21). Most economically destructive plant viruses fall into this category, including tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), cucumber mosaic virus (CMV), brome mosaic virus (BMV), and potato virus X (PVX) (22). Additionally, multiple emerging crop-damaging viruses, such as pepino mosaic virus (PepMV), tomato brown rugose fruit virus (ToBRFV), cucumber green mottle mosaic virus (CGMMV), and maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV), also use the sgRNA-dependent gene expression strategy (20, 23). Due to the intrinsically high mutation rates of +ssRNA viruses, which primarily result from the lack of proofreading activity in viral RdRP (24, 25), viral populations exist as dynamic quasispecies capable of rapid adaptation to diverse selective pressures. This potent evolutionary plasticity allows viruses to evade NLR-mediated host resistance. For example, resistance-breaking strains have been documented to overcome host resistance conferred by tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) and ToBRFV resistance genes (26, 27). Recent advances in plant immune engineering have facilitated the optimization of NLR-mediated resistance through multiple strategies, including random mutagenesis, structure-guided receptor engineering, integrated decoy engineering, and effector-mediated derepression of autoactive NLRs (28, 29). Despite these advances, durable and broadly applicable resistance approaches specifically targeting sgRNA-producing RNA viruses remain largely undeveloped.Plants maintain a dynamic balance between growth and immunity to optimize environmental adaptation. Robust immune responses strengthen disease resistance but frequently penalize plant growth and yield, a trade-off universally recognized as the “growth-defense trade-off” (30). Fortunately, multiple strategies have been developed to boost plant immunity without incurring substantial fitness costs (31). A typical paradigm is the “TBF1-cassette,” which exploits pathogen-responsive translational regulation mediated by upstream open reading frames (uORFs) within the 5′ leader sequence of the TBF1 (TL1-binding transcription factor 1). TBF1 acts as a core transcription factor that regulates the transition from growth to defense upon immune activation. Although its translation is constitutively repressed by two conserved uORFs under normal conditions, it is rapidly activated in response to pathogen challenge, ensuring the timely accumulation of defense regulators. Engineering this regulatory module to control the expression of immune genes, such as NPR1, confers broad-spectrum disease resistance without compromising plant growth (32). Further studies have revealed that uORF-dependent translational regulation is tightly associated with RNA secondary structures. Specifically, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) hairpin structures immediately downstream of the upstream AUG codons (uAUGs) of uORF, termed uAUG-ds, are critical for selective translation initiation. These structural motifs facilitate ribosome recognition of uAUGs, thereby promoting uORFs translation and repressing the translation of downstream main ORF under normal growth conditions. Upon immune activation, RNA helicases unwind these dsRNA structures, enabling ribosomes to bypass uAUGs and initiate translation of defense-related proteins. Notably, uAUG-ds serves as a functional structural partner of uORFs rather than being functionally equivalent to uORFs. While uAUGs define the start codon of uORFs, the downstream dsRNA structures modulate translational efficiency, and, together, they constitute a dynamic regulatory module that fine-tunes protein abundance (33). Previous studies have reported advanced pathogen-responsive resistance strategies. Mei et al. exploited uAUG-mediated translational regulation to modulate the expression of plant immune genes, successfully enhancing resistance against fungal, bacterial, and DNA viral pathogens with negligible fitness penalties (34). Liu’s group used the pathogen-responsive TBF1 promoter coupled with its endogenous uORFs to drive MCD1 expression in Nicotiana benthamiana, achieving broad-spectrum resistance against cross-kingdom pathogens without affecting normal plant growth (35). Engineered NLRs or elicitor peptides also confer potent resistance to potyviruses without growth penalties by activating postinfection defense responses (29, 36). Nevertheless, efficient virus-responsive resistance systems specifically tailored for sgRNA-producing RNA viruses remain largely underexplored to date.In this study, we developed a dual-layer translation inhibition–transcription activation (TI-TA) strategy for engineering resistance against sgRNA-producing +ssRNA viruses. This design is built upon two core biological principles. First, uAUG-ds elements robustly repress downstream protein translation under normal growth conditions, thereby minimizing constitutive expression-driven growth penalties typically induced by RIPs. Second, sgRNA-producing viruses specifically activate viral subgenomic promoters during infection, providing a virus-dependent transcriptional activation (TA) signal. Based on these two principles, we used uAUG-ds elements as translational inhibition (TI) modules to repress RIP expression in the absence of viral infection, while viral subgenomic promoters were used as TA modules to drive RIP expression specifically upon viral infection. For systematic evaluation, uAUG-ds motifs derived from the 5′ UTRs of TUB7 and TBF1 were designated as dsA and dsB, respectively, and a synthetic 54–nucleotide (nt) class I uAUG-ds element was named dsC and generated the enhanced translational repression module dsBC. Using this TI-TA framework, we demonstrated that the combination of dsBC with viral subgenomic promoter modules confers potent basal repression and robust virus-responsive expression. Substituting green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporters with RIP effectors (e.g., BAX) conferred effective resistance against PepMV in N. benthamiana and tomato. Furthermore, the strategy exhibits partial broad applicability toward diverse sgRNA-producing viruses, including TMV and CMV, with protective efficacy extending to other closely related viruses within the corresponding genera. Collectively, this synthetic system integrates three advantageous features: (i) potent basal translational repression, (ii) strict virus-specific activation, and (iii) partial broad-spectrum antiviral activity without detectable growth penalty. Our work therefore establishes a programmable framework for engineering durable resistance against sgRNA-producing plant RNA viruses.RESULTSStepwise optimization of TI and TA modules yields a PepMV-responsive expression systemGiven the persistent and severe threat to crop production posed by +ssRNA viruses that produce sgRNAs, we sought to develop a virus-responsive system capable of specifically activating the expression of RIPs upon viral infection. To achieve this goal, two requirements needed to be fulfilled: (i) RIP expression should remain strongly suppressed in the absence of viral infection through TI; and (ii) RIP expression should be specifically activated upon viral infection through TA. To establish an efficient TI module, we evaluated several uAUG-ds elements. The 5′ UTRs of TUB7 and TBF1 contain naturally occurring uAUG-ds elements, designated dsA (144 nt) and dsB (105 nt), respectively, whereas a 54-nt class I uAUG-ds element was designated dsC (33). The PepMV coat protein (CP) subgenomic promoter (PepMVSP1) was selected as the initial TA module (Fig. 1A). To assess the translational inhibitory activities of these elements, GFP was inserted between PepMVSP1 and the 3′ UTR to generate PepMVSP1-GFP (Fig. 1B). Individual or tandem uAUG-ds elements were subsequently fused to the 5′ end of PepMVSP1-GFP, generating dsA-, dsB-, dsC-, dsAC-, dsBC-, and ds2C-PepMVSP1-GFP constructs (Fig. 1B). Transient expression assays in N. benthamiana revealed that tandem uAUG-ds elements (dsAC, dsBC, and ds2C) conferred substantially stronger translational repression than individual elements, as evidenced by reduced GFP fluorescence and protein accumulation (Fig. 1, C and D). Among them, dsBC exhibited the strongest inhibitory effect on GFP protein accumulation (Fig. 1, C and D). Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis showed that dsBC did not substantially affect GFP transcript abundance (Fig. 1E), indicating that its inhibitory effect primarily occurred at the translational level. In addition, independent verification assays confirmed that uAUG-ds elements, in the absence of PepMVSP1, could significantly reduce GFP protein accumulation without altering mRNA levels, solidifying the translational inhibitory function of uAUG-ds modules (fig. S1). Collectively, dsBC was selected as the optimal TI element for subsequent system construction due to its strong and specific translational repression activity.Fig. 1.PepMV strongly restores GFP expression in the dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP system.(A) Schematic of the PepMV genome. TGB1–3, triple gene block proteins; CP, coat protein. (B) Schematic of uAUG-ds, PepMVSP1, and GFP constructs. The uAUG-ds elements include 144-nt dsA from the TUB7 5′ UTR, 105-nt dsB from the TBF1 5′ UTR, and a 54-nt class I element dsC (33). Tandem fusion of these elements with dsC produced dsAC, dsBC, and ds2C. Blue line indicates PepMVSP1 and 3′ UTR; pink box indicates the first 36 nt of the CP N terminus. (C to E) GFP fluorescence, protein accumulation, and mRNA levels in N. benthamiana leaves infiltrated with Agrobacterium (OD600 = 0.5) carrying GFP, PepMVSP1-GFP, or uAUG-ds-PepMVSP1-GFP constructs. EV served as the negative control. Fluorescence was observed at 2 dpi under UV light, GFP accumulation was detected by Western blot using anti-GFP and anti-actin antibodies, and GFP mRNA levels were analyzed by qRT-PCR. To date, several antiviral engineering strategies have been developed, including dominant resistance (R) genes, pathogen-derived resistance (PDR), RNA interference (RNAi), CRISPR-Cas–based genome editing, host susceptibility factor engineering, and immune signaling enhancement. Among these approaches, NLR-mediated resistance can provide strong protection against viral infection (9); however, resistance-breaking viral variants frequently emerge and compromise its durability (27, 43, 46, 47). Classical PDR and cross-protection approaches exhibit favorable biosafety and practical applicability but suffer from narrow antiviral spectra and potential risks of viral recombination and virulence reversion under field conditions (48, 49). RNAi-based strategies enable flexible and sequence-specific viral suppression; however, their efficacy can be compromised by viral sequence variation and diverse viral suppressors of RNA silencing that antagonize host silencing pathways (50, 51). CRISPR-Cas systems provide high-precision and multiplex editing for viral and host target modification, yet mutations within gRNA target sites frequently generate viral escape variants, and constitutive Cas expression may raise biosafety and regulatory concerns (52–54). Engineering host susceptibility factors, such as eIF4E family proteins, can confer durable resistance against specific groups of viruses, but their effectiveness is often limited to particular virus taxa (55–58). Likewise, manipulation of host proteins involved in virus infection through overexpression or knockout can enhance antiviral resistance, although such modifications rarely provide complete immunity (59). In addition, constitutive activation of immune pathways can confer broad-spectrum disease resistance but often results in notable growth penalties because of the well-known growth-defense trade-off (60, 61). To address these limitations, pathogen-responsive resistance systems that activate defense responses only upon pathogen infection have attracted increasing attention. Recent studies have demonstrated that translational regulation mediated by uORFs can effectively control the expression of immune-related genes and enhance resistance against fungal, bacterial, and DNA viral pathogens without obvious fitness costs (34, 35). Likewise, engineered NLRs and inducible elicitor peptide systems can provide strong resistance to potyviruses while minimizing growth penalties by activating defense responses only after infection (29, 36). These findings collectively highlight the potential of pathogen-responsive defense systems to overcome the limitations associated with constitutive resistance. Nevertheless, virus-responsive antiviral systems specifically designed for +ssRNA viruses that produce sgRNAs remain limited.Compared with existing approaches, the virus-responsive RIP system developed in this study has several notable advantages (Fig. 6). First, antiviral activity is activated only after viral infection, thereby minimizing developmental abnormalities under normal growth conditions. Second, unlike RNAi and CRISPR-based technologies that directly target viral nucleotide sequences, our strategy exploits the conserved process of viral sgRNA synthesis to activate defense responses, potentially reducing the likelihood of resistance breakdown caused by single mutational events. Third, because sgRNA production is a common feature among many +ssRNA viruses, this platform may have broader applicability than virus-specific resistance mechanisms. Additional specificity assays demonstrated that the TI-TA system was not activated by unrelated viruses, bacterial or fungal pathogens, or abiotic stresses including heat and drought (figs. S8 and S9), indicating that viral mini-replicon recognition is highly specific and that the TI-TA system is unlikely to be ectopically activated by nontarget biotic or abiotic stimuli. Such stringent specificity minimizes the risk of unintended HR activation and enhances the biosafety and practical potential of this strategy for agricultural applications. However, several limitations should also be acknowledged. Differences in the abundance, timing, and regulatory mechanisms of sgRNA accumulation among viruses may substantially influence the activation efficiency of the TI-TA system. In addition, plant species may differ in their sensitivity to RIP-induced immune responses, which could further affect system performance. Moreover, all experiments in the present study were conducted under controlled greenhouse conditions using laboratory-maintained viral isolates. Therefore, the stability, durability, and practical performance of the TI-TA system under field conditions remain to be evaluated. In agricultural environments, fluctuating temperatures, mixed infections involving multiple pathogens, and genetically diverse viral populations may influence viral replication dynamics, sgRNA production, and consequently the activation efficiency of the TI-TA circuit. Field trials using diverse viral isolates and representative environmental conditions will therefore be essential to assess the robustness and long-term effectiveness of this strategy. Another limitation is that the current study used constitutive transgenic expression of TI-TA components, which facilitated proof-of-concept validation but may not fully satisfy future regulatory requirements for commercial crop deployment. Future optimization could explore tissue-specific or infection-responsive promoters to restrict transgene expression to relevant tissues or infection sites, as well as minimized expression cassettes to simplify genetic constructs and improve biosafety and regulatory compatibility. The current TI-TA system is designed to target a specific virus or closely related viruses within the same genus. Therefore, achieving resistance against multiple unrelated viruses will likely require stacking several TI-TA modules using strategies such as tRNA- or ribozyme-mediated polycistronic expression. Although the system conferred effective immunity resistance against CMV, it did not provide complete protection against PepMV or TMV. Accordingly, further efforts are required to improve the virus-responsive activation efficiency of TI-TA upon viral challenge. Artificial intelligence–assisted screening can be adopted to identify more efficient RIPs that can potently trigger immune responses across diverse plant species. Furthermore, combining the TI-TA platform with complementary antiviral strategies, including host susceptibility factor engineering, RNAi, and CRISPR-Cas–based technologies, may provide broader-spectrum and more durable resistance against emerging plant viruses.Fig. 6.Schematic working model of the TI-TA synthetic immune module conferring plant resistance to viral infection.Our innovative system integrates three key components that combine uAUG-ds as TI, Virusmini as virus-activated transcription (TA), and RIPs to create a targeted defense that only activates upon infection. This interspecific difference might be attributed to a combination of intrinsic host-specific biological characteristics and virus-dependent variations in the activation efficiency of the TI-TA system. On one hand, interspecific variations in cell death signaling pathways, translational regulatory mechanisms, and immune response networks lead to divergent host sensitivity to BAX-induced cytotoxicity. On the other hand, the accumulation level of BAX effector protein is governed by the activation efficiency of the TA module triggered by different viral infections. Transient expression assays verified that CMV infection increased GFP transcript accumulation by ∼336%, while PepMV and TMV resulted in only 13 and 47% increases in transcript accumulation, respectively, demonstrating that CMV activates the TI-TA system far more efficiently than PepMV and TMV under the tested conditions (Figs. 4D, 1I, and 3D). Accordingly, CMV-infected A. thaliana accumulates higher levels of BAX than PepMV-infected N. benthamiana, which might be a key factor contributing to the more intense phenotypic responses in A. thaliana. The differential activation efficiency among the three viral systems may result from multiple virus-specific factors. One possibility is that differences in mini-replicon architecture, including viral UTRs, sgRNA promoter sequences, and regulatory elements required for replication complex assembly, affect the efficiency of viral activation. In addition, the ability of viral RdRps to recognize and use heterologous mini-replicons may vary among viruses, leading to differences in sgRNA production and subsequent TI-TA activation. Furthermore, virus-host compatibility and replication dynamics in different plant species may influence the abundance and timing of viral signals available for system activation. Therefore, the stronger resistance observed in the CMV system likely reflects more efficient activation of the corresponding mini-replicon rather than an inherent superiority of the TI-TA framework. Future optimization of viral regulatory elements and host-virus combinations may further enhance the performance of PepMV- and TMV-based TI-TA systems.Beyond interspecific response differences, the cross-species transferability of this TI-TA experimental platform is another critical issue worthy of discussion. Mechanistically, the platform consists of three core components: the TI module, the TA module, and the RIPs, which differ greatly in their cross-species adaptability. The TI module is based on uAUG-ds element, a mechanism that is expected to function broadly across plant species because it relies on conserved translational machinery (33). The TA module depends on viral RdRP activity and therefore should be functional in any compatible host-virus interaction (21). In contrast, the RIPs are the primary limiting factor for cross-species application. All RIPs tested in this study were only validated in dicot plants, and their functional activity in monocot crops remains uncharacterized. Meanwhile, our INF1-related experiments further confirmed the host specificity of effector proteins. In transient expression assays, CMV infection efficiently activated CMVminiRNA3-INF1 and triggered a typical HR in N. benthamiana (Fig. 4F); however, transgenic A. thaliana stably expressing CMVminiRNA3-INF1 showed no enhanced CMV resistance compared with the WT Col-0 (Fig. 4H), indicating that the ability of effectors to activate plant defense responses is highly host-dependent. Therefore, the cross-species deployment of this platform requires targeted screening and optimization of effector proteins to ensure stable biological activity in target host species. Notably, different RIPs also exhibit inconsistent antiviral efficacy even within dicot hosts. For instance, transgenic lines expressing INF1 displayed relatively weak resistance to PepMV, which was consistent with the finding that PepMV infection failed to significantly increase PR1 expression in INF1 transgenic plants (Fig. 2, D and G). An important limitation of the current study is that RIP protein accumulation could not be directly quantified after viral infection. Because specific antibodies or epitope-tagged versions of RIP proteins were unavailable in the current experimental system, we cannot exclude the possibility that the observed differences among RIPs result from variation in protein abundance, intrinsic effector activity, or downstream immune activation efficiency. Therefore, the relative contribution of these factors to RIP-mediated antiviral resistance remains unresolved. Future studies incorporating fluorescent protein fusions, optimized epitope-tagging strategies, or RIP-specific antibodies will enable direct monitoring of RIP accumulation and provide mechanistic insights into the differential performance of RIP effectors.The cross-protection spectrum of the TI-TA system is influenced by the evolutionary relatedness between the target virus and the virus-derived mini-replicon. Although TI-TA transgenic plants exhibited cross-resistance against related viruses, the extent of protection varied among virus pairs (Fig. 5). To explore the potential determinants of this variation, we compared the sequence homology of subgenomic promoters from three virus pairs: TMV/ToBRFV (69.08%), CMV-Fny/CMV-Q (65.3%), and PepMV/PVX (32.99%) (fig. S15, A to C). The relatively high promoter similarity between TMV and ToBRFV, as well as between CMV-Fny and CMV-Q, may increase the likelihood that viral replicases recognize heterologous mini-replicons. Although PepMV and PVX share relatively low promoter homology, conserved sequence elements required for potexvirus replication and sgRNA synthesis may still enable PVX RdRp to recognize the PepMV-derived mini-replicon (fig. S15D) (62, 63). Consistent with the activation efficiencies observed in Figs. 1I, 3D, and 4D, we speculate that related viruses differ in their ability to activate heterologous mini-replicons. CMV-Q most efficiently activated CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-RIPs, whereas PVX showed the weakest activation of dsBC-PepMVmini-RIPs, which may explain why CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-RIPs conferred nearly complete immunity against CMV-Q, while dsBC-TMVmini-RIPs and dsBC-PepMVmini-RIPs provided only partial resistance to ToBRFV and PVX, respectively (Fig. 5). Although the binding affinity of viral RdRps to noncognate mini-replicons was not examined in this study, it may contribute to differences in mini-replicon activation. Furthermore, variation in RIP expression levels following heterologous mini-replicon activation may further influence the final cross-resistance outcome.In addition to demonstrating the antiviral efficacy of the TI-TA system, our results also uncovered several unexpected RNA-level phenomena related to transcript stability, translational regulation, and construct architecture, which warrant further investigation. We found that PepMVmini (Fig. 1I), TMVmini (Fig. 3D), and CMVminiRNA3 (Fig. 4D) all markedly reduced GFP mRNA accumulation. In plants, RNA quality control is mediated by nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), no-stop decay (NSD), and no-go decay (NGD), with XRN4 serving as a key component of the 5′ → 3′ RNA decay pathway (64, 65). Using TRV-VIGS (66, 67), we showed that silencing NbXRN4 increased GFP mRNA levels in dsBC-PepMVmini-GFP, dsBC-TMVmini-GFP, and CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-GFP (fig. S16), indicating that XRN4-dependent RNA degradation contributes to the reduced transcript abundance of Virusmini-based constructs. NMD is known to target viral RNAs containing premature termination codons (PTCs), including those of PVX, TCV, and CGMMV (68–71). For example, PVX RNAs carrying extended 3′ UTRs are degraded through NMD (72), whereas the PEMV2 P26 protein counteracts NMD to protect viral RNAs (73). Moreover, m6A modification promotes NMD-mediated degradation of PepMV RNA (74). Because Virusmini constructs contain PTCs, it is plausible that they are recognized by the NMD machinery, thereby contributing to the reduced accumulation of GFP mRNA. Here, we also found that dsA, dsB, and dsC effectively suppressed GFP protein accumulation without reducing GFP transcript levels, suggesting that these elements primarily act through translational repression. However, tandem fusion of dsA/B/C with dsC did not further enhance TI (fig. S1). In the presence of the PepMV subgenomic promoter PepMVSP1, fusion of dsA/B/C with dsC resulted in an additional reduction in GFP protein accumulation, possibly due to the presence of a termination codon or specific RNA structural features associated with PepMVSP1. These observations suggest that combining uAUG-ds elements with viral regulatory sequences may provide a practical strategy for fine-tuning the expression of highly toxic proteins to biologically tolerable levels. In addition, unlike dsB and dsC, dsA not only inhibited GFP translation but also significantly increased GFP mRNA accumulation (Fig. 1E and fig. S1D), implying the existence of an as-yet-unknown mechanism linking dsA to transcript regulation. Another unexpected observation was that dsBC-TMVmini-INF1 lost its ability to suppress INF1 expression and triggered HR in the absence of viral infection (Fig. 3G). This leakage phenotype was eliminated in dsBC-TMVmini-INF1-2A-GFP but not in dsBC-TMVmini-GFP-2A-INF1 (Fig. 3H), suggesting that the INF1 coding sequence together with the TMVmini 3′ UTR may form a specific RNA structure that interferes with dsBC-mediated translational repression. Insertion of GFP between INF1 and the 3′ UTR may disrupt this putative structure and restore repression. Although this hypothesis requires further experimental validation, it highlights the importance of local RNA structural context in determining TI-TA performance. In addition, our results indicate that the optimal positioning of dsBC may vary among different viral mini-replicons. Unlike PepMVmini and TMVmini, in which placement of dsBC at the 5′ terminus enabled efficient virus-responsive activation, CMVminiRNA3 required internal insertion of dsBC to achieve functionality (figs. S12, B to D, and S4, B to D). Therefore, the current design principles should be considered empirical guidelines rather than fully predictive rules, as they were derived from a limited number of viral mini-replicon configurations tested in this study. The requirement for internal dsBC placement in CMVminiRNA3 highlights the current limitation that the optimal architecture for a different virus cannot yet be reliably predicted solely from viral sequence information or known regulatory elements. Specifically, 5′-terminal dsBC insertion represents a useful initial design strategy because of its successful performance in two independent viral backbones, whereas internal dsBC insertion provides an alternative configuration when 5′-terminal placement compromises mini-replicon activity or virus-responsive expression. Establishing more generalizable and predictive design principles will require systematic evaluation of diverse viral mini-replicons combined with computational analyses of RNA sequence features, secondary structures, and potential interactions between dsBC elements and viral regulatory regions. Such integrative approaches may ultimately enable rational optimization of TI-TA architectures for newly emerging viral pathogens without extensive empirical screening.In this study, we combined distinct uAUG-ds repressor elements with the viral PepMVSP1 promoter to achieve tunable, gradient attenuation of target protein expression, a tool that facilitates functional characterization of cytotoxic or growth-suppressive proteins in planta. This work innovatively fuses the dsBC translational repression module with viral mini-replicons to assemble the TI-TA synthetic immune circuit, which drives strict virus-specific activation of RIP effector expression exclusively during viral infection (Fig. 6). The dsBC-PepMVmini-BAX construct confers robust PepMV resistance in transgenic N. benthamiana and tomato lines. Separately, dsBC-TMVmini-INF1-2A-GFP and dsBC-TMVmini-NLPPya grant TMV resistance in stably transformed N. benthamiana. CMVminiRNA3-dsBC-NLPPya delivers near-complete immunity against systemic CMV infection. Furthermore, the TI-TA architecture mediates partial cross-resistance against phylogenetically related viruses within the same genus. Collectively, this programmable synthetic immune strategy provides a conceptual framework for engineering resistance against sgRNA-producing +ssRNA viruses and establishes a foundation for future optimization toward agricultural applications. Beyond agricultural deployment, this experimental framework also provides a tractable system to dissect how growth-regulatory cytotoxic proteins modulate +ssRNA virus infection dynamics in plant hosts. Last, the core TI-TA design logic offers conceptual reference and design inspiration for developing RNA-targeted synthetic immunotherapies against animal RNA viral pathogens.MATERIALS AND METHODSPlant growth conditions and plant materialsThe WT and transgenic N. benthamiana plants were grown in a climate chamber with a 15-hour daylight and 9-hour dark photoperiod at 23° to 25°C as described previously (75).
