TITLE:
Cloning of the mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) receptor: expression in human and hamster cell lines confers susceptibility to MHV.

ABSTRACT:
The cellular receptor for murine coronavirus mouse hepatitis virus (MHV)-A59 is a member of the carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) family of glycoproteins in the immunoglobulin superfamily. We isolated a cDNA clone (MHVR1) encoding the MHV receptor. The sequence of this clone predicts a 424-amino-acid glycoprotein with four immunoglobulinlike domains, a transmembrane domain, and a short intracytoplasmic tail, MHVR1 is closely related to the murine CEA-related clone mmCGM1 (Mus musculus carcinoembryonic antigen gene family member). Western blot (immunoblot) analysis performed with antireceptor antibodies detected a glycoprotein of 120 kDa in BHK cells stably transfected with MHVR1. This corresponds to the size of the MHV receptor expressed in mouse intestine and liver. Human and hamster fibroblasts transfected with MHVR1 became susceptible to infection with MHV-A59. Like MHV-susceptible mouse fibroblasts, the MHVR1-transfected human and hamster cells were protected from MHV infection by pretreatment with monoclonal antireceptor antibody CC1. Thus, the 110- to 120-kDa CEA-related glycoprotein encoded by MHVR1 is a functional receptor for murine coronavirus MHV-A59.

TITLE:

ABSTRACT:
The cellular receptor for murine coronavirus mouse hepatitis virus (MHV)-A59 is a member of the carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) family of glycoproteins in the immunoglobulin superfamily. TITLE:
Development of a CRISPR-Cas13a assay for mouse hepatitis virus detection.

ABSTRACT:
Mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) is a significant pathogen that undermines the health of laboratory animals and the reliability of research data. The development of rapid and sensitive detection methods for MHV is therefore crucial for ensuring laboratory animal quality and maintaining laboratory biosafety. Here, we established a CRISPR-Cas13a-based assay targeting the E, M, and N genes of MHV by constructing a recombinase-aided amplification (RAA)-coupled detection system. Results demonstrated that the N1 target exhibited the highest sensitivity, achieving a detection limit of 0.1 copy/μL for plasmid templates and 1 copy/μL in spiked serum samples. The system also exhibited robust specificity and a strong signal response in spiked serum samples. Furthermore, we developed a multiplex amplification-free CRISPR-Cas13a assay by combining Cas13a/crRNAs targeting different genes, which achieved a detection limit of 3.06 pM. In summary, this study presents two distinct CRISPR-Cas13a-based strategies for MHV detection, demonstrating the considerable application potential of this technology for pathogen detection in laboratory animal settings.

TITLE:
Development of a CRISPR-Cas13a assay for mouse hepatitis virus detection.

ABSTRACT:
Mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) is a significant pathogen that undermines the health of laboratory animals and the reliability of research data. The development of rapid and sensitive detection methods for MHV is therefore crucial for ensuring laboratory animal quality and maintaining laboratory biosafety. Furthermore, we developed a multiplex amplification-free CRISPR-Cas13a assay by combining Cas13a/crRNAs targeting different genes, which achieved a detection limit of 3.06 pM. TITLE:
Microbiological survey of mice (Mus musculus) purchased from commercial pet shops in Kanagawa and Tokyo, Japan.

ABSTRACT:
Information regarding the prevalence of infectious agents in mice in pet shops in Japan is scarce. This information is particularly useful for minimizing the risk of potential transmission of infections to laboratory mice. Therefore, we surveyed infectious agents in mice from pet shops in Kanagawa and Tokyo, Japan. The survey was conducted in 28 mice from 5 pet shops to screen for 47 items (17 viruses, 22 bacteria and fungi, 10 parasites) using culture tests, serology, PCR, and microscopy. The most common viral agent detected was murine norovirus (17 mice; 60.7%), followed by Theiler's murine encephalomyelitis virus (13 mice; 46.4%), and mouse hepatitis virus (12 mice; 42.8%). The most common agent amongst the bacteria and fungi was Pasteurella pneumotropica (10 mice; 35.7%), followed by Helicobacter ganmani and Pneumocystis murina (8 mice; 28.5%, for both). Tritrichomonas muris was the most common parasite (19 mice; 67.8%), followed by Spironucleus muris (13 mice; 46.4%), Aspiculuris tetraptera, and Syphacia obvelata (8 mice each; 28.5%). Remarkably, a zoonotic agent, Hymenolepis nana, was found in 7 mice (25%). Given these results, we suggest that the workers in laboratory animal facilities should recognize again the potential risks of mice outside of the laboratory animal facilities as an infectious source, and avoid keeping mice as pets or as feed for carnivorous reptiles as much as possible for risk management.

TITLE:
Microbiological survey of mice (Mus musculus) purchased from commercial pet shops in Kanagawa and Tokyo, Japan.

ABSTRACT:
Information regarding the prevalence of infectious agents in mice in pet shops in Japan is scarce. This information is particularly useful for minimizing the risk of potential transmission of infections to laboratory mice. Therefore, we surveyed infectious agents in mice from pet shops in Kanagawa and Tokyo, Japan. The survey was conducted in 28 mice from 5 pet shops to screen for 47 items (17 viruses, 22 bacteria and fungi, 10 parasites) using culture tests, serology, PCR, and microscopy. The most common viral agent detected was murine norovirus (17 mice; 60.7%), followed by Theiler's murine encephalomyelitis virus (13 mice; 46.4%), and mouse hepatitis virus (12 mice; 42.8%). The most common agent amongst the bacteria and fungi was Pasteurella pneumotropica (10 mice; 35.7%), followed by Helicobacter ganmani and Pneumocystis murina (8 mice; 28.5%, for both). Tritrichomonas muris was the most common parasite (19 mice; 67.8%), followed by Spironucleus muris (13 mice; 46.4%), Aspiculuris tetraptera, and Syphacia obvelata (8 mice each; 28.5%). Remarkably, a zoonotic agent, Hymenolepis nana, was found in 7 mice (25%). Given these results, we suggest that the workers in laboratory animal facilities should recognize again the potential risks of mice outside of the laboratory animal facilities as an infectious source, and avoid keeping mice as pets or as feed for carnivorous reptiles as much as possible for risk management.

TITLE:
Infectious microorganisms in mice (Mus musculus) purchased from commercial pet shops in Germany.

ABSTRACT:
In this study, we investigated the prevalence of infectious microorganisms (viruses, bacteria, fungi and eukaryotic parasites) in mice from different pet shops in Germany; such animals may compromise the hygienic integrity of laboratory animal vivaria if private pet holders act as unintended vectors of infections carried by them. House mice sold as pets or feed specimens were purchased from different pet shops and tested for a comprehensive panel of unwanted microorganisms. We found a number of microorganisms in these pet shop mice, the most prevalent of which were Helicobacter species (92.9%), mouse parvovirus (89.3%), mouse hepatitis virus (82.7%), Pasteurella pneumotropica (71.4%) and Syphacia species (57.1%). Several microorganisms (e.g. mouse parvovirus, Theiler's murine encephalomyelitis virus, pneumonia virus of mice, Encephalitozoon cuniculi, Clostridium piliforme) had considerably higher prevalences than those reported in similar studies on wild mice from North America, Europe or Australia. Our study shows that direct contact with pet shop mice may constitute a risk for laboratory animal vivaria if hygienic precautions are not taken. However, even relatively simple precautions seem effective enough to hold the risk at bay.

TITLE:
Infectious diseases in wild mice (Mus musculus) collected on and around the University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) Campus.

ABSTRACT:
Laboratory mice serve as important models in biomedical research. Monitoring these animals for infections and infestations and excluding causative agents requires extensive resources. Despite advancements in detection and exclusion over the last several years, these activities remain challenging for many institutions. The infections and infestations present in laboratory mouse colonies are well documented, but their mode of introduction is not always known. One possibility is that wild rodents living near vivaria somehow transmit infections to and between the colonies. This study was undertaken to determine what infectious agents the wild mice on the University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) campus were carrying. Wild mice were trapped and evaluated for parasites, viruses, and selected bacteria by using histopathology, serology, and PCR-based assays. Results were compared with known infectious agents historically circulating in the vivaria housing mice on campus and were generally different. Although the ectoparasitic burdens found on the 2 populations were similar, the wild mice had a much lower incidence of endoparasites (most notably pinworms). The seroprevalence of some viral infections was also different, with a low prevalence of mouse hepatitis virus among wild mice. Wild mice had a high prevalence of murine cytomegalovirus, an agent now thought to be confined to wild mouse populations. Helicobacter DNA was amplified from more than 90% of the wild mice (59% positive for H. hepaticus). Given the results of this study, we conclude that wild mice likely are not a source of infection for many of the agents that are detected in laboratory mouse colonies at the University of Pennsylvania.

TITLE:
Long-term storage stability of multiplex immunochromatographic assay strips for serologic monitoring of infectious diseases in laboratory rodents

ABSTRACT:
Serological monitoring of infectious diseases in laboratory rodents is vital for ensuring animal health. Therefore, we have previously developed a multiplex immunochromatographic assay (ICA) to detect antibodies against six pathogens as follows: mouse hepatitis virus, Sendai virus, and Clostridium piliforme (Tyzzer’s disease) in mice, and Seoul type orthohantavirus, Sendai virus, and sialodacryoadenitis virus in rats. However, the preparation of these strips is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the long-term storage conditions for the developed multiplex ICA strips. The multiplex ICA strips stored in the polyethylene zipper-sealed bags (poly_bags) at −30°C maintained detectable reactivity for all six targeted pathogens for 36 months, regardless of the presence or absence of desiccants, oxygen absorbers, or a vacuum state. However, when stored at 18–28°C (room temperature) and 4°C, the detectable reactivity of the multiplex ICA strips stored in poly_bags was reduced for some of the six targets pathogens at 18 months after storage. This reduction was not prevented by the storage with the desiccants and in the vacuum-sealed poly_bags (vacuum_bags). The oxygen absorber reduced detectability of the multiplex ICA strips. These results indicate that storing ICA strips in poly_bags at −30°C, which is a simple method, is able to maintain detectability long-term for the strips format and pathogen targets examined in this study.

evidence_results.verification_source: INTRODUCTIONMicrobiological monitoring of laboratory animals used in experimental studies is essential from the viewpoints of research reliability, reproducibility, and animal welfare (3Rs). The microbiological status of laboratory rodents is typically monitored by exposing sentinel animals to potentially contaminated soiled bedding or exhaust air from individually ventilated cages for several weeks. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), polymerase chain reaction (PCR), culture, and microscopic examination are the main tests used for the serological diagnosis of infectious diseases and the detection of pathogens in laboratory rats and mice. Commercially available ELISA kits, such as MONILISA® (Wakamoto Pharmaceutical, Tokyo, Japan), are mainly used for in-house monitoring.Assessment of microbial status without euthanizing and distressing test animals, including sentinels, is now considered important from the viewpoint of the 3Rs. Multiplex microbead immunoassays and PCR-based detection of antigens in feces have been reported as methods for diagnosing infectious diseases without euthanizing or distressing animals [5, 11,12,13, 15, 16]. The multiplex immunochromatographic assay (ICA) is a rapid and simple serologic test specifically designed for the detection of pathogens from a small amount of blood, thereby reducing euthanasia rates and distress in test animals. The developed multiplex ICA was used to detect mouse hepatitis virus (MHV), Sendai virus (previously known as hemagglutinating virus of Japan) (HVJ), and Clostridium piliforme, which is the pathogen causing Tyzzer’s disease (Tyzzer) in laboratory mice and HVJ, Seoul type orthohantavirus (Hanta), and sialodacryoadenitis virus (SDAV) in laboratory rats [18, 19].When an infectious disease outbreak is confirmed, rapid screening tests must be conducted to understand the extent of its spread. Therefore, the long-term storage of the developed multiplex ICA strips is important for implementing rapid response measures during an infectious outbreak, as the preparation of the strips is time-consuming and labor-intensive. The strips of the developed multiplex ICA were stored at 18–28°C (room temperature) in a dry box until use and was within 3 months [18, 19]. However, for storage of more than 3 months of the developed multiplex ICA strips, the effects of storage conditions such as temperature and humidity on detection sensitivity and specificity of antibody and storage period are unknown. Moreover, there have been also few reports on the storage conditions and stability of other ICA strips. In this study, we aim to determine suitable long-term storage conditions for the developed multiplex ICA strips for simultaneous serodetection of MHV, HVJ, and Tyzzer in mice, and Hanta, HVJ, and SDAV in rats.MATERIALS AND METHODSControl antigenInactivated fractions of purified MHV (S strain) and HVJ (MN strain) virions and a purified and inactivated Clostridium piliforme (RJ strain), which is the pathogen causing Tyzzer, were provided by the ICLAS Monitoring Center (Central Institute for Experimental Medicine and Life Science Central, Japan) [6, 8]. A recombinant antigen for Hanta diagnosis was prepared as previously described [1, 2, 23].SerumSerum samples positive for antibodies against MHV, SDAV, HVJ and Tyzzer were provided by the ICLAS Monitoring Center. These samples were diagnosed through ELISA and an immunofluorescent antibody assay as previously described [8]. The protocol for collecting positive serum samples was approved by the IACUC according to the Regulations for Central Institute for Experimental Medicine and Life Science Central, Japan. The regulations were established in compliance with the law for humane treatment and management of animals.Serum samples positive for antibodies against Hanta were diagnosed by using ELISA and an immunofluorescent antibody assay as previously described [1, 2].Lot numbers of the serum samples positive for antibodies against each antigen were as follows: mouse MHV No.1, mouse HVJ No.2, mouse Tyzzer No.9, rat SDAV No.5, rats HVJ No.5, and anti-Seoul virus strain Gou3 (Hanta). To prevent deterioration caused by freezing and thawing, the serum samples were stored at −80°C in amounts required for one analysis.Multiplex ICAThe multiplex ICA strips for detection of serum antibodies to MHV, HVJ, and Tyzzer in mice and SDAV, HVJ, and Hanta in rats were prepared as described previously [18, 19].(i) Preparation of a colloidal gold conjugate: A gold colloid solution (WRGH2, Wine Red Chemical, Tokyo, Japan) was mixed with an equal volume of 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.15). Rabbit anti-rat IgG antibody (Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA) and protein A (Nacalai tesque, Kyoto, Japan) solution were diluted to 1.5 mg/mL by using 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.15) and then mixed with 2 volumes of the colloidal gold dilution in a siliconized tube. After brief sonication, the mixture was incubated for 20 min at room temperature, after which a 1/3 volume of blocking solution (2.5% casein sodium (Wako, Osaka, Japan) in 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 9.2)) was added. The mixture was sonicated briefly, incubated for 20 min at room temperature, and centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 15 min. After removal of the supernatant, the pellet was resuspended in blocking solution to the initial volume of colloidal gold. After brief sonication, the mixture was incubated for 20 min at room temperature and then centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 15 min. Finally, the supernatant was removed, and the pellet was resuspended with 200 μL of blocking solution.(ii) Preparation of a conjugate pad: A glass-fiber conjugate pad (GFDX103000; MilliporeSigma, Billerica, MA, USA) was soaked in 0.5% casein in 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.8) for 20 min. The pad was washed with 3.0% sucrose in double-distilled water and air-dried overnight. The pad was coated with the prepared colloidal gold conjugate at a dose of 200 μL/30 cm. The pad was air-dried overnight and stored at room temperature.(iii) Preparation of a multiplex ICA strip: For diagnosis of MHV, HVJ and Tyzzer in mice, inactivated fractions of purified MHV (S strain) and HVJ (MN strain) virions and a purified and inactivated Clostridium piliforme (RJ strain) were used respectively. For diagnosis of SDAV, HVJ and Hanta in rats, inactivated fractions of purified MHV (S strain), which cross-reacts with SDAV [10], and HVJ (MN strain) virions and the recombinant antigen of Hanta were used respectively. Each antigen for test line was diluted with 0.05% casein sodium in 10 mM PB (pH 7.2) to adjust the concentrations to 1.0 mg/mL for MHV and Hanta antigens, to 0.5 mg/mL for HVJ and Tyzzer antigens. Rabbit IgG (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical, Osaka, Japan) for control line of strip for mice, and anti-rabbit IgG antibody (MP Biomedicals, Solon, OH, USA) for control line of strip for rats, were diluted with 0.05% casein sodium in 10 mM PB (pH 7.2) to adjust the concentrations to 0.15 mg/mL. These reagents were immobilized on a nitrocellulose membrane (60 mm × 300 mm) (Hi-Flow Plus 135 Membrane Card; MilliporeSigma) by using a pen (Super brush for Copic Sketch and Ciao; Too Marker Products, Tokyo, Japan) to draw thin lines for the reagents at the test line position (each antigen) and control line position (anti-rabbit IgG antibody for rats or rabbit IgG for mice).An ICA strip containing the 3 antigens and the control as separate lines was used as a multiplex ICA strip. After the membrane had been dried at room temperature for 15 min, it was soaked in 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer containing 0.5% casein (pH 7.8) for 20 min to block the unsaturated area. Then the membrane was washed twice (5 min each time) with double-distilled water, soaked in 3.0% sucrose in double-distilled water, and air-dried overnight. Finally, a sample pad (20 mm × 300 mm) (Chromatography Paper; Whatman, GE Healthcare BioSciences, Pittsburgh, PA, USA), conjugate pad, nitrocellulose membrane and absorbent pad (50 mm × 300 mm) (catalog no. CFSP20300, Cellulose fiber sample pad; MilliporeSigma, Billerica, MA, USA) were assembled on a membrane card (MilliporeSigma). The combined membranes were cut into 2-mm-wide strips by using a paper cutter. The structure of the ICA strip is shown in Fig. 1A.Fig. 1.Schematic diagram demonstrating the detection method and presentation of a multiplex immunochromatographic assay (ICA) strip. A) Structure of the multiplex ICA. Antigens were placed at the test line. Rabbit IgG and anti-rabbit IgG antibodies were placed at the control line for mice and rats, respectively. The ICA strip consisted of four membrane pads: sample pad, conjugate pad, nitrocellulose membrane, and absorbent pad. The conjugate pad contained a protein A-colloidal gold conjugate used for serologic diagnosis of infectious diseases in mice or an anti-rat IgG antibody colloidal gold conjugate, which is used for the serologic diagnosis of infectious diseases in rats. B) Detection method. Serum (0.75 μL) was diluted with 150 μL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and placed in a microtube. After the strip was dipped in the solution for 15 min, the test line (yellow arrow) and control line (red arrow) were examined visually. A sample in which only the control line appeared was regarded as negative (1), whereas a sample in which both the test and control lines appeared was regarded as positive (2).(iv) Procedure for the multiplex ICA: A 0.75 mL of the serum sample positive for antibodies against each antigen was added to 150 mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), making a 1:200 dilution. An ICA strip was put directly into a microtube containing PBS-diluted serum (Fig. 1B). After the tube had remained still for 15 min, the ICA strip was examined visually. The detectability of the ICA strips was determined visually by all co-authors. When the intensity of both the control and test lines was clear, it was regarded that detectability of the ICA strip was maintained. The following cases were regarded that detectability of the ICA strip was not maintained: 1) the intensity of both the control and test lines in each positive serum were reduced, making evaluation difficult, 2) neither the control nor test lines against each positive serum was detected, 3) the control line was detected but the test line was not detected, 4) the test line was detected but the control line was not detected. When bands were detected on the test lines of antigens other than the target antigen, it was judged as nonspecific reactions.Storage of multiplex ICA stripsAs shown in Fig. 2AFig. 2.Storage conditions of the multiplex immunochromatographic assay (ICA) strip. A) Conditions for the airtightness of storage bags of the multiplex ICA strips: (1) polyethylene zipper-sealed bags (poly_bags), (2) vacuum-sealed poly_bags (vacuum_bags). The vacuum state was achieved by removing the air using a vacuum sealer. B) Conditions of desiccants and oxygen absorbers in poly and vacuum_bags: (1) without both desiccants and oxygen absorbers, (2) with desiccants only, (3) with oxygen absorbers only, (4) with both desiccants and oxygen absorbers., the multiplex ICA strips were stored in polyethylene zipper-sealed bags (poly_bags) (140 × 100 × 0.08 mm, cold resistance temperature: −30°C) (Unipack E-8; SEISANNIPPONSHA, Tokyo, Japan) and in vacuum-sealed poly_bags (vacuum_bags) at 18–28°C (room temperature), 4°C, and −30°C in dark for 6, 18, and 36 months. The vacuum state was achieved by removing the air using a vacuum sealer (Vacuum Sealer Economy VS-400S; AS ONE, Osaka, Japan). Moreover, the following conditions were set for each storage condition: 1) stored without both desiccants (Synthetic Zeolite Plate Strong Desiccant AZ10G-100; AS ONE, Osaka, Japan) and oxygen absorbers (Oxygen absorber A-750HS; AS ONE), 2) stored with desiccants only, 3) stored with oxygen absorbers only, 4) stored with both desiccants and oxygen absorbers (Fig. 2B). It was regarded that the detectability of Tyzzer and the control lines were maintained for up to 6 months after storage, whereas the detectability of the HVJ, MHV, and control lines were maintained for up to 18 months. No effect of the desiccants was observed on the multiplex ICA strips stored in poly_bags at room temperature with respect to the detection of all three pathogens. In contrast, storing the multiplex ICA strips with oxygen absorber only in poly_bags at room temperature reduced detectability against all three pathogens compared to the strips stored in the absence of both desiccants and oxygen absorbers. In the multiplex ICA strips stored with both desiccants and oxygen absorbers, no synergistic effect was observed; however, the reduction in detectability seen during storage with only the oxygen absorbers was prevented. No effect of the vacuum state was observed on strips stored at room temperature for the detection of all three pathogens, except for those stored with oxygen absorbers only at 6 months.The intensity of immunoreactive bands for both Tyzzer and the control showed a decrease when the multiplex ICA strips were stored at 4°C in poly_bags without both desiccants and oxygen absorbers after 18 months (Table 1). Therefore, it was regarded that the detectability of Tyzzer and the control lines was maintained for up to 6 months after storage. However, the detectability of the HVJ, MHV, and control lines maintained for up to 36 months. When the strips were stored at 4°C in poly_bags, no effect of the desiccant was observed in the detection of MHV, HVJ, and Tyzzer. Conversely, storing the multiplex ICA strips with oxygen absorbers only in poly_bags at 4°C reduced detectability against HVJ and Tyzzer. No synergistic effects were observed when the strips were stored with both desiccants and oxygen absorbers, although the reduction in detectability of HVJ seen during storage with only the oxygen absorbers was prevented. The intensity of all immunoreactive bands for the control and test lines regarded as that the detectability was maintained at 36 months after storage were the same with the intensity of the control and test lines before storage (Fig. 3Fig. 3.Representative reactivity of multiplex immunochromatographic assay (ICA) strips after 36 months of storage for detection of hepatitis virus (MHV), hemagglutinating virus of Japan (HVJ), and Tyzzer in mice. Serum (0.75 μL) was diluted with 150 μL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). The strips in polyethylene zipper-sealed bags (poly_bags) were stored at room temperature in a desiccator for 36 months. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the optimal long-term storage conditions for the developed multiplex ICA strips for the simultaneous serodetection of MHV, HVJ, and Tyzzer in mice, and Hanta, HVJ, and SDAV in rats. We demonstrated that the multiplex ICA strips maintained detectable reactivity for all six target pathogens for 36 months when stored in poly_bags at −30°C, regardless of the presence or absence of desiccants, oxygen absorbers, or vacuum conditions.Although there are numerous reports on ICA using colloidal gold conjugates, there are few reports on the storage conditions and stability of ICA strips. There are reports on the storage conditions and stability of ICA strips using colloidal gold conjugates, although the detection targets are different [3, 4, 7, 9, 14, 17, 20,21,22, 24,25,26,27,28]. It has been reported that the detectability of strips stored at room temperature is maintained for at least 2 months and up to 6 months, and at 4°C, for at least 2 months and up to 12 months. Furthermore, it is necessary to examine other desiccants, such as silica gel and activated alumina to determine their effectiveness.In multiplex ICA strips stored in poly_bags with an oxygen absorber at room temperature, detectability for all six targeted pathogens was reduced compared with storage in the absence of both desiccants and oxygen absorbers. If the cause of the reduction in the detectability of the multiplex ICA strips is an oxygen-free environment, the detectability of the multiplex ICA strips stored in vacuum will also be reduced. However, the multiplex ICA strips stored in vacuum_bags at room temperature without both desiccants and oxygen absorbers had the same detectability as the poly_bags without both desiccants and oxygen absorbers. Therefore, the reason for the reduced detectability of the multiplex ICA strips stored in the poly_bags with oxygen absorbers at room temperature is not the absence of oxygen. In the multiplex ICA strips stored in poly-bags with both desiccants and oxygen absorbers, no reduction in detectability was observed. These results suggest that moisture is necessary for the oxidation reaction, which was absorbed by the desiccants, therefore inhibiting the oxidation reaction. On the other hand, the oxygen absorbers used in this study generate heat when they react with oxygen. The heat generation by the oxidation reaction might have caused denaturation of antibodies and antigens on the strips, resulting in a possible decrease in the detectability. Moreover, condensation might occur around the oxygen absorber by the heat generated during oxidation reactions. Therefore, the reduction in the detectability of ICA strips stored in the poly_bags with oxygen absorbers only at room temperature may be related to factors such as heat and condensation generated during oxidative reactions. Further studies are needed to investigate the cause of the reduction in the detectability of ICA strips stored in poly_bags with oxygen absorbers at room temperature.Previous reports indicated that the detectability of the ICA strips was maintained longer when stored at 4°C than at room temperature, regardless of the storage container. This corresponds to the findings of this study, as the detectability of the multiplex ICA strips was better maintained at lower storage temperatures, regardless of the presence or absence of desiccants, oxygen absorbers, or vacuum conditions. Although there have been no reports of storing ICA strips at −30°C, this study demonstrated that ICA strips stored in poly_bags at −30°C maintained detectability for all six targeted pathogens for 36 months.There are some limitations of this study. Firstly, the ICA strips, desiccants, and/or oxygen absorbers should have been stored in properly separated conditions to avoid the effects caused by mutual contact. Another limitation is that it would be preferable to use double-sealed bags to reduce the amount of oxygen in the experimental samples. After solving the above issues, further investigation by using a large number of specimens is needed to determine the sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility of the ICA strips stored at −30°C in poly_bags.This study showed that storing ICA strips in poly_bags at −30°C, which is a simple method, is able to maintain detectability long-term for the strips format and pathogen targets examined in this study.CONFLICT OF INTERESTThe authors declare no conflicts of interest in association with this study.

source_paper.title: Long-term storage stability of multiplex immunochromatographic assay strips for serologic monitoring of infectious diseases in laboratory rodents
source_paper.abstract: Serological monitoring of infectious diseases in laboratory rodents is vital for ensuring animal health. Therefore, we have previously developed a multiplex immunochromatographic assay (ICA) to detect antibodies against six pathogens as follows: mouse hepatitis virus, Sendai virus, and Clostridium piliforme (Tyzzer’s disease) in mice, and Seoul type orthohantavirus, Sendai virus, and sialodacryoadenitis virus in rats. However, the preparation of these strips is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the long-term storage conditions for the developed multiplex ICA strips. The multiplex ICA strips stored in the polyethylene zipper-sealed bags (poly_bags) at −30°C maintained detectable reactivity for all six targeted pathogens for 36 months, regardless of the presence or absence of desiccants, oxygen absorbers, or a vacuum state. However, when stored at 18–28°C (room temperature) and 4°C, the detectable reactivity of the multiplex ICA strips stored in poly_bags was reduced for some of the six targets pathogens at 18 months after storage. This reduction was not prevented by the storage with the desiccants and in the vacuum-sealed poly_bags (vacuum_bags). The oxygen absorber reduced detectability of the multiplex ICA strips. These results indicate that storing ICA strips in poly_bags at −30°C, which is a simple method, is able to maintain detectability long-term for the strips format and pathogen targets examined in this study.
source_paper.full_text: INTRODUCTIONMicrobiological monitoring of laboratory animals used in experimental studies is essential from the viewpoints of research reliability, reproducibility, and animal welfare (3Rs). The microbiological status of laboratory rodents is typically monitored by exposing sentinel animals to potentially contaminated soiled bedding or exhaust air from individually ventilated cages for several weeks. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), polymerase chain reaction (PCR), culture, and microscopic examination are the main tests used for the serological diagnosis of infectious diseases and the detection of pathogens in laboratory rats and mice. Commercially available ELISA kits, such as MONILISA® (Wakamoto Pharmaceutical, Tokyo, Japan), are mainly used for in-house monitoring.Assessment of microbial status without euthanizing and distressing test animals, including sentinels, is now considered important from the viewpoint of the 3Rs. Multiplex microbead immunoassays and PCR-based detection of antigens in feces have been reported as methods for diagnosing infectious diseases without euthanizing or distressing animals [5, 11,12,13, 15, 16]. The multiplex immunochromatographic assay (ICA) is a rapid and simple serologic test specifically designed for the detection of pathogens from a small amount of blood, thereby reducing euthanasia rates and distress in test animals. The developed multiplex ICA was used to detect mouse hepatitis virus (MHV), Sendai virus (previously known as hemagglutinating virus of Japan) (HVJ), and Clostridium piliforme, which is the pathogen causing Tyzzer’s disease (Tyzzer) in laboratory mice and HVJ, Seoul type orthohantavirus (Hanta), and sialodacryoadenitis virus (SDAV) in laboratory rats [18, 19].When an infectious disease outbreak is confirmed, rapid screening tests must be conducted to understand the extent of its spread. Therefore, the long-term storage of the developed multiplex ICA strips is important for implementing rapid response measures during an infectious outbreak, as the preparation of the strips is time-consuming and labor-intensive. The strips of the developed multiplex ICA were stored at 18–28°C (room temperature) in a dry box until use and was within 3 months [18, 19]. However, for storage of more than 3 months of the developed multiplex ICA strips, the effects of storage conditions such as temperature and humidity on detection sensitivity and specificity of antibody and storage period are unknown. Moreover, there have been also few reports on the storage conditions and stability of other ICA strips. In this study, we aim to determine suitable long-term storage conditions for the developed multiplex ICA strips for simultaneous serodetection of MHV, HVJ, and Tyzzer in mice, and Hanta, HVJ, and SDAV in rats.MATERIALS AND METHODSControl antigenInactivated fractions of purified MHV (S strain) and HVJ (MN strain) virions and a purified and inactivated Clostridium piliforme (RJ strain), which is the pathogen causing Tyzzer, were provided by the ICLAS Monitoring Center (Central Institute for Experimental Medicine and Life Science Central, Japan) [6, 8]. A recombinant antigen for Hanta diagnosis was prepared as previously described [1, 2, 23].SerumSerum samples positive for antibodies against MHV, SDAV, HVJ and Tyzzer were provided by the ICLAS Monitoring Center. These samples were diagnosed through ELISA and an immunofluorescent antibody assay as previously described [8]. The protocol for collecting positive serum samples was approved by the IACUC according to the Regulations for Central Institute for Experimental Medicine and Life Science Central, Japan. The regulations were established in compliance with the law for humane treatment and management of animals.Serum samples positive for antibodies against Hanta were diagnosed by using ELISA and an immunofluorescent antibody assay as previously described [1, 2].Lot numbers of the serum samples positive for antibodies against each antigen were as follows: mouse MHV No.1, mouse HVJ No.2, mouse Tyzzer No.9, rat SDAV No.5, rats HVJ No.5, and anti-Seoul virus strain Gou3 (Hanta). To prevent deterioration caused by freezing and thawing, the serum samples were stored at −80°C in amounts required for one analysis.Multiplex ICAThe multiplex ICA strips for detection of serum antibodies to MHV, HVJ, and Tyzzer in mice and SDAV, HVJ, and Hanta in rats were prepared as described previously [18, 19].(i) Preparation of a colloidal gold conjugate: A gold colloid solution (WRGH2, Wine Red Chemical, Tokyo, Japan) was mixed with an equal volume of 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.15). Rabbit anti-rat IgG antibody (Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA) and protein A (Nacalai tesque, Kyoto, Japan) solution were diluted to 1.5 mg/mL by using 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.15) and then mixed with 2 volumes of the colloidal gold dilution in a siliconized tube. After brief sonication, the mixture was incubated for 20 min at room temperature, after which a 1/3 volume of blocking solution (2.5% casein sodium (Wako, Osaka, Japan) in 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 9.2)) was added. The mixture was sonicated briefly, incubated for 20 min at room temperature, and centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 15 min. After removal of the supernatant, the pellet was resuspended in blocking solution to the initial volume of colloidal gold. After brief sonication, the mixture was incubated for 20 min at room temperature and then centrifuged at 14,000 × g for 15 min. Finally, the supernatant was removed, and the pellet was resuspended with 200 μL of blocking solution.(ii) Preparation of a conjugate pad: A glass-fiber conjugate pad (GFDX103000; MilliporeSigma, Billerica, MA, USA) was soaked in 0.5% casein in 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.8) for 20 min. The pad was washed with 3.0% sucrose in double-distilled water and air-dried overnight. The pad was coated with the prepared colloidal gold conjugate at a dose of 200 μL/30 cm. The pad was air-dried overnight and stored at room temperature.(iii) Preparation of a multiplex ICA strip: For diagnosis of MHV, HVJ and Tyzzer in mice, inactivated fractions of purified MHV (S strain) and HVJ (MN strain) virions and a purified and inactivated Clostridium piliforme (RJ strain) were used respectively. For diagnosis of SDAV, HVJ and Hanta in rats, inactivated fractions of purified MHV (S strain), which cross-reacts with SDAV [10], and HVJ (MN strain) virions and the recombinant antigen of Hanta were used respectively. Each antigen for test line was diluted with 0.05% casein sodium in 10 mM PB (pH 7.2) to adjust the concentrations to 1.0 mg/mL for MHV and Hanta antigens, to 0.5 mg/mL for HVJ and Tyzzer antigens. Rabbit IgG (FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical, Osaka, Japan) for control line of strip for mice, and anti-rabbit IgG antibody (MP Biomedicals, Solon, OH, USA) for control line of strip for rats, were diluted with 0.05% casein sodium in 10 mM PB (pH 7.2) to adjust the concentrations to 0.15 mg/mL. These reagents were immobilized on a nitrocellulose membrane (60 mm × 300 mm) (Hi-Flow Plus 135 Membrane Card; MilliporeSigma) by using a pen (Super brush for Copic Sketch and Ciao; Too Marker Products, Tokyo, Japan) to draw thin lines for the reagents at the test line position (each antigen) and control line position (anti-rabbit IgG antibody for rats or rabbit IgG for mice).An ICA strip containing the 3 antigens and the control as separate lines was used as a multiplex ICA strip. After the membrane had been dried at room temperature for 15 min, it was soaked in 20 mM sodium phosphate buffer containing 0.5% casein (pH 7.8) for 20 min to block the unsaturated area. Then the membrane was washed twice (5 min each time) with double-distilled water, soaked in 3.0% sucrose in double-distilled water, and air-dried overnight. Finally, a sample pad (20 mm × 300 mm) (Chromatography Paper; Whatman, GE Healthcare BioSciences, Pittsburgh, PA, USA), conjugate pad, nitrocellulose membrane and absorbent pad (50 mm × 300 mm) (catalog no. CFSP20300, Cellulose fiber sample pad; MilliporeSigma, Billerica, MA, USA) were assembled on a membrane card (MilliporeSigma). The combined membranes were cut into 2-mm-wide strips by using a paper cutter. A) Structure of the multiplex ICA. Antigens were placed at the test line. Rabbit IgG and anti-rabbit IgG antibodies were placed at the control line for mice and rats, respectively. The ICA strip consisted of four membrane pads: sample pad, conjugate pad, nitrocellulose membrane, and absorbent pad. The conjugate pad contained a protein A-colloidal gold conjugate used for serologic diagnosis of infectious diseases in mice or an anti-rat IgG antibody colloidal gold conjugate, which is used for the serologic diagnosis of infectious diseases in rats. After the strip was dipped in the solution for 15 min, the test line (yellow arrow) and control line (red arrow) were examined visually. An ICA strip was put directly into a microtube containing PBS-diluted serum (Fig. 1B). After the tube had remained still for 15 min, the ICA strip was examined visually. The detectability of the ICA strips was determined visually by all co-authors. When the intensity of both the control and test lines was clear, it was regarded that detectability of the ICA strip was maintained. Moreover, condensation might occur around the oxygen absorber by the heat generated during oxidation reactions. retrieved_papers.title: Microbiological survey of mice (Mus musculus) purchased from commercial pet shops in Kanagawa and Tokyo, Japan.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Information regarding the prevalence of infectious agents in mice in pet shops in Japan is scarce. This information is particularly useful for minimizing the risk of potential transmission of infections to laboratory mice. Therefore, we surveyed infectious agents in mice from pet shops in Kanagawa and Tokyo, Japan. The survey was conducted in 28 mice from 5 pet shops to screen for 47 items (17 viruses, 22 bacteria and fungi, 10 parasites) using culture tests, serology, PCR, and microscopy. The most common viral agent detected was murine norovirus (17 mice; 60.7%), followed by Theiler's murine encephalomyelitis virus (13 mice; 46.4%), and mouse hepatitis virus (12 mice; 42.8%). The most common agent amongst the bacteria and fungi was Pasteurella pneumotropica (10 mice; 35.7%), followed by Helicobacter ganmani and Pneumocystis murina (8 mice; 28.5%, for both). Tritrichomonas muris was the most common parasite (19 mice; 67.8%), followed by Spironucleus muris (13 mice; 46.4%), Aspiculuris tetraptera, and Syphacia obvelata (8 mice each; 28.5%). Remarkably, a zoonotic agent, Hymenolepis nana, was found in 7 mice (25%). Given these results, we suggest that the workers in laboratory animal facilities should recognize again the potential risks of mice outside of the laboratory animal facilities as an infectious source, and avoid keeping mice as pets or as feed for carnivorous reptiles as much as possible for risk management.

retrieved_papers.title: Infectious microorganisms in mice (Mus musculus) purchased from commercial pet shops in Germany.
retrieved_papers.abstract: In this study, we investigated the prevalence of infectious microorganisms (viruses, bacteria, fungi and eukaryotic parasites) in mice from different pet shops in Germany; such animals may compromise the hygienic integrity of laboratory animal vivaria if private pet holders act as unintended vectors of infections carried by them. House mice sold as pets or feed specimens were purchased from different pet shops and tested for a comprehensive panel of unwanted microorganisms. We found a number of microorganisms in these pet shop mice, the most prevalent of which were Helicobacter species (92.9%), mouse parvovirus (89.3%), mouse hepatitis virus (82.7%), Pasteurella pneumotropica (71.4%) and Syphacia species (57.1%). Several microorganisms (e.g. mouse parvovirus, Theiler's murine encephalomyelitis virus, pneumonia virus of mice, Encephalitozoon cuniculi, Clostridium piliforme) had considerably higher prevalences than those reported in similar studies on wild mice from North America, Europe or Australia. Our study shows that direct contact with pet shop mice may constitute a risk for laboratory animal vivaria if hygienic precautions are not taken. However, even relatively simple precautions seem effective enough to hold the risk at bay.

retrieved_papers.title: Infectious diseases in wild mice (Mus musculus) collected on and around the University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) Campus.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Laboratory mice serve as important models in biomedical research. Monitoring these animals for infections and infestations and excluding causative agents requires extensive resources. Despite advancements in detection and exclusion over the last several years, these activities remain challenging for many institutions. The infections and infestations present in laboratory mouse colonies are well documented, but their mode of introduction is not always known. One possibility is that wild rodents living near vivaria somehow transmit infections to and between the colonies. This study was undertaken to determine what infectious agents the wild mice on the University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) campus were carrying. Wild mice were trapped and evaluated for parasites, viruses, and selected bacteria by using histopathology, serology, and PCR-based assays. Results were compared with known infectious agents historically circulating in the vivaria housing mice on campus and were generally different. Although the ectoparasitic burdens found on the 2 populations were similar, the wild mice had a much lower incidence of endoparasites (most notably pinworms). The seroprevalence of some viral infections was also different, with a low prevalence of mouse hepatitis virus among wild mice. Wild mice had a high prevalence of murine cytomegalovirus, an agent now thought to be confined to wild mouse populations. Helicobacter DNA was amplified from more than 90% of the wild mice (59% positive for H. hepaticus). Given the results of this study, we conclude that wild mice likely are not a source of infection for many of the agents that are detected in laboratory mouse colonies at the University of Pennsylvania.

retrieved_papers.title: [Mouse hepatitis virus].
retrieved_papers.abstract: Mouse hepatitis virus (MHV), the coronavirus of the mouse (mus musculus), is one of the most important viral pathogens in contemporary laboratory mouse colonies. It is a highly mutable virus consisting of numerous antigenically distinct serotypes with different pathology. These can be divided according to their tissue tropism into respiratory and enterotropic strains. The course of an MHV infection is dependent on virus strain and host factors. Generally MHV causes an acute, self limiting infection which is inapparent in adult mice. Neonates are highly susceptible to disease and show high mortality. In an enzootically infected colony however, they are protected by maternally derived passive immunity. MHV's importance in biomedical research on one hand stems from its potential as an interfering agent, mainly in the field of immunology. On the other hand MHV serves as a model for coronaviruses of other species including man in studies on virus replication and tissue tropism. Since MHV infections are usually subclinical, detection depends on serological screening of colonies using Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or immunofluorescence. MHV is controlled by culling and rederivation of the affected colony using hysterectomy or embryo transfer or by elimination by cessation of breeding.

retrieved_papers.title: Cloning of the mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) receptor: expression in human and hamster cell lines confers susceptibility to MHV.
retrieved_papers.abstract: The cellular receptor for murine coronavirus mouse hepatitis virus (MHV)-A59 is a member of the carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) family of glycoproteins in the immunoglobulin superfamily. We isolated a cDNA clone (MHVR1) encoding the MHV receptor. The sequence of this clone predicts a 424-amino-acid glycoprotein with four immunoglobulinlike domains, a transmembrane domain, and a short intracytoplasmic tail, MHVR1 is closely related to the murine CEA-related clone mmCGM1 (Mus musculus carcinoembryonic antigen gene family member). Western blot (immunoblot) analysis performed with antireceptor antibodies detected a glycoprotein of 120 kDa in BHK cells stably transfected with MHVR1. This corresponds to the size of the MHV receptor expressed in mouse intestine and liver. Human and hamster fibroblasts transfected with MHVR1 became susceptible to infection with MHV-A59. Like MHV-susceptible mouse fibroblasts, the MHVR1-transfected human and hamster cells were protected from MHV infection by pretreatment with monoclonal antireceptor antibody CC1. Thus, the 110- to 120-kDa CEA-related glycoprotein encoded by MHVR1 is a functional receptor for murine coronavirus MHV-A59.

retrieved_papers.title: Gut microbiota and pathobiont exposure influences disease incidence in non-obese diabetic mice.
retrieved_papers.abstract: While the non-obese diabetic (NOD) mouse is the most widely used animal model of type 1 diabetes (T1D), it suffers from poor reproducibility in disease incidence often attributed to variables in the environment, including the gut microbiota (GM). Prior research suggests a protective effect of segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB) on disease incidence, but it is unclear whether other pathobiont organisms or resident GM affect disease incidence. The objectives of the current study were to determine the effect of supplier-origin GMs and three different microbial challenges (SFB, Helicobacter hepaticus, and Mouse Hepatitis Virus [MHV]) on early-stage insulitis and lifelong disease incidence in NOD mice. The fecal microbiome was assessed pre- and post-disease onset to identify shifts in composition and predicted function of the GM. Results show that all three microbes influence T1D incidence and insulitis severity. Overall, SFB, MHV, and a high-richness microbiome were associated with lower disease incidence, while H. hepaticus and a low-richness microbiome were associated with higher disease incidence. H. hepaticus, but not SFB or MHV, was associated with significant changes in beta-diversity of the GM. While immune outcomes were not included, these findings provide guidance on microbes affecting disease incidence in NOD mice and evidence that such microbes may contribute to poor reproducibility in NOD mice or other mouse models.

retrieved_papers.title: Effects of Extended-Release Liposomal Bupivacaine on Postoperative Mechanical and Thermal Hypersensitivity in C57BL/6 Mice (Mus musculus).
retrieved_papers.abstract: Systemic analgesics, such as opioids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, may be contraindicated in certain studies due to their mechanisms of action and risk for systemic effects. Local anesthetics (LAs) are therefore crucial in managing postoperative pain, potentially decreasing the need for systemic analgesics. However, the utility of standard formulation LAs is limited by their short duration. This study evaluated the use of a commercially available extended-release (XR) liposomal bupivacaine (LB) in a mouse paw incisional model. Our goal was to assess whether LB attenuates postoperative mechanical hypersensitivity (MH) and thermal hypersensitivity (TH). Adult female and male C57BL/6NCrl mice were randomly assigned to one of 3 groups: (1) 5 mg/kg SC meloxicam plus 3.25 mg/kg SC XR-buprenorphine (MELOX/XR-BUP); (2) 2 mg/kg intraincisional standard bupivacaine (SB); or (3) 6 mg/kg intraincisional LB. MH and TH were assessed on days -1 (baseline), 0 (2 hours postoperatively), 1, 2, 3, and 4 using von Frey and Hargreaves testing, respectively. Hind paw incisional surgery was performed on day 0. Both the MELOX/XR-BUP and SB groups demonstrated significant attenuation of MH on all postoperative days compared with baseline, while the LB group showed significant attenuation of MH on days 1-4. In the MELOX/XR-BUP group, there was a significant reduction in TH on days 1-3. In both the SB and LB groups, there was no significant reduction in TH across all postoperative days. Together, these data suggest that a single 6-mg/kg intraincisional dose of LB in C57BL/6NCrl mice does not attenuate TH over a 4-day postoperative period but does attenuate MH on postoperative days 1-4 in our incisional model. In comparing the treatments, we conclude that the relative ability of LB to attenuate postoperative MH and TH was inferior to that of MELOX/XR-BUP and comparable to that of SB in a mouse paw incisional model.

retrieved_papers.title: Defined O-acetylated Neu5Ac substrates reveal position-specific preferences of gut bacterial sialidases.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Sialic acid on intestinal glycans is modified by O-acetylation, a modification that can protect glycans from bacterial degradation and modulate immune recognition. However, the specificity of gut bacterial sialidases toward O-acetylated sialic acid remains poorly defined. Here, we characterized six GH33 sialidases from Bacteroides spp. and Akkermansia muciniphila using chemically defined 4-methylumbelliferyl substrates bearing 4-O-, 7-O-, or 8/9-O-acetylated N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac). All enzymes adopted the canonical β-propeller fold and displayed distinct substrate preferences. While 8/9-O-acetylated Neu5Ac was broadly tolerated and 7-O-acetylation variably accommodated, all commensal sialidases were unable to cleave 4-O-acetylated Neu5Ac. Endogenous murine caecal sialidase activity showed the same pattern. Removal of the 4-O-acetyl group by a viral sialate O-acetylesterase restored cleavage, demonstrating that the C4 acetyl group directly prevents hydrolysis. On primary colonic and splenic lymphocytes, the bacterial sialidases produced enzyme-, linkage-, cell-type-, and tissue-dependent changes in sialic acid-dependent lectin and Siglec-E-Fc binding. In colon tissue, however, only the broad-spectrum pathogen-derived NanI sialidase consistently reduced SNA, MAL2, and Siglec-E-Fc binding, while the commensal enzymes caused more restricted changes. These findings demonstrate pronounced position-dependent effects of Neu5Ac O-acetylation on the activity of the sialidases tested and reveal substantial enzyme-specific differences in the processing of defined O-acetylated substrates.

retrieved_papers.title: Pulmonary Thromboembolism Due to Intravenous Fibrocyte Administration in C57BL/6J Mice (Mus musculus) and Recommendations for Refinement.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Cell therapy is a promising field of study for a range of diseases for which traditional therapies have failed. A primary problem for this therapy type in human medicine is failure of treatment efficacy due to the first pass trapping effect of the lung. Consequently, in rodents where these therapies are trialed, animals can be significantly affected by pulmonary thromboembolism due to the inherently smaller vessel sizes. Several different mechanisms for this have been demonstrated for rodent models, and several pharmacologic treatments have been proposed. In a C57BL/6J mouse model of cecal ligation and puncture, significant mortality was observed immediately after intravenous adoptive transfer of cultured fibrocytes. Antemortem clinical signs consisted of peracute dyspnea and lateral recumbency. Necropsy was performed on 3 affected mice, and heart and lung tissue were evaluated histologically. Cause of death was identified as acute thromboembolism of pulmonary arterioles. Special staining supported that the thromboemboli were caused by reticular fibers produced in culture by the transferred fibrocytes that were not removed by pretransfer cell isolation techniques. Prior literature describes either de novo thrombus formation or mechanical occlusion of pulmonary capillaries by transferred cells as the primary causes for pulmonary thromboembolism in rodent models of intravenous cell transfer. We present a novel mechanism in this case series and describe refinement steps such as the use of enhanced filtration steps during cell isolation and decreased cell concentration for administration. These refinements significantly reduced mortality in follow-up intravenous adoptive transfer experiments with C57BL/6J mice, improving animal welfare and enhancing research productivity.

retrieved_papers.title: Metabolic Cage Analysis of Surgically Catheterized C57BL/6J Mice (Mus musculus) Treated with Carprofen and Sustained-Release Buprenorphine.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Federal regulations require that appropriate analgesia be provided to laboratory animals for pain control. Carprofen and buprenorphine are 2 common analgesics used for laboratory mice (Mus musculus). However, given the potential gastrointestinal side effects that these analgesics have in various species, the impact of these analgesics on mice used in metabolic studies could be concerning. To investigate the impact of carprofen and sustained-release buprenorphine on food consumption, activity level, and whole-body metabolism, we administered carprofen alone or in combination with sustained-release buprenorphine to mice that underwent jugular vein and carotid artery catheterization, or a sham surgery. The mice were individually housed in instrumented metabolic cages to continuously quantify food consumption, activity levels, and energy expenditure by indirect calorimetry. We hypothesized that catheterized mice receiving both carprofen and sustained-release buprenorphine would have decreased food consumption and increased activity level compared with mice which received sham surgery and carprofen, and that catheterized mice treated with carprofen only would have similar food consumption and activity level as sham mice which received carprofen. Our results demonstrate that during the initial 12 hours after surgery, catheterized mice that received both carprofen and sustained-release buprenorphine were more active than sham mice which received carprofen, and they were more active and consumed more food than catheterized mice which received carprofen only. Our study demonstrated that analgesia regimen can affect metabolic parameters, thus, researchers should carefully consider the effects that analgesic drugs can have on mice when designing metabolic or behavioral experiments.
