evidence_results.verification_source: 1.IntroductionIn 1984, Glenner and Wong isolated and characterized amyloidogenic protein from patients with cerebrovascular amyloidosis and Alzheimer’s disease (AD; Glenner and Wong, 1984). At the time, the sequence of discovered amyloidogenic protein did not match the sequence of any known proteins. The authors proposed that newly discovered protein may provide a diagnostic test for AD. In addition, it was suggested that this protein may play causative role in pathogenesis of AD. Cloning of amyloid precursor protein (APP) in 1987 by Kang and colleagues (Kang et al., 1987), identified this protein as a fragment of APP named amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide. Several years later, formulation of amyloid hypothesis of AD (Hardy and Alsop, 1991; Selkoe, 1991), instigated intensive investigation of the role APP and Aβ in formation of amyloid plaques in brains of AD patients. Efforts to translate accumulated knowledge into clinical practice recently culminated in FDA approval of anti-amyloid antibodies for therapeutic application in patients with mild AD (Heneka et al., 2024; Sarazin et al., 2024; Knopman, 2025; Selkoe, 2024).In contrast to numerous advances in understanding of Aβ contribution to development of AD pathology, physiological roles of APP remain incompletely understood (Cho et al., 2022). Existing literature suggests that in the central nervous system, APP plays important roles in brain development, neurogenesis, and neuronal survival (Dawkins and Small, 2014; Muller et al., 2017). APP also participates in control of structure and function of synapse and memory function (Cho et al., 2022). Of particular interest to this review, APP is expressed in the brain endothelium, however, cerebrovascular function of APP has not been studied as extensively as function of APP in neuronal and glial cells (Ristori et al., 2020a and 2020b). In this review we summarize existing evidence supporting the concept that endothelial APP plays an important role in protection and preservation of cerebrovascular function. We also address potential therapeutic implications of recognized vascular protective effects of endothelial APP.2.Expression of APP in the brain blood vesselsAPP belongs to the family of glycoproteins highly expressed in the human brain, kidney, and platelets (d’Uscio et al., 2017). APP is an integral type I transmembrane protein with large extracellular N-terminal domain and short intracellular C-terminal domain that serve important physiological functions. Alternative splicing of APP gene results in production of three different isoforms encoding 695, 751, and 770 amino acids proteins (d’Uscio et al, 2017). APP695 is predominantly expressed in the brain neurons (Muller et al., 2017), while vascular endothelial cells mostly express APP751 and APP770 (Forloni et al., 1992; d’Uscio et al., 2017). The extracellular domain of APP770 includes a cysteine-rich globular domain (E1), acidic domain (AcD), Kunitz protease inhibitor (KPI) domain, Ox-2 domain, and helix-rich domain (E2) domain (Muller et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2022; Figure 1). Aβ extends from E2 domain into the cell membrane, and it is adjacent to AICD which is C-terminal fragment of APP generated by γ-secretase-mediated cleavage of APP (Figures 1 and 2). The human APP751 does not have Ox-2 domain, and APP695 lacks both Kunitz-type serine proteinase inhibitor (KPI) and Ox-2 domains (Figure 1; Muller et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2022). High sequence identity and similarity of E1, E2, and cytoplasmic domains of APP among different species supports the concept of evolutionary conservation characteristic of proteins responsible for very important physiological functions (Shariati and De Strooper, 2013; Cho et al., 2022). Historically, APP has been annotated as “All Purpose Protein” to indicate complexity and wide range of potential functions and signaling pathways dependent on intact function of APP (Shariati and De Strooper, 2013). One of the earliest recognized APP functions relevant for preservation of vascular function is an important role of KPI domain in regulation of blood vessel thrombosis (Xu et al., 2005). Studies with recombinant KPI domain showed that KPI is strong inhibitor of prothrombotic enzymes, including factor XIa, factor IXa, factor Xa, and tissue factor VIIa complex (Van Nostrand et al., 1990; Smith et al., 1990; Schmaier et al., 1993; Mahdi et al., 1995, and 2000). These findings were extended and validated in vivo by examination of cerebrovascular thrombosis in mice overexpressing APP770 in platelets, and global APP knockout mice (Xu et al., 2005). Overexpression of APP770 in platelets inhibits while genetic inactivation of APP accelerates blood coagulation. Thus, KPI domain of APP expressed in platelets and vascular endothelium is critically important in maintenance of normal hemostasis. Ox-2 domain is involved in protein-protein interactions and cellular signaling (Dawkins and Small, 2014; Nguyen, 2015). It is homologous to the Ox-2 membrane immunoregulatory glycoprotein also known as CD200 (Shao and Owens 2023). Functionally, Ox-2 could be involved in cell-surface binding and recognition (Nguyen, 2015) however, the exact function of this region remains to be determined.Interestingly, higher expression of APP has been detected in endothelium of cerebral arteries compared to endothelium of systemic and peripheral blood vessels (Kitazume et al., 2010). The physiological relevance of this difference is not clear, but it is consistent with prominent role of APP in control of cerebrovascular endothelial function (d’Uscio et al., 2018). Enzymes responsible for α, β, and γ-processing of APP (Figure 2) are expressed in endothelial cells of cerebral blood vessels (Davies et al., 1998). High expression of APP α-secretase, disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain-containing protein 10 (ADAM10) in cerebrovascular endothelium (Yang et al., 2022) is consistent with observations demonstrating that under physiological conditions, endothelial APP is for the most part processed by α-secretase thereby resulting in production and release of soluble APPα (sAPPα; d’Uscio et al., 2018, 2021). We also wish to point out that APP processing by α-secretase activity of ADAM10 inhibits production of Aβ because APP α-cleavage site is located within the Aβ domain (Mockett and Ryan, 2023). This mechanism is an important component of overall vascular protective function of APP α-processing. Notably, two additional APP-related genes are expressed in human cerebrovascular endothelium: amyloid precursor-like protein 1 (APLP1) and amyloid precursor-like protein 2 (APLP2; Yang et al., 2022; Figure 1). Of note, in endothelium, expression of APLP2 is significantly higher as compared to expression of APLP1 (Yang et al 2022). Moreover, APLP2 (but not APLP1) has KPI domain thereby suggesting that APLP2 also plays a role in regulation of hemostasis as anticoagulant. However, systematic analyses of APLP1 and APLP2 endothelial functions have not been carried out.Previous studies demonstrated that endothelium-specific deletion of APP in mice decreases circulating levels of sAPPα by about 30% to 50%. These observations suggest that endothelium is a major source of sAPPα in circulating blood (d’Uscio et al., 2018, 2021; He et al., 2018). In contrast, circulating levels of Aβ are not affected by endothelium-specific inactivation of APP thereby suggesting that under physiological conditions, endothelial APP is predominantly processed by non-amyloidogenic α-pathway.APP is expressed in cerebrovascular smooth muscle cells but at significantly lower levels as compared to the expression of APP in endothelium. For example, in human cerebral arteries, expression of APP mRNA is about 3-fold lower in smooth muscle cells as compared to expression of APP in endothelium (Yang et al., 2022). In addition, APP protein expression is hardly detectable in smooth muscle cells of murine aorta thus indicating that in systemic arteries basal expression of APP in smooth muscle may not significantly contribute to overall control of vascular function (d’Uscio et al., 2012). Notably, α, β, and γ-secretases are expressed in smooth muscle cells of human cerebral microvessels (Auerbach and Vinters, 2006). Previous study reported that hypoxia significantly reduces expression and activity of α-secretase, ADAM10, resulting in impaired production of sAPPα in human microvascular smooth muscle cells (Auerbach and Vinters, 2006). Interestingly, production of Aβ in smooth muscle cells is not affected by hypoxia (Auerbach and Vinters, 2006). The exact role of APP and sAPPα in regulation of vascular smooth muscle function requires further investigation.3.Molecular mechanisms underlying vascular protective function of APP3.1.APP knockout mice –The first study of APP-deficient mice phenotype was published in 1995, and it was focused on phenotypic changes in the central nervous system (Zheng et al., 1995). APP-knockout mice are viable, however, they exhibit reduction in body weight, impaired grip strength and locomotor activity, long-term-potentiation (LTP) deficit, and cognitive impairment (reviewed in Cho et al., 2022). A more recent examination of endothelial function in cerebral arteries derived from global and endothelium-specific APP knockout mice revealed that deletion of APP causes impairment of endothelium-dependent relaxations to acetylcholine but does not affect relaxations to nitric oxide (NO) donor DEANONOate (diethylamine diazeniumdiolate; d’Uscio et al., 2018). These observations suggest that loss of endothelial NO rather than reduced reactivity of smooth muscle cells to NO is responsible for observed impairment of vasomotor reactivity to acetylcholine. Most notably, both global and conditional endothelium-specific inactivation of APP causes significant down-regulation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) expression in the cerebral arteries. In agreement with these findings, production of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP; second messenger for NO) is also significantly reduced thereby providing mechanistic explanation for the impairment of vasodilatation to acetylcholine in APP-deficient cerebral arteries. In agreement with observations in mice, studies on cultured human brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs) demonstrated that genetic inactivation of APP downregulates expression of eNOS whereas overexpression of neuronal or endothelial isoform of APP causes significant up-regulation of eNOS protein (d’Uscio et al., 2018; He et al., 2023). Importantly, loss of endothelial APP function in cerebral arteries enhances vasoconstriction induced by endothelin-1 (ET-1). This observation provides additional evidence that maintaining normal endothelial APP expression is critically important for preservation of vasomotor function in the cerebral blood vessels.3.2.Alpha processing of APP –As already mentioned, α-processing of APP is a predominant mechanism in proteolytic cleavage of APP in endothelium. Efforts to define the role of sAPPα in control of eNOS function in human endothelium resulted in several unexpected and novel insights (He et al., 2023). Treatment of cultured human BMECs with recombinant sAPPα significantly increased expression of eNOS protein (He et al., 2023). This effect was observed in human BMECs treated with nanomolar concentration of sAPPα thereby suggesting that loss of sAPPα may help explain downregulation of eNOS expression in cerebral arteries of APP-deficient mice (d’Uscio et al., 2018). Additional insights into pharmacological properties of sAPPα were obtained by examination of the effect of APP 17mer (peptide derived from 204–220 amino acid of human APP695 extension domain; Rice et al., 2019; Figure 6), on protein expression of eNOS (He et al., 2003). APP 17mer significantly increased expression of eNOS. In addition, APP 17mer reduced inhibitory eNOS phosphorylation at Threonine 495 resulting in increased production of NO (He et al., 2023). It is important to emphasize that APP 17mer peptide sequence is shared among APP695, APP751, and APP770 (Rice et al., 2019; Figure 6) and that like sAPPα, stimulatory effects on eNOS protein expression were caused by nanomolar concentrations of APP 17mer (He et al., 2023).Efforts to define cell signaling mechanism activated by APP 17mer were based on previous reports demonstrating that in neurons, sAPPα binds to the N-terminal sushi 1 domain of γ-aminobutyric acid type B receptor subunit 1a (GABABR1a; Rice et al., 2019). Existing evidence indicates that GABBR1 gene is expressed in human brain endothelial cells (Yang et al., 2022) and that GABAB1a receptor subunit mediates APP 17mer-induced upregulation of Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2; He et al., 2023; Figure 3). KLF2 is a transcription factor highly expressed in endothelium. KLF2 activates transcription of eNOS, as well as anti-thrombotic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant genes (Gimbrone and Garcia-Cardena, 2016). Thus, impairment of APP expression and/or α-processing of APP may cause major abnormalities of key homeostatic functions of endothelium.3.3.APP silencing in cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) –Proteomic study in HUVECs examined the effects of genetic inactivation of APP by small interfering RNA (siRNA). Loss of APP function exerted wide range of detrimental effects on morphology, biochemistry, and function of endothelial cells (Ristori et al., 2020b). The authors validated selected group of pathways that are dependent on APP for maintenance of normal endothelial function. In aggregate, generated findings provided support for important role of APP in proliferation, migration, and cytoskeletal organization of endothelium (Ristori et al., 2020b). Moreover, APP appears to be an important regulator of endothelial cells reactivity to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Consequently, silencing of APP impaired angiogenesis stimulated by VEGF (Ristori et al., 2020b). Thus, entirely new and important insights into endothelial function of APP were generated by studies on cultured HUVECs. While these findings support the hypothesis that APP is a vascular protective protein, in vivo validation of observations obtained in cultured HUVECs requires additional studies.3.4.Beta processing of APP –Proteolytic cleavage of APP by β-site amyloid precursor protein-cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) resulting in production of Aβ peptides is evolutionary conserved mechanism. Indeed, Aβ sequence is highly conserved across most vertebrate species (Moir et al., 2018). These observations suggest that Aβ may play important roles in the neuronal and cerebrovascular functions. However, elevated local concentrations of Aβ peptides exerts cytotoxic effects leading to development of endothelial dysfunction and AD pathology (Iadecola, 2003; Cortes-Canteli and Iadecola, 2020; Meakin et al., 2020; Hampel et al., 2021; Scheltens et al., 2021). Indeed, Aβ peptides are considered major culprits in pathogenesis of AD and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA; Greenberg et al., 2020; Hampel et al., 2021; Scheltens et al., 2021; Koemans et al., 2023) and inhibition of APP β-processing remains an attractive therapeutic target in prevention and treatment of AD and associated endothelial dysfunction (McDade et al., 2021; Katusic et al., 2024).Regarding potential protective cerebrovascular functions of Aβ, existing evidence indicates that low nanomolar concentrations of Aβ peptides may promote cerebral endothelial cells proliferation, migration, and tube formation thereby suggesting that Aβ peptides could have proangiogenic function (Cantara et al., 2004; Cameron et al., 2012). However, these presumably beneficial proangiogenic effects of APP β-processing are controversial (Ristori et al., 2020a). Moreover, angiogenesis in the brain is associated with the breakdown of blood-brain-barrier (BBB; Biron, 2011) thereby causing alteration in neuronal function and exacerbation of AD pathology (Boscolo et al., 2007). Moreover, in patients with AD, angiogenesis contributes to formation of nonfunctional capillaries (so called “string vessels”) lacking endothelial cells (Brown 2010; Forsberg et al., 2018). Thus, potentially beneficial angiogenic function of APP β-processing appears to be detrimental to brain function in the context of AD.Another protective function of Aβ has been proposed based on observations demonstrating that Aβ may function as antimicrobial peptide (AMP; Moir et al., 2018; Lathe et al., 2023). AMPs have 12 to 50 amino acid residues with antimicrobial activity (Moir et al., 2018; Lathe et al., 2023). They are critically important components of innate immunity (Soscia et al., 2010). As such, they can kill pathogens thereby protecting endothelium and brain parenchyma from detrimental effects of infectious agents. Interestingly, Aβ1–42 exhibits more robust antibacterial and antiviral activity than Aβ1–40 (Soscia et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2024). However, both Aβ and AMPs have dual protective/damaging effects (Kumar et al., 2016). Extensive studies of the Aβ cytotoxicity demonstrated that pathologically high concentrations of Aβ have detrimental effects on endothelial mitochondrial function, they also increase permeability of BBB and impair endothelial cells viability (Parodi-Rullan et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022).4.Vascular protective function of APP during agingAging is an important risk factor for cerebrovascular disease and neurodegeneration. During aging, blood vessels undergo complex structural and functional changes which significantly increase risk for hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke, and cognitive impairment (Paneni et al., 2017; Ungvari et al., 2018; De Silva and Faraci, 2020). Regarding APP, of particular interest is observation demonstrating that during aging, in vivo expression of APP in mouse aortic endothelial cells is significantly increased (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Moreover, aging also increases expression of APP in endothelium derived from human brain capillaries (Chen et al., 2020). Consistent with these observations, circulating levels of sAPPα are also significantly higher in plasma of aged mice (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Interestingly, in plasma of old mice lacking expression of APP in endothelium, aging-induced increase of sAPPα is blunted by ~40% thereby suggesting that endothelial cells make significant contribution to aging-induced increase in circulating sAPPα (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Furthermore, genetic inactivation of endothelial APP function in aged aortas causes down-regulation of eNOS expression and increases production of superoxide anion (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Thus, besides protection of eNOS, endothelial APP inhibits production of superoxide anion, a chemical antagonist of NO and generator of a powerful oxidant, peroxynitrite (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Consistent with findings in mice, aging causes upregulation of APP in aged human platelets (Schuk et al., 2016) and neocortical neurons (Bernstein et al., 2003). Thus, in mice and humans, aging may increase systemic and local sAPPα concentrations. This phenomenon appears to be an adaptive mechanism designed to protect blood vessel walls from detrimental effects of aging.It is however very important to emphasize that the effects of APP upregulation could be detrimental for vascular function when physiological dominance of α-processing and production of sAPPα is impaired. In this regard, hypoxia and/or impairment of eNOS function may exacerbate β-processing of APP by inhibiting of α-processing enzyme ADAM10 (Salminen et al., 2017; Austin et al., 2020). Reduced activity of cerebrovascular α-secretase may contribute to deposition and accumulation of Aβ in cerebral blood vessels thus promoting development of CAA (Austin et al., 2020).5.APP as mediator of vascular protective functions of prostacyclin (PGI2) and NOPGI2 and NO are critically important endothelium-derived vascular protective molecules (Moncada, 2006; Flammer and Lűscher, 2010; Vanhoutte et al., 2016, 2017). Prior studies established that both prostacyclin and NO synergize in the protection of blood vessels (Moncada, 2006). More recently generated evidence supports the concept that protective functions of endothelial PGI2, and NO are in part dependent on their ability to control expression and processing of APP (d’Uscio et al., 2017). PGI2 and NO function in complementary fashion, namely, PGI2 promotes α-processing of APP leading to increased production of sAPPα (Figure 4; He et al., 2017) while basal production of NO in endothelium protects α-processing by suppressing expression and function of β-site amyloid-β precursor cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) and cytotoxicity of Aβ (Austin et al., 2010, 2013; Figure 5). Importantly, partial loss of NO in cerebral microvessels of aged heterozygous eNOS knockout mice causes downregulation of α-secretase, ADAM10, and reduces production of sAPPα (Austin et al., 2020; Figure 5).5.1.Endothelial PGI2 –Treatment of cultured human BMECs with stable analogues of PGI2, iloprost and cicaprost, significantly increases expression of APP and ADAM10 resulting in elevated production of sAPPα (He et al., 2017). Consistent with these in vitro observations, analysis of cerebral microvessels derived from PGI2 receptor (IP−/−) knockout mice, demonstrated that disruption of PGI2 signaling causes significant reduction in protein expression of APP and ADAM10 (He et al., 2019). This suggests that constitutive activation of IP receptors contributes to basal production of sAPPα in the brain microvessels. Examination of PGI2 signaling mechanisms established that activation of IP receptors stimulates adenylate cyclase activity and production of cyclic AMP leading to increase in protein expression of APP and ADAM10 as well as increased production of sAPPα (He et al., 2017; Figure 4).5.2.Endothelial NO –Impairment of eNOS function and reduced production of NO in endothelium of cerebral blood vessels are considered major mechanisms in pathogenesis of endothelial dysfunction (Katusic and Austin, 2014, Katusic et al., 2023, 2024). Loss of endothelial NO functions increases expression of APP and BACE1 (Austin et al., 2010, Kwak et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013) thereby resulting in excessive production of Aβ (Figure 5). We recently reviewed the role of intact endothelial NO production in protection against excessive β-processing of APP and development of CAA and AD pathology (Katusic et al., 2023). Most notably, impaired basal production of endothelial NO in cerebral microvessels derived from aged heterozygous eNOS+/− mice causes downregulation of ADAM10 and production of sAPPα (Figure 5). Since sAPPα exerts inhibitory effect on amyloidogenic processing of APP and production of Aβ (Obregon et al., 2012), loss of sAPPα may promote deposition of Aβ in blood vessel wall thereby contributing to development of CAA in eNOS+/− mice (Tan et al., 2015). Thus, aberrant functions of PGI2 and/or NO may impair protective functions of APP and significantly contribute to initiation and progression of endothelial dysfunction and development of AD and CAA pathologies.6.Inhibitory effects of senescence and diabetes on cerebrovascular expression of APPSenescent endothelial cells significantly contribute to structural and functional changes of blood vessel wall induced by aging (Clayton et al., 2023; Mahoney et al., 2024). Number of senescent endothelial cells increases with aging and treatment with senolytic drugs improves aging-induced endothelial dysfunction for the most part by restoring local vascular concentration of NO (Clayton et al., 2023; Mahoney et al., 2024). Of particular interest is the fact that replicative senescence causes down-regulation of APP protein expression resulting in reduced production of sAPPα in cultured human BMECs (Sun et al., 2018). Analysis of this phenomenon demonstrated that maturation of APP protein is impaired by replicative senescence (Kern et al., 2006). Why senescent endothelial cells lose APP and ability to produce sAPPα, whereas non-senescent aged endothelial cells increase expression of APP and production of sAPPα during aging is unknown. Importantly, senescent endothelium exhibits senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) responsible for production of cytokines, chemokines, and inflammatory mediators that create pro-inflammatory environment in blood vessel wall (Liu et al, 2018; Gonçalves and Keyes, 2022; Suda et al., 2023). Prior studies established that pro-inflammatory cytokines stimulate production of sAPPα from human BMECs (Kitazume et al., 2012). This may help explain increased APP expression and release of sAPPα in non-senescent aged endothelial cells exposed to pro-inflammatory cytokines (d’Uscio et al., 2021). However, excessive accumulation of senescent cells and high local concentration of pro-inflammatory cytokines may also shift protective non-amyloidogenic processing to amyloidogenic processing of APP (Sun et al., 2018) thus creating vicious circle resulting in loss of cerebrovascular homeostatic functions of APP. We note that existing evidence regarding the inhibitory effects of senescence on expression of APP were obtained in cultured human endothelial cells (Sun et al., 2018) and cultured fibroblasts (Kern et al., 2006). These findings require further in vivo validation.We also wish to point out that in cerebral microvessels derived from murine experimental model of type 1 diabetes, expression of APP and α-secretase ADAM10 as well as production of sAPPα are reduced (He et al., 2017). This is an important observation suggesting that diabetes may impair endothelial function by damaging vascular protective functions of APP. Loss of microvascular APP and sAPPα in diabetic cerebral microvessels causes significant reduction of sAPPα in hippocampus (He et al., 2017). This may help explain the mechanisms underlying detrimental effects of diabetes on hippocampal neurons.7.APP dyshomeostasisAPP dyshomeostasis refers to the aberrant expression, processing, and function of APP. Existing literature supports the concept that diverse homeostatic roles of the APP protect brain from harmful effects of AD risk factors and stressors (Casselli et al., 2020). In contrast to historically dominant therapeutic approach to AD based exclusively on recognized toxicity of Aβ peptides, APP dyshomeostasis hypothesis (Casselli et al., 2020) emphasizes need for comprehensive understanding of the role of impaired homeostatic functions of entire transmembrane APP protein and all cleavage products of APP (Casselli et al., 2020; Sirisi et al., 2024). This hypothesis provides much wider therapeutic framework for the development of therapies for prevention and treatment of AD.We have already discussed the role of endothelial dysfunction as a potential cause of APP dyshomeostasis in cerebral blood vessels. In addition, we also wish to point out that the importance of APP in neurovascular homeostasis has been strikingly illustrated by the study demonstrating that APP-deficient mice experience acute mortality in response to transient global cerebral ischemia. In contrast, mortality of wild type control mice is not affected (Koike et al., 2012). Moreover, hypoxia causes an increase in cerebral blood flow of control mice but significant decrease in cerebral blood flow of APP-deficient mice (Koike et al., 2012). The exact molecular mechanisms of ischemia-induced mortality and hypoxia-induced decrease in blood flow of APP-deficient mice have not been defined. Based on current understanding of cerebrovascular function of APP, we speculate that impaired production of endothelial NO resulting from genetic inactivation of APP (d’Uscio et al., 2018) is an important contributing factor. Relevance of these observations for pathogenesis of human disease require further studies.8.Therapeutic prospects8.1.Soluble APPα –Interest in therapeutic potential of sAPPα was instigated by the recognition of beneficial effects of sAPPα on survival and growth of cultured neurons (Mattison et al., 1993; Barger and Mattison 1996; Furukawa et al., 1996). Numerous studies on neuronal cells demonstrated that sAPPα has a wide range of therapeutically useful properties that could be harnessed in prevention and treatment of neurological diseases (reviewed by Mockett et la., 2017, Mockett and Ryan, 2023). Translational efforts designed to increase brain levels of sAPPα by promoting α-processing of APP or by delivery of exogenous recombinant sAPPα are ongoing. For instance, in a pilot study on patients diagnosed with mild to moderate AD, elevation of ADAM10 activity with vitamin A analogue, acitretin, was well tolerated and resulted in significant increase of sAPPα levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF; Endres et al., 2014). However, ADAM10 has broad substrate selectivity (more than 40 ADAM10 substrates have been identified in neuronal tissue) thereby presenting major challenges in efforts to develop drugs specifically targeting α-cleavage of APP. To solve this problem, fusion protein named synthetic α-secretase (SAS) was designed and delivered into hippocampus of 5xFAD mice by adenoassociated virus-9 (AAV9; Kim et al., 2024). Design of the fusion protein was based on discovery that nuclear inclusion (Nia) from turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) is a cytosolic protease with a specificity for the α-cleavage site consensus sequence present in APP (Kim et al., 2024). Overexpression of SAS in hippocampus increased production of sAPPα, reduced levels of Aβ and normalized the impaired recognition memory in 5xFAD mice. These observations are consistent with findings demonstrating that AAV9-mediated gene delivery of recombinant sAPPα in aged APP/PS1 murine model of AD, exerts beneficial effects on cognitive function (Mockett et al., 2017). Further optimization of gene transfer techniques and testing of AAV-mediated gene transfer in large animal models is required before initiation of clinical studies.Published translational studies reporting therapeutic application of sAPPα have been exclusively focused on improving impaired function of neuronal cells. Given the fact that sAPPα has several very important vascular protective properties, it will be of major interest to determine whether overexpression of recombinant SAS in the brain endothelial cells may exert vascular protective effects in experimental models of cerebrovascular disease. Moreover, studies designed to deliver recombinant sAPPα into cerebral blood vessels, including large cerebral arteries, arterioles and capillaries may provide entirely new insights into potential therapeutic value of recombinant sAPPα. Existing evidence suggests that improved understanding of molecular mechanisms underpinning vascular protective effects of sAPPα may also help in efforts to develop new vascular protective interventions.8.2.APP-Derived Peptides –Therapeutic properties of APP have been recognized by many pre-clinical studies. Ongoing efforts to translate therapeutic effects of APP into clinical applications are focused on AD, traumatic brain injury, and stroke. However, sAPPα is large protein difficult to deliver into the brain and to achieve therapeutically useful concentrations. To overcome these challenges, novel shorter biologically active peptides derived from APP have been developed. This approach targeting neuronal tissue has been reviewed by Mockett and Ryan (2023). Beneficial effects on neuronal function have been detected with the following APP-derived peptides: APP96–110, APP204–220, APP328–330, APP328–323, and APP597–612 (Figure 6). How these peptides may affect cerebrovascular function has not been studied except for APP-17mer (APP204–220) which we have already discussed. Of interest to therapeutic targeting of cerebral blood vessels is cationic arginine-rich peptide (CARP; APP95–110; Mockett and Ryan, 2023). Prior studies showed that cationic polypeptide (poly-L-arginine) causes endothelium-dependent relaxation of canine basilar artery by activation of eNOS and production of NO (Kinoshita et al., 1997). Whether neuroprotective effects of CARP are in part mediated by NO-induced vasodilatation and increased cerebral blood flow remains to be determined. In addition, examination of vascular effects of other APP-derived peptides may provide new insights into vascular contribution to reported beneficial effects of these molecules.9.ConclusionsStrong evolutionary conservation of APP supports the concept that APP plays important roles in cerebrovascular function. Endothelial APP protects and preserves normal expression of KLF2 and eNOS thereby promoting vasodilator, antioxidant, anti-thrombotic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-aging effects of endothelial KLF2 and NO. Moreover, existing evidence suggests that vascular protective functions of NO and PGI2 are in part mediated by their ability to protect and preserve α-processing of APP and production of sAPPα. Indeed, vascular protective function of APP appears to be in part mediated by production and secretion of sAPPα from endothelial cells. Existing in vitro and in vivo studies on neuronal cells suggest that sAPPα as well as APP-derived peptides may have therapeutic potential in treatment of AD, traumatic brain injury, and stroke. Advances in understanding of vascular protective functions of APP provide opportunities for further development and optimization of novel therapies targeting dysfunctional cerebral blood vessels.

source_paper.title: Cerebrovascular protective functions of amyloid precursor protein: progress and therapeutic prospects
source_paper.abstract: Under physiological conditions, amyloid precursor protein (APP) is critically important for normal brain development, neurogenesis, neuronal survival, and synaptic signaling. Dyshomeostasis of APP increases deposition and accumulation of amyloid β (Aβ) in the brain parenchyma and cerebral blood vessels thereby leading to development of Alzheimer’s disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy. In this review, we critically examine existing literature supporting the concept that endothelial APP performs important vascular protective functions in the brain. Studies in cultured human brain microvascular endothelium and cerebral arteries derived from genetically modified mice indicate that loss of APP impairs expression and function of Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) thereby causing endothelial dysfunction. Congruency between the findings obtained in murine and human cerebrovascular endothelium is consistent with strong evolutionary conservation of APP, and reinforces the concept that APP is an important vascular protective protein. Furthermore, we highlight vascular protective effects of APP during aging. We also address the roles of endothelial prostacyclin and nitric oxide in control of expression and proteolytic cleavage of APP. Finally, we outline potential translational opportunities emerging from recent advances in understanding of cerebrovascular function of APP. Several pharmacologically active domains of APP have been identified thus providing templates for creation of novel peptides with therapeutic properties.
source_paper.full_text: 1.IntroductionIn 1984, Glenner and Wong isolated and characterized amyloidogenic protein from patients with cerebrovascular amyloidosis and Alzheimer’s disease (AD; Glenner and Wong, 1984). At the time, the sequence of discovered amyloidogenic protein did not match the sequence of any known proteins. The authors proposed that newly discovered protein may provide a diagnostic test for AD. In addition, it was suggested that this protein may play causative role in pathogenesis of AD. Cloning of amyloid precursor protein (APP) in 1987 by Kang and colleagues (Kang et al., 1987), identified this protein as a fragment of APP named amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide. Several years later, formulation of amyloid hypothesis of AD (Hardy and Alsop, 1991; Selkoe, 1991), instigated intensive investigation of the role APP and Aβ in formation of amyloid plaques in brains of AD patients. Efforts to translate accumulated knowledge into clinical practice recently culminated in FDA approval of anti-amyloid antibodies for therapeutic application in patients with mild AD (Heneka et al., 2024; Sarazin et al., 2024; Knopman, 2025; Selkoe, 2024).In contrast to numerous advances in understanding of Aβ contribution to development of AD pathology, physiological roles of APP remain incompletely understood (Cho et al., 2022). Existing literature suggests that in the central nervous system, APP plays important roles in brain development, neurogenesis, and neuronal survival (Dawkins and Small, 2014; Muller et al., 2017). APP also participates in control of structure and function of synapse and memory function (Cho et al., 2022). Of particular interest to this review, APP is expressed in the brain endothelium, however, cerebrovascular function of APP has not been studied as extensively as function of APP in neuronal and glial cells (Ristori et al., 2020a and 2020b). In this review we summarize existing evidence supporting the concept that endothelial APP plays an important role in protection and preservation of cerebrovascular function. We also address potential therapeutic implications of recognized vascular protective effects of endothelial APP.2.Expression of APP in the brain blood vesselsAPP belongs to the family of glycoproteins highly expressed in the human brain, kidney, and platelets (d’Uscio et al., 2017). APP is an integral type I transmembrane protein with large extracellular N-terminal domain and short intracellular C-terminal domain that serve important physiological functions. Alternative splicing of APP gene results in production of three different isoforms encoding 695, 751, and 770 amino acids proteins (d’Uscio et al, 2017). APP695 is predominantly expressed in the brain neurons (Muller et al., 2017), while vascular endothelial cells mostly express APP751 and APP770 (Forloni et al., 1992; d’Uscio et al., 2017). The extracellular domain of APP770 includes a cysteine-rich globular domain (E1), acidic domain (AcD), Kunitz protease inhibitor (KPI) domain, Ox-2 domain, and helix-rich domain (E2) domain (Muller et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2022; Figure 1). Aβ extends from E2 domain into the cell membrane, and it is adjacent to AICD which is C-terminal fragment of APP generated by γ-secretase-mediated cleavage of APP (Figures 1 and 2). The human APP751 does not have Ox-2 domain, and APP695 lacks both Kunitz-type serine proteinase inhibitor (KPI) and Ox-2 domains (Figure 1; Muller et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2022). High sequence identity and similarity of E1, E2, and cytoplasmic domains of APP among different species supports the concept of evolutionary conservation characteristic of proteins responsible for very important physiological functions (Shariati and De Strooper, 2013; Cho et al., 2022). Historically, APP has been annotated as “All Purpose Protein” to indicate complexity and wide range of potential functions and signaling pathways dependent on intact function of APP (Shariati and De Strooper, 2013). One of the earliest recognized APP functions relevant for preservation of vascular function is an important role of KPI domain in regulation of blood vessel thrombosis (Xu et al., 2005). Studies with recombinant KPI domain showed that KPI is strong inhibitor of prothrombotic enzymes, including factor XIa, factor IXa, factor Xa, and tissue factor VIIa complex (Van Nostrand et al., 1990; Smith et al., 1990; Schmaier et al., 1993; Mahdi et al., 1995, and 2000). These findings were extended and validated in vivo by examination of cerebrovascular thrombosis in mice overexpressing APP770 in platelets, and global APP knockout mice (Xu et al., 2005). Overexpression of APP770 in platelets inhibits while genetic inactivation of APP accelerates blood coagulation. Thus, KPI domain of APP expressed in platelets and vascular endothelium is critically important in maintenance of normal hemostasis. Ox-2 domain is involved in protein-protein interactions and cellular signaling (Dawkins and Small, 2014; Nguyen, 2015). It is homologous to the Ox-2 membrane immunoregulatory glycoprotein also known as CD200 (Shao and Owens 2023). Functionally, Ox-2 could be involved in cell-surface binding and recognition (Nguyen, 2015) however, the exact function of this region remains to be determined.Interestingly, higher expression of APP has been detected in endothelium of cerebral arteries compared to endothelium of systemic and peripheral blood vessels (Kitazume et al., 2010). The physiological relevance of this difference is not clear, but it is consistent with prominent role of APP in control of cerebrovascular endothelial function (d’Uscio et al., 2018). Enzymes responsible for α, β, and γ-processing of APP (Figure 2) are expressed in endothelial cells of cerebral blood vessels (Davies et al., 1998). High expression of APP α-secretase, disintegrin and metalloproteinase domain-containing protein 10 (ADAM10) in cerebrovascular endothelium (Yang et al., 2022) is consistent with observations demonstrating that under physiological conditions, endothelial APP is for the most part processed by α-secretase thereby resulting in production and release of soluble APPα (sAPPα; d’Uscio et al., 2018, 2021). We also wish to point out that APP processing by α-secretase activity of ADAM10 inhibits production of Aβ because APP α-cleavage site is located within the Aβ domain (Mockett and Ryan, 2023). This mechanism is an important component of overall vascular protective function of APP α-processing. Notably, two additional APP-related genes are expressed in human cerebrovascular endothelium: amyloid precursor-like protein 1 (APLP1) and amyloid precursor-like protein 2 (APLP2; Yang et al., 2022; Figure 1). Of note, in endothelium, expression of APLP2 is significantly higher as compared to expression of APLP1 (Yang et al 2022). Moreover, APLP2 (but not APLP1) has KPI domain thereby suggesting that APLP2 also plays a role in regulation of hemostasis as anticoagulant. However, systematic analyses of APLP1 and APLP2 endothelial functions have not been carried out.Previous studies demonstrated that endothelium-specific deletion of APP in mice decreases circulating levels of sAPPα by about 30% to 50%. These observations suggest that endothelium is a major source of sAPPα in circulating blood (d’Uscio et al., 2018, 2021; He et al., 2018). In contrast, circulating levels of Aβ are not affected by endothelium-specific inactivation of APP thereby suggesting that under physiological conditions, endothelial APP is predominantly processed by non-amyloidogenic α-pathway.APP is expressed in cerebrovascular smooth muscle cells but at significantly lower levels as compared to the expression of APP in endothelium. For example, in human cerebral arteries, expression of APP mRNA is about 3-fold lower in smooth muscle cells as compared to expression of APP in endothelium (Yang et al., 2022). In addition, APP protein expression is hardly detectable in smooth muscle cells of murine aorta thus indicating that in systemic arteries basal expression of APP in smooth muscle may not significantly contribute to overall control of vascular function (d’Uscio et al., 2012). Notably, α, β, and γ-secretases are expressed in smooth muscle cells of human cerebral microvessels (Auerbach and Vinters, 2006). Previous study reported that hypoxia significantly reduces expression and activity of α-secretase, ADAM10, resulting in impaired production of sAPPα in human microvascular smooth muscle cells (Auerbach and Vinters, 2006). Interestingly, production of Aβ in smooth muscle cells is not affected by hypoxia (Auerbach and Vinters, 2006). The exact role of APP and sAPPα in regulation of vascular smooth muscle function requires further investigation.3.Molecular mechanisms underlying vascular protective function of APP3.1.APP knockout mice –The first study of APP-deficient mice phenotype was published in 1995, and it was focused on phenotypic changes in the central nervous system (Zheng et al., 1995). APP-knockout mice are viable, however, they exhibit reduction in body weight, impaired grip strength and locomotor activity, long-term-potentiation (LTP) deficit, and cognitive impairment (reviewed in Cho et al., 2022). A more recent examination of endothelial function in cerebral arteries derived from global and endothelium-specific APP knockout mice revealed that deletion of APP causes impairment of endothelium-dependent relaxations to acetylcholine but does not affect relaxations to nitric oxide (NO) donor DEANONOate (diethylamine diazeniumdiolate; d’Uscio et al., 2018). These observations suggest that loss of endothelial NO rather than reduced reactivity of smooth muscle cells to NO is responsible for observed impairment of vasomotor reactivity to acetylcholine. Most notably, both global and conditional endothelium-specific inactivation of APP causes significant down-regulation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) expression in the cerebral arteries. In agreement with these findings, production of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP; second messenger for NO) is also significantly reduced thereby providing mechanistic explanation for the impairment of vasodilatation to acetylcholine in APP-deficient cerebral arteries. In agreement with observations in mice, studies on cultured human brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs) demonstrated that genetic inactivation of APP downregulates expression of eNOS whereas overexpression of neuronal or endothelial isoform of APP causes significant up-regulation of eNOS protein (d’Uscio et al., 2018; He et al., 2023). Importantly, loss of endothelial APP function in cerebral arteries enhances vasoconstriction induced by endothelin-1 (ET-1). This observation provides additional evidence that maintaining normal endothelial APP expression is critically important for preservation of vasomotor function in the cerebral blood vessels.3.2.Alpha processing of APP –As already mentioned, α-processing of APP is a predominant mechanism in proteolytic cleavage of APP in endothelium. Efforts to define the role of sAPPα in control of eNOS function in human endothelium resulted in several unexpected and novel insights (He et al., 2023). Treatment of cultured human BMECs with recombinant sAPPα significantly increased expression of eNOS protein (He et al., 2023). This effect was observed in human BMECs treated with nanomolar concentration of sAPPα thereby suggesting that loss of sAPPα may help explain downregulation of eNOS expression in cerebral arteries of APP-deficient mice (d’Uscio et al., 2018). Additional insights into pharmacological properties of sAPPα were obtained by examination of the effect of APP 17mer (peptide derived from 204–220 amino acid of human APP695 extension domain; Rice et al., 2019; Figure 6), on protein expression of eNOS (He et al., 2003). APP 17mer significantly increased expression of eNOS. In addition, APP 17mer reduced inhibitory eNOS phosphorylation at Threonine 495 resulting in increased production of NO (He et al., 2023). It is important to emphasize that APP 17mer peptide sequence is shared among APP695, APP751, and APP770 (Rice et al., 2019; Figure 6) and that like sAPPα, stimulatory effects on eNOS protein expression were caused by nanomolar concentrations of APP 17mer (He et al., 2023).Efforts to define cell signaling mechanism activated by APP 17mer were based on previous reports demonstrating that in neurons, sAPPα binds to the N-terminal sushi 1 domain of γ-aminobutyric acid type B receptor subunit 1a (GABABR1a; Rice et al., 2019). Existing evidence indicates that GABBR1 gene is expressed in human brain endothelial cells (Yang et al., 2022) and that GABAB1a receptor subunit mediates APP 17mer-induced upregulation of Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2; He et al., 2023; Figure 3). KLF2 is a transcription factor highly expressed in endothelium. KLF2 activates transcription of eNOS, as well as anti-thrombotic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant genes (Gimbrone and Garcia-Cardena, 2016). Thus, impairment of APP expression and/or α-processing of APP may cause major abnormalities of key homeostatic functions of endothelium.3.3.APP silencing in cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) –Proteomic study in HUVECs examined the effects of genetic inactivation of APP by small interfering RNA (siRNA). Loss of APP function exerted wide range of detrimental effects on morphology, biochemistry, and function of endothelial cells (Ristori et al., 2020b). The authors validated selected group of pathways that are dependent on APP for maintenance of normal endothelial function. In aggregate, generated findings provided support for important role of APP in proliferation, migration, and cytoskeletal organization of endothelium (Ristori et al., 2020b). Moreover, APP appears to be an important regulator of endothelial cells reactivity to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Consequently, silencing of APP impaired angiogenesis stimulated by VEGF (Ristori et al., 2020b). Thus, entirely new and important insights into endothelial function of APP were generated by studies on cultured HUVECs. While these findings support the hypothesis that APP is a vascular protective protein, in vivo validation of observations obtained in cultured HUVECs requires additional studies.3.4.Beta processing of APP –Proteolytic cleavage of APP by β-site amyloid precursor protein-cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) resulting in production of Aβ peptides is evolutionary conserved mechanism. Indeed, Aβ sequence is highly conserved across most vertebrate species (Moir et al., 2018). These observations suggest that Aβ may play important roles in the neuronal and cerebrovascular functions. However, elevated local concentrations of Aβ peptides exerts cytotoxic effects leading to development of endothelial dysfunction and AD pathology (Iadecola, 2003; Cortes-Canteli and Iadecola, 2020; Meakin et al., 2020; Hampel et al., 2021; Scheltens et al., 2021). Indeed, Aβ peptides are considered major culprits in pathogenesis of AD and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA; Greenberg et al., 2020; Hampel et al., 2021; Scheltens et al., 2021; Koemans et al., 2023) and inhibition of APP β-processing remains an attractive therapeutic target in prevention and treatment of AD and associated endothelial dysfunction (McDade et al., 2021; Katusic et al., 2024).Regarding potential protective cerebrovascular functions of Aβ, existing evidence indicates that low nanomolar concentrations of Aβ peptides may promote cerebral endothelial cells proliferation, migration, and tube formation thereby suggesting that Aβ peptides could have proangiogenic function (Cantara et al., 2004; Cameron et al., 2012). However, these presumably beneficial proangiogenic effects of APP β-processing are controversial (Ristori et al., 2020a). Moreover, angiogenesis in the brain is associated with the breakdown of blood-brain-barrier (BBB; Biron, 2011) thereby causing alteration in neuronal function and exacerbation of AD pathology (Boscolo et al., 2007). Moreover, in patients with AD, angiogenesis contributes to formation of nonfunctional capillaries (so called “string vessels”) lacking endothelial cells (Brown 2010; Forsberg et al., 2018). Thus, potentially beneficial angiogenic function of APP β-processing appears to be detrimental to brain function in the context of AD.Another protective function of Aβ has been proposed based on observations demonstrating that Aβ may function as antimicrobial peptide (AMP; Moir et al., 2018; Lathe et al., 2023). AMPs have 12 to 50 amino acid residues with antimicrobial activity (Moir et al., 2018; Lathe et al., 2023). They are critically important components of innate immunity (Soscia et al., 2010). As such, they can kill pathogens thereby protecting endothelium and brain parenchyma from detrimental effects of infectious agents. Interestingly, Aβ1–42 exhibits more robust antibacterial and antiviral activity than Aβ1–40 (Soscia et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2024). However, both Aβ and AMPs have dual protective/damaging effects (Kumar et al., 2016). Extensive studies of the Aβ cytotoxicity demonstrated that pathologically high concentrations of Aβ have detrimental effects on endothelial mitochondrial function, they also increase permeability of BBB and impair endothelial cells viability (Parodi-Rullan et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022).4.Vascular protective function of APP during agingAging is an important risk factor for cerebrovascular disease and neurodegeneration. During aging, blood vessels undergo complex structural and functional changes which significantly increase risk for hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke, and cognitive impairment (Paneni et al., 2017; Ungvari et al., 2018; De Silva and Faraci, 2020). Regarding APP, of particular interest is observation demonstrating that during aging, in vivo expression of APP in mouse aortic endothelial cells is significantly increased (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Moreover, aging also increases expression of APP in endothelium derived from human brain capillaries (Chen et al., 2020). Consistent with these observations, circulating levels of sAPPα are also significantly higher in plasma of aged mice (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Interestingly, in plasma of old mice lacking expression of APP in endothelium, aging-induced increase of sAPPα is blunted by ~40% thereby suggesting that endothelial cells make significant contribution to aging-induced increase in circulating sAPPα (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Furthermore, genetic inactivation of endothelial APP function in aged aortas causes down-regulation of eNOS expression and increases production of superoxide anion (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Thus, besides protection of eNOS, endothelial APP inhibits production of superoxide anion, a chemical antagonist of NO and generator of a powerful oxidant, peroxynitrite (d’Uscio and Katusic, 2021). Consistent with findings in mice, aging causes upregulation of APP in aged human platelets (Schuk et al., 2016) and neocortical neurons (Bernstein et al., 2003). Thus, in mice and humans, aging may increase systemic and local sAPPα concentrations. This phenomenon appears to be an adaptive mechanism designed to protect blood vessel walls from detrimental effects of aging.It is however very important to emphasize that the effects of APP upregulation could be detrimental for vascular function when physiological dominance of α-processing and production of sAPPα is impaired. In this regard, hypoxia and/or impairment of eNOS function may exacerbate β-processing of APP by inhibiting of α-processing enzyme ADAM10 (Salminen et al., 2017; Austin et al., 2020). Reduced activity of cerebrovascular α-secretase may contribute to deposition and accumulation of Aβ in cerebral blood vessels thus promoting development of CAA (Austin et al., 2020).5.APP as mediator of vascular protective functions of prostacyclin (PGI2) and NOPGI2 and NO are critically important endothelium-derived vascular protective molecules (Moncada, 2006; Flammer and Lűscher, 2010; Vanhoutte et al., 2016, 2017). Prior studies established that both prostacyclin and NO synergize in the protection of blood vessels (Moncada, 2006). More recently generated evidence supports the concept that protective functions of endothelial PGI2, and NO are in part dependent on their ability to control expression and processing of APP (d’Uscio et al., 2017). PGI2 and NO function in complementary fashion, namely, PGI2 promotes α-processing of APP leading to increased production of sAPPα (Figure 4; He et al., 2017) while basal production of NO in endothelium protects α-processing by suppressing expression and function of β-site amyloid-β precursor cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1) and cytotoxicity of Aβ (Austin et al., 2010, 2013; Figure 5). Importantly, partial loss of NO in cerebral microvessels of aged heterozygous eNOS knockout mice causes downregulation of α-secretase, ADAM10, and reduces production of sAPPα (Austin et al., 2020; Figure 5).5.1.Endothelial PGI2 –Treatment of cultured human BMECs with stable analogues of PGI2, iloprost and cicaprost, significantly increases expression of APP and ADAM10 resulting in elevated production of sAPPα (He et al., 2017). Consistent with these in vitro observations, analysis of cerebral microvessels derived from PGI2 receptor (IP−/−) knockout mice, demonstrated that disruption of PGI2 signaling causes significant reduction in protein expression of APP and ADAM10 (He et al., 2019). This suggests that constitutive activation of IP receptors contributes to basal production of sAPPα in the brain microvessels. Examination of PGI2 signaling mechanisms established that activation of IP receptors stimulates adenylate cyclase activity and production of cyclic AMP leading to increase in protein expression of APP and ADAM10 as well as increased production of sAPPα (He et al., 2017; Figure 4).5.2.Endothelial NO –Impairment of eNOS function and reduced production of NO in endothelium of cerebral blood vessels are considered major mechanisms in pathogenesis of endothelial dysfunction (Katusic and Austin, 2014, Katusic et al., 2023, 2024). Loss of endothelial NO functions increases expression of APP and BACE1 (Austin et al., 2010, Kwak et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013) thereby resulting in excessive production of Aβ (Figure 5). We recently reviewed the role of intact endothelial NO production in protection against excessive β-processing of APP and development of CAA and AD pathology (Katusic et al., 2023). Most notably, impaired basal production of endothelial NO in cerebral microvessels derived from aged heterozygous eNOS+/− mice causes downregulation of ADAM10 and production of sAPPα (Figure 5). Since sAPPα exerts inhibitory effect on amyloidogenic processing of APP and production of Aβ (Obregon et al., 2012), loss of sAPPα may promote deposition of Aβ in blood vessel wall thereby contributing to development of CAA in eNOS+/− mice (Tan et al., 2015). Thus, aberrant functions of PGI2 and/or NO may impair protective functions of APP and significantly contribute to initiation and progression of endothelial dysfunction and development of AD and CAA pathologies.6.Inhibitory effects of senescence and diabetes on cerebrovascular expression of APPSenescent endothelial cells significantly contribute to structural and functional changes of blood vessel wall induced by aging (Clayton et al., 2023; Mahoney et al., 2024). Number of senescent endothelial cells increases with aging and treatment with senolytic drugs improves aging-induced endothelial dysfunction for the most part by restoring local vascular concentration of NO (Clayton et al., 2023; Mahoney et al., 2024). Of particular interest is the fact that replicative senescence causes down-regulation of APP protein expression resulting in reduced production of sAPPα in cultured human BMECs (Sun et al., 2018). Analysis of this phenomenon demonstrated that maturation of APP protein is impaired by replicative senescence (Kern et al., 2006). Why senescent endothelial cells lose APP and ability to produce sAPPα, whereas non-senescent aged endothelial cells increase expression of APP and production of sAPPα during aging is unknown. Importantly, senescent endothelium exhibits senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) responsible for production of cytokines, chemokines, and inflammatory mediators that create pro-inflammatory environment in blood vessel wall (Liu et al, 2018; Gonçalves and Keyes, 2022; Suda et al., 2023). Prior studies established that pro-inflammatory cytokines stimulate production of sAPPα from human BMECs (Kitazume et al., 2012). This may help explain increased APP expression and release of sAPPα in non-senescent aged endothelial cells exposed to pro-inflammatory cytokines (d’Uscio et al., 2021). However, excessive accumulation of senescent cells and high local concentration of pro-inflammatory cytokines may also shift protective non-amyloidogenic processing to amyloidogenic processing of APP (Sun et al., 2018) thus creating vicious circle resulting in loss of cerebrovascular homeostatic functions of APP. We note that existing evidence regarding the inhibitory effects of senescence on expression of APP were obtained in cultured human endothelial cells (Sun et al., 2018) and cultured fibroblasts (Kern et al., 2006). These findings require further in vivo validation.We also wish to point out that in cerebral microvessels derived from murine experimental model of type 1 diabetes, expression of APP and α-secretase ADAM10 as well as production of sAPPα are reduced (He et al., 2017). This is an important observation suggesting that diabetes may impair endothelial function by damaging vascular protective functions of APP. Loss of microvascular APP and sAPPα in diabetic cerebral microvessels causes significant reduction of sAPPα in hippocampus (He et al., 2017). This may help explain the mechanisms underlying detrimental effects of diabetes on hippocampal neurons.7.APP dyshomeostasisAPP dyshomeostasis refers to the aberrant expression, processing, and function of APP. Existing literature supports the concept that diverse homeostatic roles of the APP protect brain from harmful effects of AD risk factors and stressors (Casselli et al., 2020). In contrast to historically dominant therapeutic approach to AD based exclusively on recognized toxicity of Aβ peptides, APP dyshomeostasis hypothesis (Casselli et al., 2020) emphasizes need for comprehensive understanding of the role of impaired homeostatic functions of entire transmembrane APP protein and all cleavage products of APP (Casselli et al., 2020; Sirisi et al., 2024). This hypothesis provides much wider therapeutic framework for the development of therapies for prevention and treatment of AD.We have already discussed the role of endothelial dysfunction as a potential cause of APP dyshomeostasis in cerebral blood vessels. In addition, we also wish to point out that the importance of APP in neurovascular homeostasis has been strikingly illustrated by the study demonstrating that APP-deficient mice experience acute mortality in response to transient global cerebral ischemia. In contrast, mortality of wild type control mice is not affected (Koike et al., 2012). Moreover, hypoxia causes an increase in cerebral blood flow of control mice but significant decrease in cerebral blood flow of APP-deficient mice (Koike et al., 2012). The exact molecular mechanisms of ischemia-induced mortality and hypoxia-induced decrease in blood flow of APP-deficient mice have not been defined. Based on current understanding of cerebrovascular function of APP, we speculate that impaired production of endothelial NO resulting from genetic inactivation of APP (d’Uscio et al., 2018) is an important contributing factor. Relevance of these observations for pathogenesis of human disease require further studies.8.Therapeutic prospects8.1.Soluble APPα –Interest in therapeutic potential of sAPPα was instigated by the recognition of beneficial effects of sAPPα on survival and growth of cultured neurons (Mattison et al., 1993; Barger and Mattison 1996; Furukawa et al., 1996). Numerous studies on neuronal cells demonstrated that sAPPα has a wide range of therapeutically useful properties that could be harnessed in prevention and treatment of neurological diseases (reviewed by Mockett et la., 2017, Mockett and Ryan, 2023). Translational efforts designed to increase brain levels of sAPPα by promoting α-processing of APP or by delivery of exogenous recombinant sAPPα are ongoing. For instance, in a pilot study on patients diagnosed with mild to moderate AD, elevation of ADAM10 activity with vitamin A analogue, acitretin, was well tolerated and resulted in significant increase of sAPPα levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF; Endres et al., 2014). However, ADAM10 has broad substrate selectivity (more than 40 ADAM10 substrates have been identified in neuronal tissue) thereby presenting major challenges in efforts to develop drugs specifically targeting α-cleavage of APP. To solve this problem, fusion protein named synthetic α-secretase (SAS) was designed and delivered into hippocampus of 5xFAD mice by adenoassociated virus-9 (AAV9; Kim et al., 2024). Design of the fusion protein was based on discovery that nuclear inclusion (Nia) from turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) is a cytosolic protease with a specificity for the α-cleavage site consensus sequence present in APP (Kim et al., 2024). Overexpression of SAS in hippocampus increased production of sAPPα, reduced levels of Aβ and normalized the impaired recognition memory in 5xFAD mice. These observations are consistent with findings demonstrating that AAV9-mediated gene delivery of recombinant sAPPα in aged APP/PS1 murine model of AD, exerts beneficial effects on cognitive function (Mockett et al., 2017). Further optimization of gene transfer techniques and testing of AAV-mediated gene transfer in large animal models is required before initiation of clinical studies.Published translational studies reporting therapeutic application of sAPPα have been exclusively focused on improving impaired function of neuronal cells. Given the fact that sAPPα has several very important vascular protective properties, it will be of major interest to determine whether overexpression of recombinant SAS in the brain endothelial cells may exert vascular protective effects in experimental models of cerebrovascular disease. Moreover, studies designed to deliver recombinant sAPPα into cerebral blood vessels, including large cerebral arteries, arterioles and capillaries may provide entirely new insights into potential therapeutic value of recombinant sAPPα. Existing evidence suggests that improved understanding of molecular mechanisms underpinning vascular protective effects of sAPPα may also help in efforts to develop new vascular protective interventions.8.2.APP-Derived Peptides –Therapeutic properties of APP have been recognized by many pre-clinical studies. Ongoing efforts to translate therapeutic effects of APP into clinical applications are focused on AD, traumatic brain injury, and stroke. However, sAPPα is large protein difficult to deliver into the brain and to achieve therapeutically useful concentrations. To overcome these challenges, novel shorter biologically active peptides derived from APP have been developed. This approach targeting neuronal tissue has been reviewed by Mockett and Ryan (2023). Beneficial effects on neuronal function have been detected with the following APP-derived peptides: APP96–110, APP204–220, APP328–330, APP328–323, and APP597–612 (Figure 6). How these peptides may affect cerebrovascular function has not been studied except for APP-17mer (APP204–220) which we have already discussed. Of interest to therapeutic targeting of cerebral blood vessels is cationic arginine-rich peptide (CARP; APP95–110; Mockett and Ryan, 2023). Prior studies showed that cationic polypeptide (poly-L-arginine) causes endothelium-dependent relaxation of canine basilar artery by activation of eNOS and production of NO (Kinoshita et al., 1997). Whether neuroprotective effects of CARP are in part mediated by NO-induced vasodilatation and increased cerebral blood flow remains to be determined. In addition, examination of vascular effects of other APP-derived peptides may provide new insights into vascular contribution to reported beneficial effects of these molecules.9.ConclusionsStrong evolutionary conservation of APP supports the concept that APP plays important roles in cerebrovascular function. Endothelial APP protects and preserves normal expression of KLF2 and eNOS thereby promoting vasodilator, antioxidant, anti-thrombotic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-aging effects of endothelial KLF2 and NO. Moreover, existing evidence suggests that vascular protective functions of NO and PGI2 are in part mediated by their ability to protect and preserve α-processing of APP and production of sAPPα. Indeed, vascular protective function of APP appears to be in part mediated by production and secretion of sAPPα from endothelial cells. Existing in vitro and in vivo studies on neuronal cells suggest that sAPPα as well as APP-derived peptides may have therapeutic potential in treatment of AD, traumatic brain injury, and stroke. Advances in understanding of vascular protective functions of APP provide opportunities for further development and optimization of novel therapies targeting dysfunctional cerebral blood vessels.

PAPER:

TITLE:
Cerebrovascular protective functions of amyloid precursor protein: progress and therapeutic prospects

ABSTRACT:
Under physiological conditions, amyloid precursor protein (APP) is critically important for normal brain development, neurogenesis, neuronal survival, and synaptic signaling. Dyshomeostasis of APP increases deposition and accumulation of amyloid β (Aβ) in the brain parenchyma and cerebral blood vessels thereby leading to development of Alzheimer’s disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy. In this review, we critically examine existing literature supporting the concept that endothelial APP performs important vascular protective functions in the brain. Studies in cultured human brain microvascular endothelium and cerebral arteries derived from genetically modified mice indicate that loss of APP impairs expression and function of Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) thereby causing endothelial dysfunction. Congruency between the findings obtained in murine and human cerebrovascular endothelium is consistent with strong evolutionary conservation of APP, and reinforces the concept that APP is an important vascular protective protein. Furthermore, we highlight vascular protective effects of APP during aging. We also address the roles of endothelial prostacyclin and nitric oxide in control of expression and proteolytic cleavage of APP. Finally, we outline potential translational opportunities emerging from recent advances in understanding of cerebrovascular function of APP. Several pharmacologically active domains of APP have been identified thus providing templates for creation of novel peptides with therapeutic properties.

TITLE:
Cerebrovascular protective functions of amyloid precursor protein: progress and therapeutic prospects

ABSTRACT:
Under physiological conditions, amyloid precursor protein (APP) is critically important for normal brain development, neurogenesis, neuronal survival, and synaptic signaling. Dyshomeostasis of APP increases deposition and accumulation of amyloid β (Aβ) in the brain parenchyma and cerebral blood vessels thereby leading to development of Alzheimer’s disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy. In this review, we critically examine existing literature supporting the concept that endothelial APP performs important vascular protective functions in the brain. Studies in cultured human brain microvascular endothelium and cerebral arteries derived from genetically modified mice indicate that loss of APP impairs expression and function of Krüppel-like Factor 2 (KLF2) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) thereby causing endothelial dysfunction. Congruency between the findings obtained in murine and human cerebrovascular endothelium is consistent with strong evolutionary conservation of APP, and reinforces the concept that APP is an important vascular protective protein. Furthermore, we highlight vascular protective effects of APP during aging. We also address the roles of endothelial prostacyclin and nitric oxide in control of expression and proteolytic cleavage of APP. Finally, we outline potential translational opportunities emerging from recent advances in understanding of cerebrovascular function of APP. Several pharmacologically active domains of APP have been identified thus providing templates for creation of novel peptides with therapeutic properties.

retrieved_papers.title: The Lotus japonicus alpha Expansin EXPA1 is recruited during intracellular and intercellular rhizobial colonization
retrieved_papers.abstract:
ABSTRACT

Most legumes establish a mutualistic association with rhizobia, a group of nitrogen-fixing bacteria. In Lotus japonicus , the symbiotic colonization occurs intracellularly, via root-hair infection threads by Mesorhizobium loti , or intercellularly, with Agrobacterium pusense IRBG74. In both mechanisms, cell wall remodeling is presumably an essential process. In plants, alpha-Expansins (EXPA) promote cell wall loosening by non-enzymatically triggering a pH-dependent relaxation. In this study, we show that LjEXPA1, is critical for the intracellular and intercellular symbiotic program in L. japonicus . Promoter activity and subcellular localization analyses revealed that EXPA1 is recruited at essential compartments and structures of epidermal and cortical cells in both mechanisms of rhizobial infection, such as the infection chambers, infection pockets and transcellular infection threads. Additionally, EXPA1-YFP abundantly accumulated in dividing cortical cells during nodule formation. The expression profile of EXPA1 correlates with the symbiotic phenotype observed in homozygous mutants disrupted in the EXPA 1 gene ( expA1 -1 and expA1 -2). Infection thread formation and intercellular colonization was drastically reduced in expA1 -1 and expA1 -2 mutants, respect to wild type plants. Similarly, nodule formation was significantly reduced in these mutants after M. loti or IRBG74 inoculation. Our results indicate that non-enzymatic cell wall remodeling by the alpha Expansin EXPA1 is crucial for the successful establishment of Lotus -rhizobia symbiosis, regardless of the infection mechanism.

retrieved_papers.title: Consequences of double virus infections on host plant preference and performance of <i>Aphis gossypii</i> (Hemiptera: Aphididae).
retrieved_papers.abstract: Understanding virus-vector-host interactions in the context of mixed infections is crucial to predict virus spread and develop effective control measures in economically important crops. The virus transmission process plays a central role in plant disease epidemiology and is particularly influenced by vector behavior and life-history traits. However, how mixed virus infections shape vector fitness and host preference remains poorly understood. Here, we determined the effects of double infections with the noncirculative cucumber mosaic virus (CMV, Cucumovirus) and the circulative cucurbit aphid-borne yellows virus (CABYV, Polerovirus) on the fitness and host plant preference of the aphid Aphis gossypii Glover on the host plant, melon (Cucumis melo L.). We revealed that aphids feeding on melon infected only with CMV (single-infected) weighed less and had lower fecundity than those feeding on uninfected plants or CABYV single- or double-infected plants. The mean relative growth rate and, consequently, the intrinsic rate of natural increase were also lower in aphids on CMV single-infected plants, indicating a negative impact of CMV single-infection on aphid fitness. In choice experiments, aphids were initially attracted to CABYV/CMV double-infected plants, but this was followed by a shift in host preference toward mock-inoculated plants over time. These findings suggest that mixed infections can modulate vector behavior in complex and dynamic ways. The pattern of early attraction followed by dispersal appears to promote CMV spread while having limited consequences for CABYV transmission, indicating an asymmetrical benefit between these 2 viruses.

retrieved_papers.title: Adaptation of turnip mosaic virus to Arabidopsis thaliana involves rewiring of VPg-host proteome interactions.
retrieved_papers.abstract: The outcome of a viral infection depends on a complex interplay between the host physiology and the virus, mediated through numerous protein-protein interactions. In a previous study, we used high-throughput yeast two-hybrid (HT-Y2H) to identify proteins in Arabidopsis thaliana that bind to the proteins encoded by the turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) genome. Furthermore, after experimental evolution of TuMV lineages in plants with mutations in defense-related or proviral genes, most mutations observed in the evolved viruses affected the VPg cistron. Among these mutations, D113G was a convergent mutation selected in many lineages across different plant genotypes, including cpr5-2 with constitutive expression of systemic acquired resistance. In contrast, mutation R118H specifically emerged in the jin1 mutant with affected jasmonate signaling. Using the HT-Y2H system, we analyzed the impact of these two mutations on VPg's interaction with plant proteins. Interestingly, both mutations severely compromised the interaction of VPg with the translation initiation factor eIF(iso)4E, a crucial interactor for potyvirus infection. Moreover, mutation D113G, but not R118H, adversely affected the interaction with RHD1, a zinc-finger homeodomain transcription factor involved in regulating DNA demethylation. Our results suggest that RHD1 enhances plant tolerance to TuMV infection. We also discuss our findings in a broad virus evolution context.

retrieved_papers.title: Genome-Wide Analysis and Expression Profiling of Soybean RbcS Family in Response to Plant Hormones and Functional Identification of GmRbcS8 in Soybean Mosaic Virus.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Rubisco small subunit (RbcS), a core component with crucial effects on the structure and kinetic properties of the Rubisco enzyme, plays an important role in response to plant growth, development, and various stresses. Although Rbcs genes have been characterized in many plants, their muti-functions in soybeans remain elusive. In this study, a total of 11 GmRbcS genes were identified and subsequently divided into three subgroups based on a phylogenetic relationship. The evolutionary analysis revealed that whole-genome duplication has a profound effect on GmRbcSs. The cis-acting elements responsive to plant hormones, development, and stress-related were widely found in the promoter region. Expression patterns based on the RT-qPCR assay exhibited that GmRbcS genes are expressed in multiple tissues, and notably Glyma.19G046600 (GmRbcS8) exhibited the highest expression level compared to other members, especially in leaves. Moreover, differential expressions of GmRbcS genes were found to be significantly regulated by exogenous plant hormones, demonstrating their potential functions in diverse biology processes. Finally, the function of GmRbcS8 in enhancing soybean resistance to soybean mosaic virus (SMV) was further determined through the virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) assay. All these findings establish a strong basis for further elucidating the biological functions of RbcS genes in soybeans.
