They play significant roles in regulating growth and development, cell differentiation, immune responses, the occurrence and progression of cancer, as well as virus transmission.1 PENs exhibit structural characteristics similar to mammalian exosomes and represent a safer alternative with reduced risks, owing to their lower immunogenicity, high biocompatibility, and negligible risk of pathogen transmission or tumorigenic contamination commonly associated with animal derived counterparts.2 They not only exert positive effects on various physiological processes but also carry an abundance of bioactive molecules, such as polyphenols, flavonoids, polysaccharides, and terpenoids.3 These molecules are abundant in organisms and play significant roles. Plant and fruit extracts have long been studied for their anticancer properties. Fruit derived ENs are scalable and biocompatible, offering a novel strategy for cancer therapy.4 This characteristic enables them to meet the growing demand for delivering natural bioactive compounds through nutrition or as therapeutic delivery systems. Moreover, PENs have demonstrated efficacy in modulating inflammation and oxidative processes, as well as promoting skin wound healing.5,6The skin is one of the largest and most vital organs of the human body, composed of three structural layers: the outermost epidermis, the middle dermis, and the deepest subcutaneous tissue.7 As the primary protective barrier against the external environment, the skin performs multiple physiological functions in maintaining overall health, such as barrier protection, sensory perception, thermoregulation, immune defense, and metabolic activities.8 Skin damage can be caused by physical, chemical, biological, or pathological factors (such as burns, cuts, infections, or chronic diseases), leading to compromised barrier function, moisture loss, increased risk of infection, and reduced immune function. Severe damage may also trigger systemic inflammatory responses, posing life threatening risks.In recent years, the biological and functional properties of ENs have begun to be extensively studied, with the beneficial effects of PENs on human health gradually gaining attention.9 This article provides a comprehensive review of the current research status of PENs and their impacts on human tissue physiological functions, skin inflammation, wound healing, and related areas. The aim is to explore the roles and mechanisms of PENs in the skin and to establish a theoretical foundation for better safeguarding human health.Traditional therapeutic approaches for skin wounds, including surgical debridement, skin grafting, and the application of synthetic dressings or growth factor formulations, have considerably improved acute wound management.10 However, these strategies often face significant limitations, such as poor bioavailability of bioactive agents, insufficient penetration into deep tissue layers, suboptimal control over the inflammatory microenvironment, and unsatisfactory outcomes in chronic or large area wounds due to impaired angiogenesis and re-epithelialization.11 Consequently, there is an urgent need for innovative therapeutic platforms that can simultaneously modulate inflammation, promote tissue regeneration, and restore skin appendages. PENs offer distinct advantages that directly address the aforementioned limitations of conventional wound therapies. On one hand, their lipid bilayer membrane structure enables efficient encapsulation and protection of bioactive molecules, significantly improving bioavailability and allowing sustained release at wound sites;12 on the other hand, PENs possess intrinsic bioactive cargo that exerts anti-inflammatory effects, for instance, downregulating NF-κB, IL-6, and TNF-α while promoting M2 macrophage polarization and facilitate angiogenesis and re-epithelialization through PI3K-Akt and TGF-β signaling pathways.13,14 These multifunctional properties position PENs as a next generation therapeutic platform that actively participates in tissue repair.The translational potential of PENs has gained considerable momentum in recent years. Plant sources offer abundant raw materials and scalability, overcoming yield constraints of mammalian derived exosomes,12 while advances in isolation technologies have improved batch-to-batch reproducibility.13 Moreover, integration of PENs with functional biomaterials (eg, hydrogels and microneedles) enhances skin penetration and targeted delivery.15 Notably, recent preclinical studies have demonstrated efficacy in diabetic wound healing, with lemon derived nanovesicles promoting macrophage reprogramming and angiogenesis.16,17 Although clinical translation remains in early stages, the expanding evidence supports the feasibility of PENs for skin repair.12Despite these promising prospects, the rapid growth of this field has exposed several critical bottlenecks that must be resolved prior to widespread clinical application. Primary challenges include the lack of standardized isolation protocols affecting reproducibility, incomplete understanding of tissue specific targeting mechanisms, and insufficient long term biosafety data.18 To overcome the scalability and standardization hurdles, advanced downstream processing technologies, such as tangential flow filtration (TFF) and microfluidic based isolation, are increasingly being adopted to replace conventional ultracentrifugation, thereby securing high yield, current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) compliant manufacturing.19 Furthermore, to circumvent off-target effects and enhance deep-tissue penetration, cutting-edge bioengineering strategies are emerging. By modifying the lipid surface of PENs with specific targeting ligands or co-assembling them into stimuli-responsive smart hydrogels, researchers can achieve spatiotemporally controlled release perfectly synchronized with the dynamic phases of wound healing.20 From a regulatory standpoint, establishing comprehensive multi-omics databases (eg, lipidomics and transcriptomics) and rigorous Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) criteria will be pivotal in translating PENs from benchtop discoveries into approved nanomedicines.21 Importantly, while numerous reviews have summarized the general bioactivities of PENs, a comprehensive analysis integrating their regulatory roles across the entire cascade of skin repair is still lacking. For instance, a recent comprehensive review by Lou et al thoroughly discussed the immunomodulatory functions of PENs in skin health.22 In contrast, the present review adopts a distinct and complementary tissue regeneration-axis perspective, systematically dissecting how PENs orchestrate macrophage polarization during the inflammatory phase, promote fibroblast keratinocyte crosstalk in the proliferative phase, enhance vascular remodeling, and stimulate nerve and appendage regeneration (eg, hair follicles and sebaceous glands). This regenerative centric framework bridges the mechanistic actions of PENs with the practical requirements of functional skin restoration, while also critically assessing translational challenges in scale up production, quality control, and regulatory pathways. This article ultimately aims to provide a holistic and forward looking resource for researchers and clinicians, establishing a theoretical foundation for leveraging PENs based nanotherapeutics to safeguard human dermatological health.The Concept of PENsPENs are nanoscale vesicles with a lipid bilayer structure actively secreted or released by plant cells into the extracellular environment. Their diameter typically ranges from 30 to 1000 nanometers, and they resemble animal derived exosomes in morphology, size, and certain biosynthetic mechanisms, thus often referred to as “exosome-like” nanovesicles.23 PENs possess unique structures and compositions, enabling them to participate in various biological functions such as intercellular communication, material transport, immune regulation, antioxidant activity, and tissue repair.24 Based on their origin and function, they can be further categorized into various types such as exosomes, apoptotic bodies, micro vesicles, and apoptotic body derived vesicles, all of which hold significant biological functions and potential application value. Three major pathways for PENs secretion have been identified (Figure 1). ① MVBs pathway: multivesicular bodies (MVBs) fuse with the cell membrane, releasing intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) into the extracellular space, thereby forming PENs.25 ②EXPO pathway: Exocyst positive organelles (EXPOs) are double membraned structures that fuse with the plasma membrane to release vesicles. This is a plant specific unconventional pathway.26 ③Vacuolar pathway: the central vacuole fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing hydrolases and defense related proteins, and may also contribute to PENs formation.27 Among the three pathways for PENs secretion, the MVBs pathway is considered dominant.25,28 In the MVBs pathway, early endosomes mature into MVBs, encapsulating RNA, DNA, lipids, and proteins into ILVs, which are released as PENs upon fusion with the plasma membrane.3,29 This process is highly similar to mammalian derived exosomes (MDEs).30–33 The EXPO pathway releases single membrane vesicles via fusion of double membraned structures with the plasma membrane.26 The vacuolar pathway mainly functions in plant defense, releasing hydrolytic enzymes and defense proteins during pathogen attack.34 Figure 1Diverse secretory pathways mediating the extracellular release of PENs.The diagram illustrates the secretion of plant extracellular nanovesicles (PENs) from a plant cell. Three pathways are depicted: multivesicular bodies (MVBs), exocyst positive organelles (EXPO) and vacuolar pathways. The EXPO pathway involves double membraned structures that fuse with the plasma membrane to release vesicles. The nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum and other cellular components are labeled within the plant cell structure.Diagram of plant cell showing PENs secretion via MVBs, EXPO and vacuolar pathways with labeled components.These ENs feature a phospholipid bilayer structure and contain a variety of bioactive molecules, including lipids, proteins, RNA, and other metabolites.35 Therefore, these ENs are recognized as important mediators of intercellular communication among plant cells and also serve as cross-kingdom communication carriers. They participate in key physiological processes such as signal transduction, nutrient transport, and plant immune responses, enabling information exchange between plants and pathogens.36,37 PENs play a critical role in signal transduction. When plants are subjected to biotic or abiotic stress, PENs can transport signaling molecules to neighboring cells, thereby triggering a series of defense responses. This mechanism is referred to as the “signalosome”, which effectively regulates plant immune responses and enhances resistance against pathogens. By transferring information and substances, PENs promote intercellular interactions and coordination, supporting plant growth, development, and adaptation to environmental stress. Notably, PENs are not limited to communication within plant cells; they also participate in interactions between plants and microorganisms. By carrying specific small RNAs, PENs enable cross-kingdom communication between plants and pathogens. Such cross-boundary signaling allows plants to better recognize and respond to pathogen invasion, thereby activating their own defense mechanisms.38 PENs also play a significant role in nutrient transport and substance translocation. They can serve as carriers for transporting essential nutrients and signaling molecules required by plants, ensuring nutritional balance and material exchange between cells. This mechanism is crucial for plant growth and development, especially under environmental stress, where PENs assist plants in adjusting their metabolic processes to adapt to varying growth conditions.24,39,40 In the plant immune system, they rapidly respond to pathogen attacks by mediating intercellular signal transmission. When pathogens invade plants, the plants release vesicles to convey alarm signals, stimulating neighboring cells to enhance their defensive capabilities. Furthermore, these ENs can carry specific molecules for combating pathogens, thereby directly participating in the plant’s defense responses.41PENs may play an important role in regulating the gut microbiome in recent studies. By modulating the composition of intestinal microorganisms, plants can indirectly influence their own growth and health. This indicates that PENs not only function within plants but may also impact health and disease states through interactions with the gut microbiota of animals, including humans.42Isolation and Characterization of PENsIsolation and PurificationCommonly employed isolation techniques primarily encompass the following: ultracentrifugation (UC), polymer based precipitation, sucrose density gradient ultracentrifugation, immunoaffinity capture, ultrafiltration, nanotechnology-based methods, size exclusion chromatography (SEC), and commercial kits (Figure 2). Figure 2Isolation of PENs: Overview of Major Methods.The diagram illustrates six methods for isolating PENs. Ultracentrifugation involves low and high-speed centrifugation. Polymer-based precipitation uses PEG and a 12-hour process. Sucrose density gradient ultracentrifugation involves layering a sucrose solution and centrifugation. Nanotechnology includes pre-filtration and DLD. SEC (size exclusion chromatography) is based on time and volume. Immunoaffinity capture-based method uses specific binding interactions.Diagram of six methods for isolating PENs, including ultracentrifugation and nanotechnology.Ultracentrifugation (UC) remains the most prevalent technique for isolating PENs and is widely regarded as the “gold standard”.43 The fundamental principle involves the application of centrifugal force to segregate PENs from biological fluids. Specifically, ENs of similar diameters are isolated through alternating cycles of low speed and high speed centrifugation. While this method is characterized by high efficiency and relative technical simplicity, its primary drawbacks include prolonged processing times and the potential for mechanical damage or aggregation of the vesicles.43Polymer based precipitation leverages solubility differentials to isolate ENs. By employing hydrophilic polymers, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), a hydrophobic microenvironment is induced around the ENs, thereby reducing their solubility and causing them to precipitate. The resulting precipitate is subsequently collected via low speed centrifugation. This technique has gained increasing prominence in recent years,44,45 offering advantages such as operational simplicity, cost effectiveness, broad sample compatibility, minimal ENs damage, and high recovery yields. However, it may result in lower purity due to the risk of residual polymer contaminants, which necessitates additional purification steps and may interfere with downstream analyses; furthermore, the processing duration is relatively extensive.46Sucrose Density Gradient Ultracentrifugation isolates ENs based on density gradients. During ultracentrifugation, vesicles and biomolecules of varying densities settle into distinct layers within a sucrose gradient, enabling high purity isolation.47 The strengths of this approach lie in its superior purity and effective removal of impurities, such as proteins and lipoproteins, while avoiding exogenous chemical contamination by relying solely on physical density differences. Conversely, the method is time consuming (often exceeding 4 hours), requires substantial initial sample volumes (rendering it unsuitable for micro scale samples), and is highly dependent on expensive ultracentrifugation equipment. Additionally, recovery rates may be compromised as a portion of ENs can be lost during the process.45Immunoaffinity capture based technique utilizes the specific binding between antibodies and antigens to isolate ENs. This technique targets specific surface protein markers (eg, TET8, CD63) using antibody functionalized magnetic beads or solid-phase substrates to selectively capture target vesicles, followed by purification through low-speed centrifugation or magnetic separation.48 Its advantages include high specificity, allowing for the precise isolation of ENs subpopulations expressing specific markers (such as PENs) and significantly reducing contamination from non-target proteins to yield high-purity analytes.45 The process is rapid and can be integrated with density gradient centrifugation to further enhance purity. Its limitations, however, include the potential omission of ENs lacking specific markers, resulting in a loss of heterogeneity information and lower overall yield. Furthermore, it necessitates prepurification steps, involves high antibody costs, and carries a risk of non-specific binding, making it less suitable for large-scale sample processing. Its application is also restricted by the requirement for predefined surface markers.49Nanotechnology is emerging as a cutting-edge paradigm for the isolation of ENs, utilizing precise physical and chemical modalities to overcome the long standing bottlenecks in purity and efficiency associated with conventional isolation techniques. By leveraging microfluidic chip technology for the sophisticated manipulation of micro/nanofluidics integrating precision architectures such as nanopore filtration and Deterministic Lateral Displacement (DLD) arrays, high resolution fractionation of exosomes from complex biological matrices has been achieved.50 Furthermore, the implementation of noninvasive manipulation via acoustic, magnetic, and electric force fields at the nanoscale, coupled with advanced materials such as functionalized magnetic beads, ZnO nanoarrays, and click chemistry, has significantly enhanced the sensitivity of specific capture. These advancements facilitate a highly integrated workflow transitioning from rapid isolation to in situ molecular characterization, establishing a robust foundation for the application of exosomes in clinical Point-of-Care Testing (POCT).50Size exclusion chromatography (SEC), also known as gel filtration chromatography, is an efficient separation technique based on particle size and hydrodynamic volume, particularly suitable for isolating PENs of varying sizes.43,51 The principle involves utilizing a porous gel matrix or resin filtration, where larger particles elute rapidly with the mobile phase, while smaller PENs traverse a longer path through the internal pores of the solid phase matrix, achieving precise molecular separation.52,53 This method has been successfully applied to extract PENs from cabbage; its core advantage lies in maintaining the structural integrity and biological activity of the vesicles under mild conditions, yielding high purity samples for downstream analysis.54,55 Although traditional SEC faces limitations such as sample dilution, potential loss, and the challenge of excluding impurities of similar size, the development of specialized commercial columns like the Izon qEV® size exclusion chromatography columns has enabled standardized and rapid processing (approximately 15 min), significantly enhancing the concentration and purity of the isolates.56–58 Consequently, SEC, especially when integrated with other techniques to balance yield and purity, is widely recognized as a preferred strategy for the separation of PENs.54The isolation and extraction technologies for PENs are diverse, with each methodology possessing distinct advantages and inherent limitations (Table 1). Ultracentrifugation remains the most widely utilized isolation technique, frequently regarded as the “gold standard” in the field. In contrast, polymer based precipitation (eg, PEG-based) and immunoaffinity chromatography offer enhanced flexibility and superior specificity for target subpopulations. As technological frontiers continue to advance, the emergence of novel isolation methodologies is anticipated to further augment the efficiency and purity of vesicle separation, thereby providing robust support for the mechanistic investigation and clinical application of PENs. Regarding particle size and surface charge analysis, Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA) and Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) are the most frequently employed methodologies. While DLS offers advantages in rapid detection and high sensitivity, its resolution remains relatively limited. In contrast, NTA, as a high throughput single particle tracking technology, exhibits superior performance in resolution and concentration quantification, effectively overcoming the limitations of DLS in distinguishing subtle variations in particle size.67,68 Research indicates that the average diameter of PENs typically ranges from 30 to 400 nm (Figure 3A), with a characteristically negative zeta potential (frequently between −6 mV and −30 mV). endotoxin quantification and PAMP profiling are mandatory quality control steps for medical applications.98Orchestrating Skin Tissue Regeneration: Mechanistic Paradigms of PENs-Based NanotherapeuticsWound healing is a highly coordinated, spatiotemporal biological process comprising four core phases, hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling, among which the precise regulation of cellular behaviors during the proliferative phase critically determines the quality of tissue repair (Figure 4). However, during impaired wound repair, dysregulated immune responses frequently result in the persistence of inflammation, trapping the tissue in a hostile microenvironment. This pathological niche is characterized by the excessive accumulation of pro-inflammatory cells, the marked upregulation of inflammatory mediators such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-1β (IL-1β), as well as the sustained elevation of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. The concomitant overactivation of MMPs and accumulation of ROS create a destructive hydrolytic and oxidative microenvironment that severely suppresses the proliferation and migration of multiple skin cell types, including fibroblasts, ultimately impairing tissue repair and contributing to the development of chronic, non-healing wounds.99 Therefore, downregulating proinflammatory cell differentiation and inflammatory mediator secretion, reducing excessive ROS production, suppressing oxidative stress, and restoring immune homeostasis represent critical therapeutic strategies for overcoming chronic inflammatory skin wounds and facilitating the transition to the proliferative phase.100 Figure 4Wound healing process.101Illustration of wound healing phases: bleeding, inflammation, proliferation and remodeling.To address these pathophysiological barriers, PENs naturally occurring nanoscale vesicles enriched in bioactive cargos such as lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids have recently been demonstrated to play pivotal regulatory roles in bridging the transition from inflammation to active tissue repair. Accumulating evidence indicates that ENs derived from diverse plant sources can effectively reprogram the hostile wound microenvironment, thereby selectively promoting the proliferation and migration of skin resident cells and other key cell populations involved in tissue repair. By acting through multiple signaling pathways and molecular mechanisms, these multifaceted nanoplatforms offer novel therapeutic avenues for accelerating high quality wound healing and comprehensive skin regeneration.PENs as Immunomodulatory Nanoplatforms: Restoring Systemic and Local Tissue HomeostasisPENs have emerged as promising immunomodulatory nanoplatforms capable of maintaining gastrointestinal (GI) homeostasis and regulating broad spectrum inflammatory responses.102 Inflammation is a critical component of innate immunity; however, persistent or dysregulated inflammatory signaling contributes to the development of acute and chronic inflammatory disorders as well as multiple chronic diseases.30 Increasing evidence indicates that PENs exert potent anti-inflammatory effects primarily through the dynamic modulation of host immune cells, cross-kingdom regulation of microbiota, and the targeted inhibition of pathological intracellular signaling cascades. After internalization into recipient cells, PENs initiate multiple signaling cascades that resolve excessive inflammation and promote tissue homeostasis.102Macrophage Reprogramming and Cytokine Network ModulationIn various inflammatory disorders, macrophages often lose their tolerogenic phenotype. PENs efficiently reverse this by driving anti-inflammatory macrophage polarization and reshaping the local cytokine milieu. macrophages.106 Notably, exploiting their natural nanocarrier properties, grapefruit ENs have been engineered to co-deliver the chemotherapeutic drug methotrexate to inflammatory sites, synergistically amplifying the suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and improving therapeutic outcomes in colitis models.42,103,106Cross-Kingdom Microbiota Regulation and Mucosal ImmunityA unique IBD.42,106Targeted Inhibition of Inflammasomes and Intracellular Stress SensorsAt the molecular level, PENs exert profound systemic anti-inflammatory effects by directly inhibiting critical intracellular stress sensors. PENs effectively regulate inflammation through the inhibition of NLRP3 inflammasome activation.24 Shiitake mushroom and leek derived ENs suppress NLRP3 formation in macrophages and reduce IL-6 expression, protecting against drug induced acute liver injury.24,115 GENs additionally protect the liver by activating the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway via TLR4/TRIF signaling.116Crucially, owing to their nanoscale dimensions and unique lipid composition, certain PENs can traverse physiological barriers such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to mitigate neuroinflammation. GaENs are efficiently taken up by brain microglia and ameliorate brain inflammation through AHR and c-GAS/STING signaling pathways.117 Oat derived ENs also cross the BBB and reduce alcohol induced neuroinflammation.118 Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PENs function as highly versatile nanotherapeutics, orchestrating systemic immune resolution through immune modulation, microbiota regulation, cytokine suppression, inflammasome inhibition, and precise signaling pathway regulation across multiple tissues.Targeted Cellular Reprogramming: PENs Mediated Proliferation and Migration in Wound HealingDuring the proliferative phase of tissue repair, PENs function as highly biocompatible nanocarriers, delivering bioactive cargos that directly reprogram the cellular behaviors of fibroblasts, keratinocytes, and endothelial cells. This targeted modulation orchestrates the rapid spatiotemporal reconstruction of damaged cutaneous tissues and restores the critical barrier function of the skin.Coordinated Reprogramming of Dermal Fibroblasts and Epidermal KeratinocytesFibroblasts are the central effector cells in the dermal layer; their proliferative capacity directly dictates extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and wound contraction. Mechanistically, PENs accelerate fibroblast proliferation primarily through two interconnected pathways: cell cycle acceleration and TGF-β/SMAD signaling activation. Multiple PENs including those derived from Lithospermum erythrorhizon callus (LENs),119 Physalis (PDNCs),120 Panax ginseng (GNENs)121 and Aloe saponaria (AS-ENs)122 have been shown to upregulate key cyclin dependent kinases (eg, Cyclin D1, Cyclin E). This upregulation drives the G1-to-S and G2-to-M phase transitions, significantly shortening the cell division cycle. Concurrently, these nanovesicles stimulate the TGF-β/SMAD cascade and ERK1/2 phosphorylation (as seen with Rosa damascena stem cell ENs),123,124 upregulating COL1A1 transcription and repressing matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-1/3), thereby establishing a synergistic “proliferation matrix synthesis” microenvironment.Furthermore, mitigating excessive ROS is critical for preventing fibroblast senescence in chronic wounds. PENs from balloon flower roots,125 coriander,20 and tomatoes126 exert potent intracellular ROS scavenging effects, frequently by activating the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway. This not only protects DNA and lipids from oxidative damage but also promotes a pro-regenerative macrophage polarization (M1 to M2 phenotype), fostering a stable niche for cellular expansion.Epidermal Keratinocyte Regulation: Promoting Re-EpithelializationKeratinocyte migration and proliferation are decisive for epidermal barrier reconstruction. PENs precisely regulate these processes without inducing the pathological hyperproliferation associated with disorders like psoriasis. For instance, ginseng derived ENs modulate the ERK and AKT/mTOR pathways to safely enhance HaCaT cell viability.127 Additionally, ROS induced keratinocyte damage can be robustly mitigated by the intrinsic antioxidant cargos of Aloe vera peel and grapefruit derived nanovesicles, which drive cell cycle entry and ECM synthesis.24,43,128To facilitate directed cellular migration (re-epithelialization), certain PENs carry adhesion molecules that interact with cell membrane integrins. Tomato derived ENs, for example, trigger focal adhesion kinase (FAK) phosphorylation and downstream Rho family GTPases (Rac1, Cdc42).6,129 This initiates cytoskeletal reorganization such as actin polymerization and lamellipodia formation accelerating targeted keratinocyte migration toward the wound bed.Endothelial Cell Activation and NeovascularizationCoupled with ECM synthesis, neovascularization is essential for supplying oxygen and nutrients to healing tissues. PENs from wheat5 and grapefruit6 have demonstrated concentration dependent enhancement of human umbilical vein endothelial cell (HUVEC) tube formation. Furthermore, Morinda officinalis derived ENs can activate the MAPK/YAP1 signaling pathway, simultaneously stimulating endothelial proliferation and tubular networking.13Highlighting the potential of advanced nanomedicine platforms, broccoli derived ENs have been engineered into integrated therapeutic systems (eg, SK@E-Au@Exos). By combining the innate spatiotemporal immunomodulatory properties of PENs (suppressing NF-κB while upregulating TGF-β/IL-10) with active antibacterial agents, such bioengineered platforms significantly boost endothelial and basal epidermal cell proliferation, ultimately enabling scar-free healing in challenging MRSA infected wounds.130Translational Perspectives: Advantages and ChallengesAs next generation nanomedicines, PENs offer profound advantages for wound therapy. Their native lipid bilayer structure preserves cargo stability against enzymatic degradation, while their high biocompatibility, negligible immunogenicity, and lack of in vivo toxicity bypass the safety concerns of synthetic liposomes or mammalian cell derived exosomes.131 Moreover, their widespread availability ensures cost effective scalability.However, translating PENs from benchtop discovery to clinical wound therapy faces critical hurdles. Current efficacy data is predominantly derived from rodent models, necessitating rigorous human clinical trials.132 Technologically, standardizing isolation protocols to completely separate PENs from plant impurities remains challenging. Future research must prioritize scaling up yields under current cGMP guidelines, optimizing targeted delivery vehicles (eg, smart hydrogels), and establishing comprehensive pharmacokinetic profiles.131,133Nanotherapeutic Regulation of Angiogenesis: Multi Pathway Orchestration by PENsThe reconstruction of a functional microvascular network is a prerequisite for successful skin regeneration, whereas impaired angiogenesis remains the pathological hallmark of chronic diabetic ulcers. Consequently, PENs have emerged as highly biocompatible nanoplatforms that orchestrate vascular repair through integrated metabolic, immune, and cellular signaling cascades.Pro-Angiogenic Mechanisms: Metabolic Remodeling and Microenvironmental CrosstalkPENs drive endothelial cell (EC) behavior and tube formation through distinct nanotherapeutic mechanisms. A primary pathway involves the metabolic reprogramming of ECs via horizontal miRNA transfer. For instance, ginseng derived nanovesicles (GExos) deliver ptc-miR396f to upregulate critical glycolytic enzymes (PFKM, PGK1, ENO1), thereby amplifying ATP production to fuel cell migration and sprouting.134,135 Beyond direct endothelial targeting, PENs actively remodel the inflammatory and oxidative microenvironment to indirectly promote neovascularization. Vesicles from lemon and cactus drive macrophage polarization toward a pro-healing M2 phenotype, triggering robust VEGF secretion for endothelial activation.17,136Concurrently, specific PENs (eg, from coriander and tomato) activate the Nrf2/Keap1 antioxidant axis to scavenge ROS, shielding nascent capillary networks from oxidative damage and preserving functional CD31 expression.20,137 These microenvironmental regulations are further amplified by the direct activation of classical prosurvival cascades including PI3K/Akt and ERK/mTOR pathways yielding multi-fold increases in capillary branching.5,138,139Bi Directional Modulation: Context Dependent Angiogenic RegulationInterestingly, PENs function as smart nanomedicines capable of context dependent angiogenic modulation. In pathological microenvironments such as tumor associated skin lesions, specific PENs exhibit potent anti-angiogenic properties. GExos can silence the c-MYC oncogene via ptc-miR396f to reduce VEGF secretion,76 while Brucea javanica derived vesicles suppress the PI3K/Akt/mTOR axis to inhibit aberrant vessel formation.140 This unique bidirectional regulatory capacity highlights the precision medicine potential of PENs in complex cutaneous lesions.Comparative Assessment and Translational Advantages of PENs in AngiogenesisIn the context of angiogenesis, PENs, animal derived EVs, and microbial EVs exhibit distinct biological characteristics and translational advantages. Animal derived EVs (eg, MSC exos and deer antler blood derived EVs) directly upregulate VEGF/TGF-β and promote endothelial proliferation, benefiting from well characterized mechanistic pathways.141–143 Recently, cutting edge therapies have successfully integrated these mammalian EVs with smart biomaterials such as trace element dictated modules or Mn-doped ZIF-8 hydrogels to orchestrate profound angiogenesis and antibacterial responses in diabetic ulcers.144,145 However, their broader translation remains severely constrained by complex cell culture dependencies, high production costs, batch variability, and potential immunogenic risks.141 Similarly, while microbial EVs (eg, bacterial OMVs) induce angiogenesis via robust early stage immune recruitment, their highly immunogenic profile necessitates strict regulation to prevent endotoxin driven hyper inflammation.146In contrast, PENs provide a biosafety favorable alternative characterized by scalable, cost effective production, low immunogenicity, and an abundance of intrinsic bioactive phytocompounds (eg, flavonoids, polyphenols, plant miRNAs).134,147 They serve as highly accessible nanoplatforms that seamlessly couple anti-inflammatory regulation with safe vascular reconstruction. Despite this immense therapeutic potential, critical translational bottlenecks remain. The inherent compositional heterogeneity of PENs necessitates the urgent development of standardized production protocols, multi-omics-guided quality control, and comprehensive long term biosafety evaluations prior to their widespread clinical application.Neurovascular Synergy: Mechanisms and Nanotherapeutic Delivery of PENs in Skin InnervationThe integumentary system is densely innervated, and cutaneous reinnervation actively orchestrates keratinocyte proliferation, angiogenesis, and immune recruitment during tissue repair.148–150 When this neuroregenerative cascade is compromised as is prevalent in diabetic chronic wounds healing is substantially delayed.151 Consequently, PENs have emerged as potent nanotherapeutic mediators of neurovascular crosstalk, offering a highly accessible “dual-targeting” approach that simultaneously addresses nerve and vessel deficits with remarkably low toxicity.76Mechanistic Paradigms of PENs Mediated Neural Repair and CrosstalkPENs intrinsically modulate neural differentiation and neurovascular crosstalk through diverse, multi-target molecular cascades. A defining feature of certain PENs is their capacity for horizontal miRNA transfer, which effectively reprograms endogenous signaling networks. For instance, ginseng derived GExos deliver specific miRNAs into bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), triggering PI3K/Akt pathway activation to drive the expression of neural progenitor and mature neuron markers homeostasis.148,149,152 Similarly, the Lycium barbarum ISL@PE formulation exerts robust neuroprotection by simultaneously modulating the PI3K/Akt axis and Bax/Bcl2 anti-apoptotic pathways, thereby reducing neuronal apoptosis.153,154 Beyond direct neurogenesis, PENs actively enhance paracrine crosstalk between neural and vascular compartments. Kelp derived CA@Exos activate Camk2a mediated Erk1/2 and cGMP-PKG pathways, significantly upregulating the coordinated neurotrophic and angiogenic factors (VEGF, CD31, BDNF, NGF) required for integrated neurovascular repair.149Microenvironmental Remodeling: Anti-Ferroptotic and Antioxidant CascadesPENs exhibit profound antioxidant and anti-ferroptotic capacities, which are crucial for neurovascular niche regeneration under high-oxidative-stress conditions. Kelp derived CA@Exos effectively scavenge ROS and inhibit advanced glycation end products (AGEs), creating a permissive microenvironment for Schwann cell survival.149Remarkably, Salvia miltiorrhiza derived EVs (SMEVs) counteract macrophage ferroptosis following peripheral nerve injury by upregulating protective factors (GPX4, Fth1) and suppressing lipid peroxidation.155 This anti-ferroptotic mechanism simultaneously restores VEGFA expression, establishing a direct, innovative molecular link between macrophage survival, neurogenesis, and angiogenesis at the injury site.156Advanced Delivery Systems for Cutaneous Neurovascular TranslationTo overcome cutaneous physiological barriers and achieve sustained neurovascular restoration, PENs are increasingly integrated with advanced bio-instructive materials. For example, the incorporation of kelp derived CA@Exos into conductive microneedles (CA@Exos-MNs) leverages mild electrical stimulation to enhance vesicle cellular uptake, synergistically promoting M2 macrophage polarization and deep tissue neurovascular crosstalk.149Likewise, photocrosslinked hydrogels and 3D printed bionic scaffolds loaded with PENs (eg, G-Exos and ISL@PE) significantly prolong vesicle retention, sustain chemokine mediated stem cell recruitment, and accelerate both in situ axonal repair and comprehensive wound closure.148,153,157 However, precisely matching scaffold degradation rates to vesicle release kinetics remains a crucial parameter for optimizing long term functional recovery.158Comparative Translational Potential and Future PerspectivesIn the realm of neurovascular regeneration, animal derived EVs (particularly from MSCs and Schwann cells) provide a crucial reference standard, featuring well characterized repair mechanisms such as miR-22-3p-mediated AKT/mTOR activation and PI3K/Akt-dependent axonal growth alongside established clinical translation pathways.159,160 However, their broader application is fundamentally constrained by complex cell culture dependencies, high production costs, and potential immunogenic risks.161 Concurrently, while microbial derived EVs (eg, bacterial EVs) exhibit robust pro-angiogenic and immunomodulatory properties,162,163 their application in neurovascular regeneration is severely restricted by the inherent presence of pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), which risk inducing endotoxin driven hyper inflammation in delicate neural tissues.164In contrast, PENs emerge as a biosafety favorable nanotherapeutic platform characterized by scalable, cost effective extraction from renewable sources and a complete absence of zoonotic or endotoxin related risks.161 Crucially, specific PENs harbor intrinsic phytocompound bioactivities such as caffeic acid mediated anti-glycation, ferroptosis regulating lipid cargos, and unique plant miRNAs (eg, pab-miR482c) that are entirely absent in mammalian or microbial vesicles.149,155,165 By systematically modulating PI3K/Akt, NF-κB, and Erk1/2 pathways, PENs seamlessly couple axonal growth with microvascular stabilization. This “dual-targeting” neurovascular synergy makes PENs exceptionally advantageous for treating chronic wounds characterized by persistent neurodegeneration and vascular dysfunction,155,166 especially when integrated with smart nanobiomaterials for sustained delivery.167Despite this immense therapeutic potential, critical translational bottlenecks remain. The inherent compositional heterogeneity of PENs necessitates the development of standardized, multi-omics-guided quality control and purification protocols.168–170 Furthermore, comprehensive pharmacokinetic profiles, long term biosafety evaluations, and large animal clinical validations are currently absent.171,172 Future research should prioritize engineered combinational strategies that integrate structurally standardized PENs with intelligent biomaterials, ultimately accelerating their safe and precise clinical translation in cutaneous neurovascular reconstruction.Targeting Skin Appendage Homeostasis: The Apex of Regenerative NanomedicineIn the preceding sections, the multifaceted nanotherapeutic effects of PENs in cutaneous repair have been systematically elucidated spanning immune polarization, oxidative stress attenuation, and neurovascular cellular reprogramming. Collectively, these spatiotemporal events prime a microenvironment conducive to tissue repair. However, genuine skin regeneration extends beyond mere wound closure and inflammation resolution. The ultimate apex of cutaneous regenerative nanomedicine is complete, scar free healing, a milestone that strictly depends on the structural and functional neogenesis of skin appendages (primarily hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands).These appendages are far more than accessory structures; they play indispensable roles in maintaining epidermal barrier integrity, thermoregulation, and cutaneous microecological balance via lipid and sweat secretion. Crucially, hair follicles serve as vital adult stem cell reservoirs that drive sustained re-epithelialization and high-quality tissue remodeling. Therefore, transitioning from a purely systemic or microenvironmental perspective to an organ and structure oriented paradigm is essential. Understanding how PENs leverage the previously described neurovascular crosstalk and immunomodulatory networks to orchestrate appendage homeostasis will provide deeper mechanistic insights, ultimately unlocking their full translational potential for functional skin regeneration.Direct Modulation of Hair Follicle Cycling: A Paradigm Shift in Epigenetic TherapyHair follicles (HFs) are currently the most thoroughly studied target among skin appendages in PEN research. PENs directly promote the transition of HFs from the telogen to the anagen phase and protect them from immune mediated damage through multiple mechanisms, introducing a novel “cross-kingdom epigenetic modulation” paradigm.Polygoni Multiflori Radix-derived ENs (PMENs) deliver plant miRNAs (aof-miR168a, osa-miR164a) that cross-kingdom suppress the human AR. This downregulates DKK1 and stabilizes β-catenin, thereby reversing androgen-induced HFs miniaturization.173 This suggests that PENs can act as natural, programmable gene-silencing vectors, offering a highly specific alternative to conventional small-molecule alopecia drugs. Similarly, Iris germanica rhizome derived nanovesicles activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling via AKT, ERK, and GSK3β phosphorylation while restoring the inductive capacity of dermal papilla cells by mitigating mitochondrial ROS.174Building upon the angiogenic and inflammatory paradigms discussed earlier, garlic derived nanovesicles exert a synergistic dual effect: they upregulate Wnt-1, β-catenin, and growth factors (VEGF, PDGF, TGF-β) to drive anagen entry and perifollicular angiogenesis (aligning with Nanotherapeutic Regulation of Angiogenesis: Multi Pathway Orchestration by PENs), while simultaneously suppressing NF-κB and MAPK pathways to resolve perifollicular inflammation (aligning with PENs as Immunomodulatory Nanoplatforms: Restoring Systemic and Local Tissue Homeostasis).175,176 Additionally, ENs derived from germinated Cannabis sativa seeds promote HFSC differentiation and protect follicles from immunological damage by downregulating BMP4, suppressing the AR-SP1 axis, and modulating IL-15R and STAT1 pathways.177,178 Collectively, these actions orchestrate an “immune privileged” niche vital for HFs survival.Microenvironmental Niche Reprogramming: The “Seed and Soil” ParadigmFrom a regenerative perspective, appendage stem cells act as the “seed”, while the dermal macroenvironment serves as the “soil”. PENs effectively act as “soil conditioners”, facilitating post injury HFs neogenesis indirectly by optimizing the local injury microenvironment rather than exclusively targeting follicular progenitors. For instance, cactus derived PENs promote follicle regeneration by scavenging ROS, polarizing macrophages toward the pro-healing M2 phenotype, and stimulating angiogenesis.136 Similarly, PENs derived from Allium fistulosum179 and Portulaca oleracea180 resolve inflammation and enhance vascularization in acute and diabetic wounds.At the molecular level, PENs shift the wound environment from a chronic inflammatory state to a regenerative one by activating the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant axis and suppressing NF-κB and STAT3 signaling, which downregulates key pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-17, IL-23, and TNF-α).181,182 Clinically, RSCEs deliver Let-7 family miRNAs to suppress inflammation and promote collagen synthesis, restoring the atrophic dermal architecture flanking HFs.124 Furthermore, a hydrogel loaded with curcumin containing nanovesicles restores skin barrier function and mitigates oxidative stress in atopic dermatitis,183 while tomato derived vesicles facilitate the coordinated migration of keratinocytes and fibroblasts essential for follicle neogenesis.126 Dandelion derived nanovesicles neutralize Staphylococcus aureus exotoxins, preserving follicle integrity in infected wounds.184Crucially, because sweat gland functional recovery strictly depends on low oxidative and low inflammatory niches, the robust Nrf2/ARE activating properties of PENs185,186 theoretically offer potent indirect protection against inflammation induced glandular atrophy, circumventing the hostile microenvironment that typically drives glandular apoptosis.Pilosebaceous Tropism and Trans Annexal Nanotherapeutic DeliveryThe pilosebaceous unit is a lipid rich microenvironment where PENs exhibit unique biophysical and translational advantages. While direct studies of PENs in sebaceous glands remain scarce, preliminary evidence suggests PENs can modulate key lipid metabolism pathways, such as PPARγ and SREBP1c, to limit sebum overproduction and alleviate acne associated perifollicular inflammation.13From a nanotherapeutics delivery perspective, PENs demonstrate a remarkable biomimetic tropism for follicular sebaceous pathways. The lipid bilayer of PENs exhibits a “like dissolves like” interaction with sebum, allowing them to act as a physical shunt bypassing the highly impermeable stratum corneum.187 Notably, cucumber derived nanovesicles can disrupt stratum corneum lipid packaging to significantly enhance transdermal drug delivery via the follicular sebaceous pathway.188 This intrinsic trans annexal permeability positions PENs not merely as active regenerative agents, but as ideal next generation nanocarriers for targeted drug co-loading in deep skin glandular disorders, overcoming a major anatomical hurdle in dermatology.189Translational Paradigms, Comparative Advantages, and Future BioengineeringPENs offer multiple advantages in dermatological applications. Compared with animal derived EVs (costly and ethically restricted) and microbial derived EVs (immunogenic and endotoxin prone), PENs are characterized by low immunogenicity, high biosafety, and a rich cargo of bioactive compounds (polyphenols, flavonoids, miRNAs) that exert multi-target effects. Overall, PENs present a more favorable balance across safety, accessibility, and functional versatility (See Table 3 for detailed cross source comparisons). Table 3Comparison Among PENs, Animal-Derived EVs and Microbial-Derived EVsComparison AspectPENsAnimal-Derived EVsMicrobial-Derived EVsSource and ProductionDerived from plant tissues with abundant and renewable resources, free from ethical concerns related to animal or human tissues, and suitable for scalable production due to relatively simple isolation procedures.161,190Mainly derived from MSCs, Schwann cells, and other mammalian cells, requiring complex cell culture systems with relatively high production costs.141,159,160Sourced from bacterial or fungal fermentation; exceptionally scalable and highly cost-effective to produce.191Biosafety and ImmunogenicityExhibit high safety, low immunogenicity, and excellent biocompatibility with minimal risk of immune rejection.134,161,175,192Possess good biocompatibility but still carry potential risks of immunogenicity, viral transmission, and biosafety concerns.141Act as strong immune adjuvants due to PAMPs; excellent for vaccines but require stringent detoxification for tissue regeneration to prevent excessive inflammation.193Bioactivity and Regenerative FunctionsEnriched with natural bioactive cargos, including flavonoids, vitamins, lipids, and plant miRNAs, which regulate inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB and TLR4 to promote anti-inflammatory effects, angiogenesis, and tissue repair.149,155,165Mechanisms are more comprehensively characterized, promoting neuroregeneration, angiogenesis, and cellular repair through pathways including PI3K/Akt, AKT/mTOR, and Wnt/β-catenin.150,159,160Potent immunomodulators and antibacterial agents; effectively regulate local microbiome balance and competitively inhibit wound pathogens.194Translational PotentialOffer advantages of low cost, high yield, and intrinsic pharmacological activity; however, most studies remain limited to in vitro and animal models, with insufficient clinical evidence.132Benefit from more established animal evaluation systems, standardized isolation protocols, and a relatively advanced clinical translation pathway.159,160High translational potential for tumor immunotherapy and vaccines; emerging applications in infected wound management when properly engineered.195LimitationsChallenges include strong compositional heterogeneity, lack of standardized production methods, and insufficient long-term biosafety evaluation.13,133Limited by low yield, high production costs,142 batch variability, and potential ethical and biosafety concerns.141,161Inherent high immunogenicity, challenging endotoxin removal, and the potential to trigger detrimental localized hyper-inflammation.196However, their functional efficacy varies significantly by plant source. High cost stem cell derived PENs (eg, RSCEs) excel in anti-inflammation and dermis remodeling,124 whereas traditional medicinal herbs (Polygoni Multiflori,173 Iris germanica,174 Garlic176) directly target HFs regeneration through conserved developmental pathways. In contrast, agricultural and food derived PENs (Allium fistulosum,179 Portulaca oleracea,180 tomato,126 dandelion184) offer low cost, scalable platforms for wound closure and toxin neutralization, though they suffer from lower concentrations of active payloads and high batch-to-batch variation.The primary limitations for the clinical translation of PENs lie in their profound heterogeneity across different species and anatomical origins, which severely complicates standardization and scalable cGMP manufacturing. Additionally, direct evidence demonstrating their therapeutic efficacy on sebaceous and sweat glands is still lacking. To overcome these shortcomings, future research should focus on establishing robust characterization frameworks and quality control standards (standardizing size, zeta potential, surface markers, and miRNA profiles). Echoing the integrated SK@E-Au@Exos platform discussed in Targeted Cellular Reprogramming: PENs Mediated Proliferation and Migration in Wound Healing, future strategies must pivot towards bioengineering PENs via surface ligand modification or synergistic drug co-loading in smart hydrogels to improve targeting resolution. Finally, employing single vesicle sequencing and spatial transcriptomics to map the precise targeting of PENs within the follicle sebaceous sweat gland axis, alongside longitudinal investigations into their long term biosafety, will be imperative for unlocking their full clinical potential.ConclusionPENs have emerged as promising natural nanocarriers in wound healing and regenerative medicine. They exert pleiotropic regulatory effects such as suppressing inflammatory pathways (eg, NF-κB), promoting fibroblast and epithelial cell proliferation, and enhancing angiogenesis driven by their intrinsic bioactive cargos, including miRNAs, proteins, and polyphenols. Within the landscape of nanoscale delivery, mammalian derived EVs exhibit excellent biocompatibility and tissue specific targeting, whereas microbial derived extracellular vesicles offer high amenability to genetic engineering. However, their broad clinical translation is often hindered by complex ethical considerations, prohibitive mammalian cell culture costs, and stringent requirements for endotoxin clearance. In this context, PENs offer unique and complementary advantages.197 They effectively preclude the risk of zoonotic pathogen transmission, possess an inherently immuno-silent profile, and maintain robust structural stability even in harsh acidic microenvironments. Consequently, PENs represent a safe, economically viable, and highly scalable alternative for sustained skin regeneration therapies.To successfully transition PENs into clinical practice, their in vivo pharmacokinetic (ADME) profiles require comprehensive elucidation. Current evidence suggests that the cellular uptake of PENs is primarily mediated by non-endocytic membrane fusion and macrophage-dependent phagocytosis, while their systemic biodistribution is highly dependent on both the specific plant source and the route of administration.86,198 Following internalization, PENs predominantly enter the endosomal pathway, where efficient endo-lysosomal escape within this acidic microenvironment is a prerequisite for releasing bioactive cargos into the host cytoplasm.199 Despite these insights, precisely defining their terminal metabolic and excretory pathways (eg, hepatic versus renal clearance) remains a critical knowledge gap. Future studies must move beyond static end point observations by integrating advanced isotopic or near infrared fluorescent tracking technologies. Establishing physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models will be essential to quantitatively map their dynamic ADME processes within complex physiological environments, ultimately guiding precise clinical dosing regimens.A major barrier hindering the widespread clinical application of PENs is the lack of standardized isolation technologies and unified quality control protocols. Current isolation techniques are often constrained by low yields, batch-to-batch inconsistency, and the co-purification of plant impurities.21 Transitioning to large-scale, cGMP compliant production requires overcoming the inherent biological variability of plant sources, which fluctuate based on climate, harvest timing, and genetic background. Establishing robust physicochemical profiling, defining specific molecular biomarkers, and ensuring product stability during industrial scale up are imperative milestones for achieving reproducible and standardized manufacturing.21 Despite these manufacturing challenges, PENs hold profound translational potential as cost effective, natural nanoplatforms for precision tissue repair. However, navigating the complex regulatory landscape requires highly proactive strategies. Developers must clarify the specific regulatory classification of PENs early in the development pipeline determining whether they fall under medical devices, botanical drugs, biological products, or combination products based on their degree of manipulation and intended therapeutic claims.200 To streamline the approval process, it is highly recommended to implement Quality by Design (QbD) principles and maintain GMP compliant documentation starting from the preclinical stages. Transparent reporting of botanical sourcing, reproducible validation of biological activity, and early pre-submission engagement with regulatory agencies (such as the FDA or EMA) will pave a definitive pathway from bench to bedside.21In conclusion, PENs represent a highly promising and transformative nanoplatform. With continuing advances in nanotechnology, multi-omics, and biomaterials engineering, future research must focus on deciphering the precise molecular mechanisms underlying their cross-kingdom regulation. By continuously optimizing isolation efficiencies and employing surface engineering strategies to enhance targeted delivery, PENs are poised to evolve into safe, highly efficient, and clinically viable therapeutic nanocarriers for regenerative medicine.

retrieved_papers.title: Ubiquitin-Conjugating Enzyme Positively Regulates Salicylic Acid and Jasmonic Acid Biosynthesis to Confer Broad-Spectrum Antiviral Resistance in <i>Nicotiana benthamiana</i>.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (UBC) plays a significant role in plant hormone signal transduction. In this study, we observed that TuMV infection markedly upregulates UBC mRNA expression, suggesting a close association between UBC and viral infection. Using Tobacco rattle virus (TRV)-based virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) to downregulate UBC expression in Nicotiana benthamiana, we found that UBC-silenced plants exhibited enhanced susceptibility to TuMV compared with control plants. Conversely, transient overexpression of UBC protein suppressed viral propagation. Further analysis by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) revealed a substantial downregulation in the expression of SA and JA biosynthetic genes in UBC-silenced plants. Accordingly, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) confirmed a marked decrease in the accumulation of the corresponding hormones. Exogenous application of SA or JA partially restored antiviral resistance in UBC-silenced plants, indicating that hormonal deficiency contributes to enhanced viral susceptibility. Collectively, our results demonstrate that UBC positively regulates SA and JA biosynthesis. UBC silencing impairs both SA- and JA-mediated defense pathways, thereby facilitating viral infection in N. benthamiana.

retrieved_papers.title: The Transcription Factor DPB Confers Antiviral Defence Against Potato Virus X by Modulating MYB-Dependent Signalling.
retrieved_papers.abstract: As a transcriptional co-factor of E2F, DP proteins are typically involved in the regulation of plant cell-cycle-related processes. However, whether DP proteins participate in transcriptional regulation associated with plant antiviral defence remains largely unclear. This study demonstrates that NbDPB, a DP family protein in Nicotiana benthamiana, positively regulates resistance to potato virus X (PVX) by functioning as a transcription factor. Knockout of NbDPB increased plant susceptibility to PVX, while its overexpression significantly suppressed viral accumulation. Furthermore, we identified that NbDPB binds to the promoter of NbMYB (a MYB transcription factor) and positively regulates its expression. Silencing NbMYB enhanced PVX infection, whereas exogenous application of jasmonic acid (JA) and salicylic acid (SA) partially rescued this phenotype. Hormone levels of JA and SA, as well as the expression levels of their marker genes, were significantly reduced in the silenced NbMYB plants. These findings suggest that the NbDPB-NbMYB module mediates antiviral defence through the JA and SA signalling pathways. This study reveals a previously uncharacterized role of DP proteins in antiviral transcriptional regulation, indicating that they may play a crucial role in plant antiviral defence.

retrieved_papers.title: Transient Expression of Hen Egg White Lysozyme (EWL) in <i>Nicotiana benthamiana</i> Influences Plant Pathogen Infection.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Lysozyme is an enzyme that hydrolyzes bacterial cell walls, which is functional for destroying the integrity of bacteria, enhancing the activity of immune cells, participating in immune signal transmission, helping to maintain the micro-ecological balance of the gastrointestinal tract, etc. Egg white lysozyme (EWL), as one of the typical representatives of lysozyme, is the most widely used enzyme in production so far, and is also one of the most complex structures of lysozyme. EWL also helps protect plants from fungal and bacterial diseases. Here, we report the effect of EWL on infections from plant viruses. The EWL gene was cloned and characterized. The EWL protein sequence analysis identified a conserved domain of lysozyme activity and the sharing of a 100% identical EWL protein from the Coturnix japonica lysozyme. Then, the EWL gene was cloned into the plant expression vector pEAQ-HT-DEST3 and transiently expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana (N. benthamiana). We found that EWL expression in N. benthamiana significantly contributed to infections by the turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) but not by the tobacco mosaic virus (TMV). Plants that transiently expressed EWL showed an obvious increase in resistance to Botrytis cinerea (B.cinerea). Our results suggested a new research point for the application of EWL on plant pathogen infections.

retrieved_papers.title: Resveratrol synthase homologs participate in infection of <i>Nicotiana benthamiana</i> by pathogenic plant viruses and fungi.
retrieved_papers.abstract:
Introduction

Resveratrol synthase (RS) is a key enzyme involved in the synthesis of stilbene and resveratrol. Resveratrol has many biological pharmacological activities that are beneficial to human health including anti-cancer, cardiovascular protection, estrogen regulation, antibacterial, antiviral, and reduction of tissue and organ damage. In plants, RS catalyzes the production of resveratrol, which helps to protect against fungal and bacterial diseases.

Methods

We analyzed RS homologues from peanuts (Arachis hypogaea L.) during infection by plant viruses and fungi. The peanut RS gene was cloned and characterized. The peanut RS gene was cloned into the pEAQ-HT-DEST3 plant binary expression vector and transiently expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana.

Results

Sequence analysis of the protein revealed a conserved stilbene synthase activity domain. The protein displayed high phylogenetic identity to RS from A. hypogaea (100%), Vitis vinifera (72.42%), and Polygonum cuspidatum (69.51). The results showed that RS expression in plants significantly contributed to infection by turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) and silghtly contributed to viral infection of tobacco mosaic virus (TMV). However, no significant influence of RS expression on infection by tobacco vein mottling virus (TVMV) was observed. Expression of the RS gene was transiently increased upon fungal infection of Botrytis cinerea in N. benthamiana.

Discussion

This finding suggests that transient expression of the RS gene could significantly contribute to infection by turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) and improve the resistance of N. benthamiana to B. cinerea.

retrieved_papers.title: Potato purple top phytoplasma infection induces autophagy-associated lipid dynamics that support pathogen proliferation.
retrieved_papers.abstract: Phytoplasmas are unculturable, phloem-restricted bacterial pathogens responsible for devastating diseases in crops and ornamentals worldwide. Their mechanism for nutrient acquisition from host plants remains largely unknown. This study demonstrated that infection with potato purple top phytoplasma induced extensive remodeling of lipid metabolism in tomato plants, closely linked to autophagy activation. Western blot and confocal analyses revealed increased ATG8 lipidation and autophagosome formation at endoplasmic reticulum stress sites, alongside the redistribution of lipid droplets toward phytoplasma cells. Lipidomic profiling showed a decline in chloroplast galactolipids and phospholipids with a concomitant rise in triacylglycerol, indicating accelerated membrane turnover and neutral lipid sequestration. Transmission electron microscopy further revealed frequent spatial proximity between lipid droplets and phytoplasmas. Inhibition of autophagy with 3-methyladenine blocked lipid droplet breakdown, disrupted endoplasmic reticulum organization, and reduced phytoplasma titers, suggesting that host autophagy contributes to phytoplasma proliferation. In addition, genome analysis identified a conserved phytoplasma-encoded alpha/beta hydrolase (potato purple top-lipase), predicted to be related to monoacylglycerol lipases. In vivo assays in yeast and Nicotiana benthamiana confirmed that potato purple top-lipase reduced neutral lipids, mainly triacylglycerol, and that catalytic triad mutations abolished activity. Because potato purple top-lipase lacks a predicted secretory signal peptide, it likely functions intracellularly within phytoplasma cells and may participate in the metabolism of lipid intermediates. These findings support a model in which phytoplasma infection is associated with host autophagy-associated lipid droplet mobilization and a phytoplasma lipase that may contribute to host-derived lipid resources, providing insight into potential nutrient acquisition strategies of phloem-restricted pathogens.

TITLE:
25th Annual Meeting of the Rocky Mountain Virology Association

ABSTRACT:
Located on the traditional and ancestral homelands of the Arapaho, Cheyenne, and Ute Nations, Colorado State University’s Mountain Campus hosted the 25th Annual Rocky Mountain Virology Association meeting. The three-day event, held from 26 September to 28 September 2025, welcomed 152 participants focused on the following topics: viruses, prions, immunology, transmission, structural biology, and vector biology. This year’s Randall Jay Cohrs Keynote Presentation summarized ongoing research on viral glycoproteins in relation to viral entry and assembly. Understanding the role of viral glycoproteins is essential in vaccine and antiviral development for enveloped RNA viruses. Alongside rigorous scientific discourse and networking, attendees made the most of their time by hiking amidst beautiful fall colors, wildlife, and young aspens starting the forest anew. On behalf of the Rocky Mountain Virology Association, this report summarizes select presentations from the 25th annual meeting.

IntroductionJust 50 miles from Fort Collins, Colorado State University’s Mountain Campus is the home to the Rocky Mountain Virology Association annual meeting. Founded in 2000, the Rocky Mountain Virology Club (RMVC) opened its doors to virologists at any stage in their careers, providing them a place to share their expertise and collaborate with others. In 2009, RMVC expanded to include prion biologists. The following year, RMVC was renamed the Rocky Mountain Virology Association (RMVA). Like the few aspens emerging from burn scars to begin a new forest, what started as a meeting of a handful of people has grown dramatically over the last 25 years. Attendees gathered at Colorado State University’s Mountain Campus from 26 September to 29 September 2025 (Figure 1 and Figure 2). The conference featured five sessions, six invited speakers, 33 oral presentations, and 57 poster presentations.The meeting started with the Randall Jay Cohrs Keynote Presentation delivered by Dr. Hector Aguilar-Carreno from the University of California, Los Angeles’ Department of Microbiology, Immunology, and Molecular Genetics. He presented on enveloped RNA virus glycoproteins and their roles in viral entry and assembly, and how this research can be used for vaccine and antiviral development.The Richard A. Bessen Memorial Lecture was delivered by Dr. David Harris from Boston University. Dr. Harris spoke on elacridar’s effects on lysosomal sterol and lipid metabolism in relation to the scrapie isoform of the prion protein. Dolan from the Quantitative Virology and Evolution Unit, Laboratory of Viral Diseases, NIH-NIAID Division of Intramural Research, Bethesda, MD, presented their research using mutational scanning to understand how viral capsids sense their environment. Viral capsids are remarkable molecular machines. They have evolved to be robust to the environmental stresses encountered, which often include changes in pH, salinity, and temperature, while maintaining precise mechanisms to release their genomic cargo when specific criteria are met—usually when receptors and co-receptors are presented within the right chemical environment. Here, they use a mutational library encompassing all possible substitutions in the capsid proteins of Enterovirus D68 and Enterovirus A71 to probe capsid functions involved in entry and uncoating. The results highlight specific regions that respond to chemical and biophysical changes and how mutational preferences shift in response, and identify functional sequences that may engage host factors to initiate and facilitate uncoating and entry. They are also recognized as reservoirs for zoonotic diseases, making them important laboratory models for studying emerging infections. Public scrutiny surrounding bat research escalated during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Public posts and comments were collected from Facebook, X, and Instagram via Google Social Search. After removing duplicates, 139 relevant posts from Colorado, Montana, Kansas, and Texas were analyzed across pre-, during, and post-COVID periods. All studies using human subjects or tissue samples have been either approved or deemed non-human-subject research by the Institutional Review Board of Colorado State University.Priscilla Yang from Microbiology and Immunology at Stanford University conducted a research study on small-molecule-induced proximity as an antiviral strategy. Conventional direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) bind to and inhibit (or derange) the function of their viral targets. Their pharmacology is driven by target binding to the viral protein (occupancy), and any loss of binding due to point mutations reduces antiviral potency. This underlies the narrow-spectrum activity and propensity for resistance to DAAs used as monotherapies. In addition, it is difficult to design inhibitors of viral proteins that are not enzymes. Instead of using small-molecule binding to inhibit viral proteins, Yang’s group has been developing small molecules that achieve antiviral activity by inducing the proximity of the viral protein target with another protein. One example of this is small-molecule “degraders,” which bind to their viral target of interest and to a host E3 ubiquitin ligase. By inducing proximity between these two proteins, the small molecule can cause ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of the viral protein by the proteasome. The pharmacology is driven by the removal of the viral protein from the cell—once the protein has been ubiquitinated, no further binding to the viral protein is required. They hypothesized that this type of mechanism could have advantages in developing broad-spectrum activity, raising barriers to drug resistance, and providing an easier way to achieve antiviral activity against non-enzymatic viral proteins. They will describe their group’s proof-of-concept work developing antiviral degraders and comparing the ability of these compounds to address viral genetic diversity when compared to functional inhibitors. GSS is an inherited, sporadic disease linked to several point mutations in the human prion protein (PrP). Uniquely, GSS does not produce PK-resistant PrP, thus making it difficult to investigate with typical methods. The objective of this study was to determine if there was a biochemical procedure that could detect GSS prions similar to the use of PK for conventional prions. When they assessed the progression of disease in Tg(GSS) mice, they found distinctive plaque and lesion profiles in the CNS that temporally correlate to the presence of Thermolysin-resistant PrP. Moreover, the occurrence of neuropathology in Tg(GSS) mice and the accumulation of Thermolysin-resistant PrP coincided with the decline of sensorimotor function. These results continue to broaden our understanding of GSS as an unconventional prion disease with undiscovered qualities. Useful models for studying spontaneous disease have historically been limited, raising challenges for the development of therapeutics for GSS and other prion diseases linked to PrP point mutations. The use of their model allows for the investigation of GSS in cell-free systems as well as the ability to assess future therapeutics as they apply to human disease. Zoonotic spillover, where pathogens jump from animals to humans, poses a major threat to global health, with emerging coronaviruses responsible for multiple high-impact, cross-species outbreaks over the past two decades. Intermediate host animals have played a pivotal role in these events, acting not only as transmission vessels but also as environments where viruses can acquire adaptive mutations that enhance their zoonotic potential. Therefore, understanding the zoonotic role of intermediate hosts is crucial, since these animals serve as evolutionary bridges between wildlife reservoirs and humans. Farmed minks are of particular concern due to their documented capacity to harbor wildlife coronaviruses at the animal–human interface. Yet, their role, particularly their evolutionary capacity to drive viral adaptation, remains poorly understood. During the pandemic, they served as hosts where SARS-CoV-2 rapidly evolved, raising critical questions about their role in future coronavirus emergence, especially in regions where mink farming intersects with wildlife-rich ecosystems, potentially creating spillover hotspots. This project aims to elucidate the evolutionary mechanisms by which coronaviruses adapt in minks, driving spillover potential. Specifically, their research team aims to define the molecular signatures of entry-related (spike protein) mutations that arise during coronavirus adaptation in minks and determine how these changes contribute to the risk of viral spillover into humans. By integrating high-throughput receptor binding assays, deep mutational scanning, and pseudovirus entry assays, this study will provide a comprehensive understanding of how farmed minks may serve as key evolutionary intermediates driving the emergence of zoonotic coronaviruses.
